docs.text: Migrating

docs.title: Coming from reservoirpy or ReservoirComputing.jl
docs.text:
If you have built echo-state networks in reservoirpy (Python/NumPy) or ReservoirComputing.jl (Julia/SciML), the building blocks of ResDAG will feel familiar — a reservoir, a ridge readout, a warmup, a forecast. What differs is the mental model:

  • Models are PyTorch modules, not a bespoke graph runtime. A ResDAG model is an ordinary nn.Module. It moves with .to("cuda"), serializes with state_dict(), and embeds inside a larger network. There is no separate "node" abstraction or compile step.
  • Composition is the API, not a feature. Where reservoirpy connects nodes with >> and RC.jl wires fixed ESN slots, ResDAG builds an arbitrary DAG with the pytorch_symbolic functional API. State augmentation, parallel reservoirs, and multiple readout heads are a few lines of composition.
  • The common workflow accepts 2-D or batch-first 3-D tensors. Use (time, features) for one trajectory or (batch, time, features) for a batch. Raw graph APIs use the 3-D layout.
  • Start with model.fit(data). rd.ESN handles shifted targets, washout and training-only scaling. A custom rd.Model uses the same commands. Raw ESNTrainer and graph factories remain available for explicit data windows.

The rest of this page maps concepts and API surface side by side, then walks the same Lorenz forecast through all three libraries.

docs.title: Phase-five compact weights and PyTorch hooks
docs.text:
For sparse=True, recurrent weights now live only in compressed component buffers. cell.weight_hh is a CSR Tensor view rather than a dense Parameter; use .to_dense() for explicit inspection and .values() for existing edge updates. State dictionaries store compressed arrays instead of a dense square matrix. Dense models retain their existing representation. See memory and sparse models for initialization, device, numerical and trainability details.

Forecasting now honors native PyTorch hooks, including output-changing hooks on layers and the outer model. Models with hooks use a compatible execution path; hook-free models retain the lean path. compile=True with relevant hooks warns and uses eager execution. Existing forecasts that relied on hooks being ignored can change. Put recurrent memory in declared DAG nodes so explicit state and checkpointing can track it; arbitrary Python state hidden in hooks is not a model-state interface. See execution capabilities.

readout="lsmr" is a new explicit low-memory CPU solver. Existing solver defaults remain unchanged; its guide explains convergence and accelerator transfers.

docs.title: CPU initialization follow-up
docs.text: Sparse cycles and other matrices with at most one stored entry per row now use their analytic weighted-cycle spectrum. Large cycles can therefore normalize without an iterative eigensolver converging. Newly scaled weights may differ in their last digits from earlier successful Arnoldi estimates; saved weights remain unchanged. General CSR matrices still raise on an unsuccessful sparse estimate without allocating a dense fallback.

docs.title: Independent initialization streams
docs.text:
New ESN, continuous, Euler, edge-of-stability, residual ESN, gated reservoir and LIF models now use separate random streams for feedback, external inputs, recurrent weights and bias, including the gated cell's candidate and gate roles. Previously, mixing a named or custom initializer with a default could restart the same random sequence: a bias could repeat a feedback prefix, or recurrent weights could reuse feedback draws. Changing one role no longer shifts the other roles, even when an optional input is added or removed.

New seeded models can have different weights and forecast results. This includes graph-based recurrent initializers, whose fallback seed now belongs to the recurrent role. Repeat comparisons and tuning for newly constructed models; do not treat older accuracy measurements as evidence for these new initializations. Loading an existing checkpoint keeps its materialized weights and reservoir state; it does not replace them with new seeded draws.

An integer seed fixes every local role without consuming the global RNG. Passing a torch.Generator now uses its initial_seed() without advancing it, matching the named-initializer convention. With seed=None, the cell draws one master integer from Torch's CPU global RNG and derives its local roles from that value; torch.manual_seed still reproduces construction. Explicit initializer seeds, including an explicitly bound seed=None, and RNGs owned by custom initializer objects or callbacks keep their own policies. The standalone create_torch_generator utility still returns and advances an explicitly supplied generator when callers use it for draws. Advancing a generator does not change its initial_seed(). For distinct models within one experiment, pass different integer seeds or use SeedStreams.

docs.title: Phase-four training and persistence changes
docs.text:
The common rd.ESN and rd.Model now support model.save("run.pt") and rd.load("run.pt"), including the complete graph. Use .svg, .png, .pdf or .dot for diagrams. Portable custom components need registration; optional notebook-code bundles require explicit trusted=True at save and load. See save and load.

Batch fitting evaluates one continuous warmup-plus-training prefix. Readout regression still excludes warmup, and downstream reservoirs use fitted upstream outputs throughout the prefix. Temporal layers now see one sequence instead of a separate warmup call and training call. Ordinary hooks consequently observe one combined graph call. Stochastic layers, including reservoir noise and dropout, follow the new traversal order, so old noisy-training results can change even for the same seed; new seeded runs remain repeatable. Custom outer ESNModel.forward bodies are rejected rather than bypassed; put custom behavior in graph operations or module hooks.

A readout object may fan out from one invocation but cannot occupy several fitted graph positions. Use distinct readout instances there. Internal readouts can receive readout_targets={"name": values} without becoming public outputs. The raw trainer mutates in place; the common workflow commits a fit only after it succeeds. fit_stream retains its independent incremental-readout contract.

Raw plot_model(save_path=...) now infers the suffix and returns the saved path; without a path it returns a notebook-displayable source. It no longer opens a system viewer or silently writes SVG when a PNG filename was requested.

docs.title: Forecast timing after v0.11
docs.text:
The default low-level forecast now starts at the immediate unseen sample after all observations. It agrees with the common workflow and with next-sample training. Previously, core and coupled forecasts skipped that first prediction.

pred = model.forecast(observed, horizon=H)
truth = full_series[:, observed.shape[1]:observed.shape[1]+H]

prepare_esn_data now includes the final supervised target in forecast warmup. Validation still starts after that target, and training/target/validation windows are unchanged. Prepared predictions continue to align directly with val; remove any manual shift added around older custom observed histories.

Other intentional interface changes:

  • Future drivers begin after observed history and need H-1 samples, since the final observed driver already produced prediction zero. For H=1, omit them.
  • initial_feedback is a distinct additional input after full warmup. It needs H drivers. Do not repeat the final warmup observation as this seed.
  • return_warmup=True has length W-1+H, since the boundary prediction occurs once. Explicit seeds and legacy alignment retain length W+H.
  • ParallelESN already used immediate unseen timing. Its default future trajectory keeps that convention; its combined prefix now contains historical predictions instead of raw observations, with the same W-1+H length as other models.

To reproduce an older prepared-data core or ensemble experiment:

warmup, train, target, f_warmup, val = rd.prepare_esn_data(
    data, warmup_steps=W, train_steps=L, val_steps=H, alignment="legacy",
)
rd.ESNTrainer(model).fit((warmup,), (train,), {"output": target})
pred = model.forecast(f_warmup, horizon=H, alignment="legacy")

Both legacy arguments matter: preparation restores the earlier history window, and forecasting restores its skipped-boundary rollout. Golden fixtures for the new default use version 2, with unchanged numerical tolerances and quality rules; frozen version 1 fixtures additionally check legacy reproduction. The migration is backed by exact integer and driver recurrence tests before fixture regeneration. Timing explains the indices and saved-state continuation.

docs.title: Coming from reservoirpy
docs.text: reservoirpy composes Nodes — Reservoir, Ridge, Input — with the >> pipe operator, or wraps the common case in the ESN class. ResDAG composes layers with the functional API and wraps them in named rd.Model inputs and outputs. Use rd.ESN for a preset with the same fitting/forecasting interface.

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text:
The following examples show the two APIs. The reservoirpy example evaluates teacher-forced predictions; the ResDAG example rolls forward autonomously. They illustrate usage, not an accuracy comparison. reservoirpy:

from reservoirpy.nodes import Reservoir, Ridge
from reservoirpy.datasets import lorenz, to_forecasting

X = lorenz(n_timesteps=5000)
x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = to_forecasting(X, forecast=1, test_size=0.2)

reservoir = Reservoir(units=300, sr=0.9, lr=0.3, seed=42)
readout = Ridge(ridge=1e-6)
esn = reservoir >> readout

esn.fit(x_train, y_train, warmup=100)
predictions = esn.run(x_test)

ResDAG — fitting prepares the targets and scaling automatically:

import torch
import resdag as rd

data = rd.lorenz(5000, seed=42).double()  # (1, 5000, 3)
model = rd.ESN(
    reservoir_size=300, input_size=3, washout=100,
    spectral_radius=0.9, leak_rate=0.3, alpha=1e-6,
    seed=42, dtype=torch.float64,
)
model.fit(data[:, :4000])
forecast = model.forecast(horizon=200)    # estimates data[:, 4000:4200]

The closest one-call analogue to reservoirpy's ESN is rd.ESN. Build custom branches and heads with the same common model workflow. For explicit low-level training, the graph factories return raw ESNModel instances that work with ESNTrainer.

docs.title: Coming from ReservoirComputing.jl
docs.text: ReservoirComputing.jl (current LuxCore-based API) builds an ESN from initializer functions, runs setup to obtain parameters and state, trains with train!, and forecasts with predict in a Generative rollout. ResDAG folds the parameter/state handling into the stateful nn.Module and the trainer.

docs.title: Concept mapping
docs.text: ReservoirComputing.jl ResDAG Notes ESN(in, res, out; …) ESNLayer(res, feedback_size=in) + CGReadoutLayer(res, out) RC.jl bundles reservoir + readout in one type; ResDAG keeps them as composable layers. init_reservoir = rand_sparse(; radius, sparsity) spectral_radius=…, topology=("erdos_renyi", {"p": …}) Radius → spectral radius; sparsity → topology density. init_input = weighted_init(; scaling) / scaled_rand input_initializer / feedback_initializer A named initializer. state_modifiers = NLAT2 a transform layer or premade model (e.g. ott_esn) Nonlinear state augmentation is a composed layer. ps, st = setup(rng, esn) (implicit) — the layer owns its parameters and state No separate params/state objects; it is a stateful module. train!(esn, X, Y, ps, st, StandardRidge(λ)) ESNTrainer(model).fit(warmup_inputs=…, train_inputs=…, targets=…) λ of StandardRidge ↦ alpha on the readout. predict(esn, len, ps, st; initialdata=…) model.forecast(warmup, horizon=len) initialdata ↦ the warmup tensor that re-syncs the reservoir. Generative prediction mode model.forecast(...) (closed loop) The autoregressive rollout. Predictive prediction mode model(inputs) (teacher-forced one-step) Run the model directly on the inputs.

docs.text: ReservoirComputing.jl ResDAG res_size (e.g. 300) reservoir_size=300 rand_sparse(; radius=1.2) spectral_radius=1.2 rand_sparse(; sparsity=6/300) topology=("erdos_renyi", {"p": 6/300}) weighted_init(; scaling=0.1) input_initializer=("random", {"input_scaling": 0.1}) StandardRidge(1e-6) CGReadoutLayer(..., alpha=1e-6) predict(esn, predict_len, …) model.forecast(warmup, horizon=predict_len)

docs.title: Side by side
docs.text:
The same Lorenz forecast. ReservoirComputing.jl (current API):

using ReservoirComputing, Random

esn = ESN(3, 300, 3;                       # in_size, res_size, out_size
    init_reservoir = rand_sparse(; radius = 1.2, sparsity = 6 / 300),
    init_input = weighted_init(; scaling = 0.1),
    state_modifiers = NLAT2,
)
ps, st = setup(MersenneTwister(17), esn)
ps, st = train!(esn, input_data, target_data, ps, st, StandardRidge(1e-6))
output, st = predict(esn, predict_len, ps, st; initialdata = test_data[:, 1])

ResDAG — the reservoir and readout are separate composable layers, and the parameter/state bookkeeping (ps, st, setup) is folded into the stateful module:

import torch
import resdag as rd
from resdag import ESNLayer, ESNModel, reservoir_input, lorenz
from resdag.layers import CGReadoutLayer

data = lorenz(5000, seed=17)               # (1, 5000, 3)
warmup, train, target, f_warmup, val = rd.utils.prepare_esn_data(
    data, warmup_steps=100, train_steps=3000, val_steps=1000, normalize=True
)

inp = reservoir_input(3)
states = ESNLayer(
    300, feedback_size=3,
    spectral_radius=1.2,                                   # rand_sparse radius
    topology=("erdos_renyi", {"p": 6 / 300}),             # rand_sparse sparsity
    feedback_initializer=("random", {"input_scaling": 0.1}),  # weighted_init scaling
)(inp)
out = CGReadoutLayer(300, 3, name="output", alpha=1e-6)(states)   # StandardRidge(1e-6)
model = ESNModel(inp, out)

rd.ESNTrainer(model).fit(
    warmup_inputs=(warmup,),
    train_inputs=(train,),
    targets={"output": target},
)
output = model.forecast(f_warmup, horizon=200)            # predict(...; Generative)

The NLAT2 nonlinear state-augmentation modifier has a direct analogue in ResDAG: ott_esn squares the even-indexed reservoir features and concatenates them back — the same trick used to break the odd symmetry that hampers Lorenz forecasting — as a composed architecture rather than a modifier flag.

docs.title: Build your own components
docs.text: Start with existing layers and replace only the part you need. A custom initializer builds weights; a cell defines one recurrent update; a Torch module transforms signals; a readout solver fits the final prediction map. They all work inside the same functional rd.Model.

docs.title: Give branches independent, repeatable seeds
docs.text:
import torch
from torch import nn
import resdag as rd

seeds = rd.SeedStreams(42)
fast_seed = seeds["fast"]
slow_seed = seeds["slow"]
assert fast_seed != slow_seed
assert rd.SeedStreams(42)["fast"] == fast_seed

Explicit names keep the same seeds when you reorder branches or add another one. Reusing a name gives the same seed; it does not share parameters or memory between layers. The fixed blake2b-v1 algorithm uses Python's standard hashlib, consumes no global random state and accepts names such as "encoder/fast". Keep those names stable in experiments.

This controls initialization, not numerical nondeterminism in accelerator kernels or the current position of a noise generator. Pass the derived seeds to your components; constructing Model never reinitializes supplied layers.

docs.title: Register a weight initializer
docs.text:
@rd.init.register_recurrent_initializer("tutorial_cycle", prescaled=True)
def tutorial_cycle(size, gain=0.8, *, device=None, dtype=None):
    return gain * torch.eye(size, device=device, dtype=dtype).roll(1, dims=0)

reservoir = rd.ESNLayer(
    8, feedback_size=2, seed=fast_seed, dtype=torch.float64,
    recurrent_initializer=("tutorial_cycle", {"gain": 0.7}),
)

prescaled=True means the builder owns its recurrent scale. Otherwise the layer applies its requested spectral radius. Random builders should accept seed and use a local Torch or NumPy generator. Registration is per process: import your registration module on each worker. Direct callables work too. See custom initialization for input, feedback, bias and reset-state builders.

docs.title: Define one recurrent update
docs.text:
The cell below keeps an exponentially weighted memory. It uses the existing state and sequence machinery rather than writing another time loop:

class MovingAverageCell(rd.ReservoirCell):
    def __init__(self, width, rate=0.3):
        super().__init__()
        self.width = width
        self.register_buffer("rate", torch.tensor(rate, dtype=torch.float64))

    @property
    def state_size(self):
        return self.width

    @property
    def output_size(self):
        return self.width

    def init_state(self, batch_size, device, dtype):
        return torch.zeros(batch_size, self.width, device=device, dtype=dtype)

    def forward(self, inputs, state):
        updated = (1 - self.rate) * state + self.rate * inputs[0]
        return updated, updated

memory = rd.BaseReservoirLayer(MovingAverageCell(2))

The layer handles carried state, explicit state, batch iteration and device moves. Register learnable quantities as nn.Parameter and fixed tensors as buffers. Keep state in the returned state tensor. For a faster cell, the optional public project_inputs and step methods can separate the batched input projection from recurrence.

docs.title: Add a framewise transform
docs.text:
class SignedSquare(nn.Module):
    supports_framewise = True

    def forward(self, data):
        return data.sign() * data.square()

The declaration means that splitting time into individual frames gives the same result. It is valid here because each value is transformed independently. A temporal operation such as a running sum needs a recurrent cell or history execution.

docs.title: Supply a readout solver
docs.text:
Implement the public solve(states, targets) method. The base class owns shape checks, fitted flags and copying coefficients into its PyTorch layer:

class LeastSquaresReadout(rd.ReadoutLayer):
    def solve(self, states, targets):
        coefficients = torch.linalg.lstsq(states, targets).solution
        return coefficients, None

Inputs are flattened (samples, features) matrices. Return coefficients of shape (input_features, output_features) and an optional output intercept. This example uses bias=False. A solver supporting bias should estimate and return that intercept. Use fit as the training entrypoint; solve is its extension hook and may update solver diagnostics or online fitting statistics. For example, the incremental and RLS solvers update their accumulated or recursive state. Use the supplied dtype/device and standard Torch linear algebra, keeping transfers explicit.

docs.title: Connect them and use the common workflow
docs.text:
x = rd.reservoir_input(2, dtype=torch.float64)
fast = reservoir(x)
slow = memory(x)
features = rd.Concatenate()(SignedSquare()(fast), slow)
y = LeastSquaresReadout(10, 2, bias=False).double()(features)
custom = rd.Model(inputs={"state": x}, outputs={"prediction": y}, washout=5)

t = torch.linspace(0, 8, 90, dtype=torch.float64)
training = torch.stack((t.sin(), t.cos()), dim=-1)
custom.fit(training)
prediction = custom.forecast(horizon=5)
assert prediction.shape == (5, 2)
assert torch.isfinite(prediction).all()

Expose each reservoir as a separate functional node so explicit-state and forecast execution can thread its state. Add branches with new layer instances; share weight tensors explicitly when desired. See the common model guide for PyTorch pipelines and the roadmap for tuning and complete model artifacts.

docs.title: Custom preprocessing
docs.text: Use input_transforms and output_transforms to override preprocessing by port name. Each transform preserves the signals and their feature count; the workflow fits it on training rows, runs the graph in transformed units, and returns predictions in the original units. Put temporal operations or feature construction inside the functional graph instead.

docs.title: Reuse Standardize or disable one port
docs.text:
rd.Standardize(num_features=D) works directly. Use nn.Identity() to disable preprocessing for one port while retaining the global fallback for other ports.

import io
import torch
from torch import nn
import resdag as rd

training = torch.arange(1, 21, dtype=torch.float64)[:, None]
x = rd.reservoir_input(1, dtype=torch.float64)
head = rd.RidgeReadoutLayer(1, 1, alpha=0).double()
incoming = rd.Standardize(num_features=1)
model = rd.Model(
    inputs={"state": x},
    outputs={"prediction": head(x)},
    washout=2,
    preprocessing="standard",
    input_transforms={"state": incoming},
    output_transforms={"prediction": nn.Identity()},
).fit(training)
assert model.input_scalers[0] is incoming
torch.testing.assert_close(
    model.forecast(horizon=3), torch.arange(21, 24).double()[:, None]
)

Keys match the names declared by Model(inputs=..., outputs=...). The ESN preset uses "input" and "output". Explicit overrides also run when preprocessing="off"; unspecified ports use the global preprocessing policy.

docs.title: Define a reversible Torch module
docs.text:
A custom transform is an ordinary nn.Module with:

  • fit(training), accepting (batch, time, features) and returning self;
  • forward(data) and inverse(data), preserving the exact shape, dtype and device;
  • supports_framewise = True, declaring that splitting the time axis into individual frames gives the same result;
  • all learned state in persistent, pre-registered buffers or parameters with fixed names and shapes.

Allocate state for the known feature width in the constructor. Fit by copying values into it, rather than adding or resizing registered tensors:

class CenterScale(nn.Module):
    supports_framewise = True

    def __init__(self, num_features):
        super().__init__()
        self.register_buffer("center", torch.zeros(num_features))
        self.register_buffer("scale", torch.ones(num_features))

    @torch.no_grad()
    def fit(self, training):
        self.center.copy_(training.mean(dim=(0, 1)))
        self.scale.copy_(training.std(dim=(0, 1), unbiased=False).clamp_min(0.01))
        return self

    def forward(self, data):
        return (data - self.center) / self.scale

    def inverse(self, data):
        return data * self.scale + self.center


class Asinh(nn.Module):
    supports_framewise = True

    def fit(self, training):
        return self

    def forward(self, data):
        return data.asinh()

    def inverse(self, data):
        return data.sinh()

A fixed unit converter can use the same no-op fit recipe as Asinh. nn.Identity() is the standard exception that needs neither fit nor inverse methods. The workflow owns fittedness; a custom is_fitted property is unnecessary.

Fit and forecast apply transforms in evaluation mode, restoring every module's previous mode afterward. Their evaluation behavior must be pure, deterministic, framewise and reversible, without modifying inputs or learned state. Keep temporal state in a visible reservoir node using BaseReservoirLayer; see custom components and forecast execution.

docs.title: Train in transformed units and forecast in physical units
docs.text:
The output override fits the actual target rows. This example learns a nonlinear physical map by making its transformed targets linear:

def make_model():
    signal = rd.reservoir_input(1, dtype=torch.float64)
    readout = rd.RidgeReadoutLayer(1, 1, alpha=0).double()
    return rd.Model(
        inputs={"state": signal},
        outputs={"prediction": readout(signal)},
        washout=0,
        preprocessing="off",
        input_transforms={"state": CenterScale(1)},
        output_transforms={"prediction": Asinh()},
    )

values = torch.linspace(-2, 2, 40, dtype=torch.float64)[:, None]
custom = make_model().fit(values, targets=(0.2 * values + 0.05).sinh())
current = values[-1:]
expected = []
for _ in range(3):
    current = (0.2 * current + 0.05).sinh()
    expected.append(current)
torch.testing.assert_close(
    custom.forecast(horizon=3), torch.cat(expected), rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12
)

source = values[:4].clone().requires_grad_()
custom(source).sum().backward()
torch.testing.assert_close(
    source.grad, 0.2 * (0.2 * source.detach() + 0.05).cosh()
)

Only supervised rows after washout fit each transform. Custom output transforms use the aligned targets, including next-step targets when targets are omitted. An unspecified output keeps the built-in fallback: for implicit next-step training it fits the original input's supervised rows. It does not inherit a custom input transform. Feedback always converts through physical units: output inverse, then receiving input forward.

docs.title: State, refitting and checkpoints
docs.text:
Fitting stages independent copies, validates reversible behavior on a bounded sample and checks that loading registered tensor state alone reproduces it. It also checks finite transformed training data. A failed staged fit leaves the fitted workflow unchanged. Successful fits preserve the supplied module and parameter identities, so an optimizer created before fitting keeps its references. Distinct ports need independent modules and tensor storage; sharing state with another port or the raw graph is rejected. Expanded or overlapping state tensors must be cloned into writable independent storage.

Standard .to(...) moves the registered state. Ordinary transforms can be fitted inside torch.inference_mode() and used with autograd afterward; construct custom parameters outside inference mode. At inference, shape, dtype and device checks remain active, while NaN and infinity propagate according to the transform's Torch operations.

Save and load a matching workflow's state with standard Torch tools:

buffer = io.BytesIO()
torch.save(custom.state_dict(), buffer)
buffer.seek(0)
state = torch.load(buffer, weights_only=True, map_location="cpu")
restored = make_model()
restored.load_state_dict(state)
torch.testing.assert_close(
    restored.forecast(horizon=3), custom.forecast(horizon=3), rtol=0, atol=0
)

Reconstruct the same transform classes, feature widths and Python configuration before loading. The checkpoint validates registered tensor schema and sampled behavior; arbitrary Python settings remain your responsibility. Store fitted quantities in registered tensors, including flags that affect fitted behavior. Ordinary Torch load_state_dict(assign=True) can replace parameters, so construct an optimizer after such a load.

docs.title: Custom layers in forecasting
docs.text:
Ordinary graph execution accepts standard torch.nn.Module layers, including whole-sequence transformations. Forecasting must also decide how those layers receive future inputs.

The default execution="fast" processes the observed history once, then consumes one frame per future tick. Built-in feature transforms, pointwise PyTorch layers, readouts, and visible BaseReservoirLayer nodes support this execution. Explicit reservoir states carry their temporal memory between ticks.

PyTorch execution hooks also apply during forecasting and explicit-state execution. ResDAG detects local, nested and global registrations automatically and uses ordinary module calls when needed. A hook on an rd.Model or rd.ESN sees its usual original-unit inputs and outputs; named feedback and delays use those modified predictions. Hook-free models retain the lean executor. On backends that support compiled forecasts, requesting compile=True with execution hooks emits a warning and uses eager execution. Full-history execution and parallel/coupled workflow backends reject compile=True independently of hooks. Hooks may change output dtype or device. In fast mode, a prehook can convert the next feedback frame back to the graph's required placement, just as in an ordinary model call. History replay uses torch.cat to extend each input prefix: normal dtype promotion applies, but frames on different devices cannot be concatenated. Use compatible hook placement for history replay; ResDAG does not move the saved prefix between devices automatically.

Hooks still follow the selected temporal contract: fast execution calls the model on the full observed history and then one frame at a time; history execution replays the growing prefix. A hook that itself needs the full prefix should use execution="history". Hooks on methods that ordinary module execution never calls, such as a cell's low-level step, are not dispatched as module-forward hooks. Explicit-state execution restores carried reservoir buffers even when a hook raises; other hook side effects follow ordinary PyTorch behavior. Recurrent modules must remain in the declared graph's named state contract. Explicit-state and forecast calls reject reservoirs attached outside model.graph; ordinary model(x) remains available. Python counters or other hidden mutable state inside a hook follow the hook author's own lifecycle. Portable checkpoints omit active execution hooks. Put behavior that must survive loading in a registered module, or use an explicitly trusted bundle; see saving and loading.

docs.title: Declare a framewise custom module
docs.text:
Set supports_framewise = True when splitting along the time axis preserves the module's behavior. For inputs shaped (batch, time, features), the module must preserve the batch and time axes and apply the same operation independently at each time. Feature widths may change inside the graph. The declaration also applies to a custom coupled aggregator's time axis, immediately before its final feature axis.

import torch
from torch import nn
import resdag as rd

class SignedSquare(nn.Module):
    supports_framewise = True

    def forward(self, values):
        return values.sign() * values.square()

source = rd.reservoir_input(1, dtype=torch.float64)
graph = rd.ESNModel(source, SignedSquare()(source))
observed = torch.tensor([[[0.5], [1.0], [2.0]]], dtype=torch.float64)
prediction = graph.forecast(observed, horizon=2)
torch.testing.assert_close(prediction, torch.tensor([[[4.0], [16.0]]]).double())

An unchanged inherited implementation retains its declaration. A subclass that overrides forward must declare the capability again. An existing module instance can instead set its own supports_framewise = True after its behavior has been checked. A declaration is a semantic promise; ResDAG does not infer a custom function's temporal behavior by trying sample inputs.

Known scalar symbolic arithmetic such as source + 1, source ** 2, and feature-only slices remains fast. Generic lambdas, arbitrary tensor methods, and unknown module classes require a declaration or explicit history execution. ResDAG validates the graph before warmup, hooks, or recurrent-state changes.

docs.title: Replay the complete observed prefix
docs.text:
A cumulative sum depends on every earlier input. Giving it isolated future frames would discard that information. Wrap the graph with rd.Model and select execution="history" to rerun its complete input prefix at each future tick.

import torch
from torch import nn
import resdag as rd

class PrefixSum(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, values):
        return values.cumsum(dim=1)

source = rd.reservoir_input(1, dtype=torch.float64)
features = PrefixSum()(source)
head = rd.RidgeReadoutLayer(1, 1, alpha=1e-6).double()
model = rd.Model(
    inputs={"observed": source},
    outputs={"prediction": head(features)},
    preprocessing="off",
    washout=0,
)
observed = torch.arange(1, 21, dtype=torch.float64)[:, None]
model.fit(observed)
prediction = model.forecast(history=observed, horizon=3, execution="history")
assert prediction.shape == (3, 1)
assert torch.isfinite(prediction).all()

Each replay starts visible reservoirs from their configured reset state and recomputes the full supplied history plus every subsequently consumed forecast frame. It keeps the final prediction unconsumed, matching normal forecast timing. History execution costs more computation and memory as the prefix grows, and requires compile=False.

Graphs that need history execution retain their complete observed fitting history, so omitted history replays that prefix. Fast graphs retain a compact observed tail. Supplying history explicitly starts from that observed prefix; include every earlier sample the temporal operation needs. Within a forecast call, replay never shortens the supplied prefix.

Both execution choices expect custom modules to behave as pure input functions in evaluation mode. Temporal operations such as cumulative sums can compute their memory from the supplied prefix. Arbitrary mutable Python state or per-call temporal buffers cannot be reset automatically. Implement streaming memory through a ReservoirCell wrapped in BaseReservoirLayer, exposing that reservoir as its own functional graph node. Reservoirs hidden inside arbitrary containers remain outside the explicit-state contract.

The low-level ESNModel.forecast provides fast execution. Use the common rd.Model(graph=...) workflow for explicit history replay. Direct graph forward and whole-sequence forward_stateless remain available for custom operations without a framewise declaration.

docs.title: Raw HPO runner
docs.text: Advanced

docs.title: Raw HPO runner
docs.text: Use this lower-level runner when you want to prepare every training and forecast tensor yourself and build raw ESNModel graphs. The usual model.tune(...) workflow handles chronological validation, preprocessing, named ports and installing a fitted winner. run_hpo returns an Optuna study and leaves winner reconstruction to you. Both workflows use the same managed joblib executor and parent-owned Optuna bookkeeping. This raw entry point keeps its explicit data and loss contracts.

docs.title: Parameters to explore
docs.text:
Useful search dimensions include:

Parameter Controls Range First move reservoir_size model capacity 100–2000 double it until gains stall spectral_radius memory horizon, stability 0.8–1.2 sweep ±0.1 around 0.9 leak_rate state update timescale 0.05–1.0 lower it for slow signals bias_scaling diversity of unit operating points 0.0–2.0 leave at 1.0; 0.0 recovers a zero-bias reservoir topology recurrent connectivity structure registry names default (dense random) first, graphs after feedback_initializer how the signal enters registry names default first; scale before structure alpha readout ridge regularization 1e-8–1e-2 step by ×100 on a log scale warmup length state synchronization 100–500 steps raise it until forecasts stop changing

Spectral radius scales the recurrent matrix so its largest eigenvalue magnitude hits the target, which sets how long an input echoes through the state. Small values forget fast and stay stable; values near one remember longer and produce richer transients at the edge of instability — for driven, leaky reservoirs the best value often sits slightly above 1.0. Factories default to 0.9; a bare ESNLayer leaves the matrix unscaled unless you pass a value.

Leak rate blends the previous state into the new one: \(x_t = (1-a)\,x_{t-1} + a\,\tilde{x}_t\). At 1.0 the state is fully replaced each step (the standard ESN); smaller values integrate slowly, matching the reservoir's timescale to the signal's. Slow, smooth signals call for small leak rates; leak_rate=0.1 with a spectral radius near 1.0 is a standard configuration for long-period oscillations.

Alpha sets the bias–variance tradeoff of a ridge readout such as CGReadoutLayer. Too small, and the readout amplifies state noise and forecasts diverge within a few steps; too large, and predictions over-smooth toward the mean. The optimum shifts with reservoir size and training length, which is why it belongs in every search space.

docs.title: Searching with run_hpo
docs.text:
Three callables define a study: a model factory, a search space, and a data loader. Each trial builds a fresh model, fits the readout, forecasts over the validation window, and scores it.

import torch
import resdag as rd
from resdag.hpo import run_hpo

t = torch.arange(2300, dtype=torch.float32) / 20
data = torch.sin(t[:, None] * torch.tensor([0.7, 1.0, 1.3]))[None]
# data has shape (1, 2300, 3): batch, time, features
warmup, train, target, f_warmup, val = rd.utils.prepare_esn_data(
    data, warmup_steps=200, train_steps=1600, val_steps=300
)

def model_creator(reservoir_size, spectral_radius, leak_rate, alpha, seed=None):
    """One fresh model per trial. Must accept every key of search_space."""
    return rd.classic_esn(
        reservoir_size=reservoir_size, feedback_size=3, output_size=3,
        spectral_radius=spectral_radius, leak_rate=leak_rate,
        readout_alpha=alpha, seed=seed,
    )

def search_space(trial):
    return {
        "reservoir_size": trial.suggest_int("reservoir_size", 100, 500, step=100),
        "spectral_radius": trial.suggest_float("spectral_radius", 0.5, 1.2),
        "leak_rate": trial.suggest_float("leak_rate", 0.2, 1.0),
        "alpha": trial.suggest_float("alpha", 1e-8, 1e-2, log=True),
    }

def data_loader(trial):
    """Must include these five keys, each (batch, time, features)."""
    return {"warmup": warmup, "train": train, "target": target,
            "f_warmup": f_warmup, "val": val}

study = run_hpo(
    model_creator=model_creator,
    search_space=search_space,
    data_loader=data_loader,
    n_trials=100,
    loss="efh",
    seed=42,
    storage="study.log",                    # journal file: resumable
)
print(study.best_params)

The data contract is validated per trial: the dict must contain "warmup", "train", "target", "f_warmup", "val", all 3-D tensors. The forecast horizon defaults to val.shape[1]. Input-driven models add drivers_keys=["driver"] and supply warmup_driver, train_driver, f_warmup_driver, and forecast_driver entries — the last one sliced with the pinned alignment.

Invalid trials and debugging

catch_exceptions=True continues after an invalid evaluation, but the default error_policy="fail" records it as an Optuna FAIL trial so it cannot win. Details remain in the trial's "error" attribute. A study with no valid completed evaluation raises clearly. Pass catch_exceptions=False to see the original exception immediately. The explicit error_policy="penalty" records numeric penalties; it still cannot return an invalid winner. Low-level TrialRunner and build_objective have a penalty default: pass error_policy="fail" when driving those helpers directly. If every attempt is pruned, the returned study has no best trial.

The actual forwarded model seed is recorded as trial.user_attrs["model_seed"] when the creator accepts a seed; "trial_seed" records the trial RNG seed. Use that model seed when reconstructing the winner. Forecast evaluation uses temporary evaluation mode, restoring each module's earlier training flag.

docs.title: Resume and reuse settings
docs.text:
n_trials is the number of new attempts in this call. Failed and pruned attempts count too. Running with the same storage and study name adds that many attempts; it does not mean a target total study length. For example, n_trials=10 followed by n_trials=5 creates 15 attempts.

Use prior results as starting settings for a new experiment:

from resdag.hpo import export_best_config

best = export_best_config(study)
next_study = run_hpo(
    model_creator, search_space, data_loader, n_trials=10,
    transfer_from=study, seed=42, verbosity=0,
)

transfer_from queues complete settings for re-evaluation by default. Single-objective sources are queued best-first, with trial number breaking ties. Multi-objective sources retain their source order. Suggestions used only by data_loader and fixed model values are preserved; nothing is silently dropped to make an old score fit a different model. Queued configurations consume new attempts when evaluated. Remaining configurations stay WAITING if the new budget is smaller than the queue.

warm_start=[best] queues specific settings. export_best_config includes fixed model settings alongside suggestions. The destination factory must accept its model settings; adapt a configuration explicitly if changing architectures. Trial attributes record full resolved settings and source study/trial provenance under "resdag_transfer".

Copying old scores requires the explicit transfer_mode="scores" and an identical bound task protocol, including data, validation, objective and settings. Raw resume and score import replay each historical configuration's data preparation with Optuna's FixedTrial and compare the actual prepared tensor contents. A changed file loaded by the same callback/path is rejected before its old scores can compete. Use a fresh study with settings reuse for changed tasks.

If a data callback needs live-study resources that FixedTrial cannot replay, supply task_context="my-dataset-v3" (or a portable metadata mapping). This is an explicit assertion of the external resources' identity; change it whenever those resources change. A successful replay still checks tensor contents. Callbacks may run again for historical validation on resume, so keep data preparation free of side effects. New attempts receive a real Optuna Trial.

docs.title: Losses
docs.text:
Key Behavior "efh" Expected forecast horizon — soft survival sum (default, chaotic systems) "forecast_horizon" Hard count of contiguous below-threshold steps "lyapunov" Error weighted by \(e^{-t/\tau}\) with lyapunov_t "standard" Mean geometric-mean error — stable or periodic signals "soft_horizon" Hill-gated survival horizon — smoother search landscape "attractor_dimension" Correlation-dimension mismatch for long-term attractor fidelity

All are minimized; the horizon losses are negated internally, so lower study values mean longer usable forecasts. loss_params passes kwargs (thresholds, metrics) to the chosen loss; monitor_losses=["standard"] logs extra metrics on every trial without optimizing on them.

With torch_scoring=True (the default), the five horizon/error losses score directly on the forecast device; each checkpoint transfers only its final scalar. The attractor-dimension loss uses NumPy. Custom losses can accept torch tensors for the same device-local path, or use the automatic NumPy fallback. Forecasts are generated in chunks. Checkpoint pruning stops future generation as soon as the parent pruner rejects a growing prefix. Reports use 1-based checkpoint indices, not physical sample counts. Raw losses retain their existing prefix-dependent normalization, so raw scoring can keep a complete prediction prefix in memory: O(horizon) storage. Custom/monitor losses receive the same full-horizon tensors when an evaluation completes.

docs.title: Multi-worker studies
docs.text:
study = run_hpo(..., n_trials=200, n_workers=8, storage="study.log", seed=42)

One worker runs in the caller; multiple workers use managed joblib/loky processes. Notebook factories and loss closures work through joblib's standard serialization. Search-space functions, data loaders, user trial callbacks, samplers, pruners and storage all remain in the parent. Numerical workers receive prepared data and return scores/diagnostics, with no study connection. In-memory studies therefore also work with multiple workers.

Submission uses finite windows, so failures and pruning cannot overshoot the new-attempt budget. On errors or interruption, outstanding work is canceled through joblib and this call's unfinished reservations are marked FAIL. Successfully completed pools follow joblib's normal reuse policy. Journal and SQLite storage are optional persistence choices; SQLite URLs use normal SQLAlchemy parsing, including query options.

inner_max_num_threads=1 limits native library threads inside worker processes. The parent thread settings, environment variables, logging levels and RNG streams are restored/preserved. seed initializes the parent sampler; each new trial uses seed + trial.number. Data preparation's RNG consumption is preserved before model initialization in the worker. An explicit model seed in the resolved settings takes precedence. Adaptive suggestions can differ when you change worker count because the sampler sees different completed windows; concurrency is not a reproducibility guarantee across schedules/devices.

docs.title: Optional memory planning
docs.text:
Arbitrary raw factories require a custom estimate when a budget is supplied:

from resdag.hpo import MemoryBudget, MemoryEstimate

def memory_estimator(params, context):
    # Complete peak estimate for this particular factory, not just weights.
    n = params["reservoir_size"]
    state_bytes = context.refit_samples * n * 8
    solver_bytes = 4 * n * n * 8
    return MemoryEstimate(
        host_bytes=context.dataset_host_bytes + state_bytes + solver_bytes
        + context.retained_forecast_bytes,
        details={"solver": "factory-specific estimate"},
    )

planned = run_hpo(
    model_creator, search_space, data_loader, n_trials=10, n_workers=2,
    memory_budget=MemoryBudget("2GiB", worker_overhead="256MiB"),
    memory_estimator=memory_estimator, seed=42, verbosity=0,
)

context contains immutable shape/dtype/device/storage metadata, never live model or data objects. The estimate is a complete host/device peak for your factory; known resident data, device copies and retained forecast storage set a minimum. Include custom layers, solver workspaces and other temporary allocations in your estimate. The example above illustrates a CPU estimate; adapt host/device accounting to your chosen factory and accelerator.

An oversized candidate becomes PRUNED before model construction; candidates that fit individually run with reduced numerical concurrency when necessary. trial.user_attrs["memory_estimate"] records requested/known-minimum accounting. Preparation itself still occurs in the parent before estimation, and a pending configuration may be retained while an admitted window runs. These are planning estimates, not process, RSS or accelerator allocation limits. The default without memory_budget imposes no memory admission policy.

docs.title: Reading a study
docs.text:
run_hpo returns a plain optuna study, so optuna's visualization module works on it directly: optuna.visualization for interactive plotly figures, optuna.visualization.matplotlib for static ones like the four below. These plots replay the recorded Lorenz validation search from the independent-trajectory robustness study: 24 configurations, each scored across three validation trajectories, three reservoir seeds and three forecast starts. The objective is the median of trajectory medians at the 0.3 normalized-error threshold, in Lyapunov times. Final test forecasts are absent from this study and these plots. Scores at the ten-Lyapunov-time evaluation limit are lower bounds, not measured later forecast failures.

from optuna.visualization import plot_optimization_history   # plotly, interactive
from optuna.visualization.matplotlib import plot_contour     # static

plot_optimization_history(study)

Recorded validation objectives and their running best. Failed trials retain their failed state and supply no completed score.

Optuna PED-ANOVA estimates of parameter importance within this small validation search. They describe this sampled region and objective; they are not causal effects or conclusions about final-test accuracy.

Slice plots: the objective against each parameter individually.

Optuna interpolation of sampled validation scores over spectral radius and leak rate. Other settings also vary, so this is not an isolated two-parameter experiment or evidence of an optimum between observations.

docs.title: Tuning resources
docs.text: Advanced · Tune

docs.title: Plan tuning resources
docs.text:
Ordinary tuning evaluates every candidate with the full configured seeds and forecast starting points. These optional controls help when a search has large models or many candidates. They do not change a model's architecture or precision.

Start with the tuning workflow if you have not tuned a model yet.

docs.title: Give tuning a memory budget
docs.text:
model.tune(
    development,
    preset="balanced",
    horizon=100,
    n_jobs=4,
    memory_budget="8GiB",
)

The tuner estimates each candidate before constructing it. It admits fewer candidates at once when their combined estimates would exceed the budget. A candidate that cannot fit by itself is skipped and recorded in the tuning report. A giant lazy ESN base can also be rejected before its initial reservoir is allocated; choose a smaller base or provide a suitable construction recipe.

The budget is a planning estimate, not an operating-system, RSS or GPU allocator limit. Other processes, cached allocations, Python objects, backend workspaces and custom layers can use additional memory. Leave headroom. The tuner does not resize a reservoir, lower precision or change your model to make it fit.

"8GB" means 8,000,000,000 bytes. "8GiB" means 8 × 1,073,741,824 bytes. Integer byte counts and values such as "1.5GiB" are also accepted.

docs.title: Separate accelerator memory
docs.text:
from resdag.hpo import MemoryBudget

budget = MemoryBudget(
    limit="16GiB",
    device_limit="8GiB",
    worker_overhead="512MiB",
)
model.tune(development, horizon=100, n_jobs=4, memory_budget=budget)

limit covers estimated host plus device memory and one worker-overhead reserve per active candidate. device_limit adds a separate device-only check. The default overhead reserve is 256 MiB per candidate. This is conservative logical accounting; host/device accounts can overlap on unified-memory systems.

Automatic estimates account for shared tensor storage, retained/staged model copies, complete refit data, feature traces, forecast outputs and 8-byte readout workspaces. Accelerator estimates also reserve host space for a stable CPU solve bridge. Seeds and starting points run sequentially within a candidate, so the estimate does not multiply its peak by their count.

Later forecast starting points can have more observed history than the original fit. Their warmup traces are included too. History-replay execution also reserves its growing input history and concatenation copies. A custom factory that changes which execution mode the architecture needs must include those requirements in its own estimate.

For the built-in parallel model, the planner includes the patch count. A batch of B fields split into P patches produces B * P reservoir sequences; the shared readout fits their pooled supervised rows. Its estimate includes patch windows, projected inputs, feature traces, local targets and recurrent state. Warmup takes trace memory but contributes no fitted rows. This also accounts for candidates that sample a shorter washout.

docs.title: Optionally shortlist candidates
docs.text:
from resdag.hpo import Screening

model.tune(
    development,
    preset="balanced",
    horizon=100,
    screening=Screening(),
    memory_budget="8GiB",
)

Balanced tuning normally checks all 24 candidates with three initialization seeds and three forecast starting points. With this optional screen, it first checks all 24 using one seed and one starting point. The best eight then receive the full evaluation. The winner must come from that full evaluation.

Screening saves work, but can discard a configuration that would perform well across other seeds or starting points. Leave it disabled when every candidate needs the full comparison.

Customize the screen explicitly:

screen = Screening(
    seed_count=1,
    origin_count=2,
    keep_fraction=0.5,
    cohort_size=12,
)

This screens cohorts of 12 and promotes the best six from each cohort. A partial cohort rounds promotion upward, retaining at least one candidate. Screening counts cannot exceed the full evaluation's seed/origin counts. cohort_size=None uses the requested new-trial budget as one cohort.

docs.title: Supply an estimate for a custom recipe
docs.text:
A custom factory can change the model's topology. With a memory budget, provide memory_estimator(params, context) so the tuner can check the candidate before calling its factory. Without a memory budget, no estimate is required.

The context contains immutable shapes, dtype/device, full refit sample counts, shared dataset/model storage counts and readout widths. It contains no live model or data tensors. Return a MemoryEstimate, or an integer for a complete host-only estimate. The result replaces the automatic estimate; it is not an extra surcharge. Worker overhead is added separately by MemoryBudget.

context.train_samples and context.refit_samples count observations as before. For supported parallel models, readout_train_samples and readout_refit_samples give each head's actual pooled supervised row counts; sequence_layout records the immutable fit, refit and forecast-history shapes. These optional facts default to empty tuples/mappings for other contexts. Custom parallel implementations with different patching or hooks need their own estimate rather than assuming the built-in layout.

For a custom recipe that still builds a classic dense ESN, reuse the standard estimator instead of writing another memory formula:

from dataclasses import replace

import torch
import resdag as rd
from resdag.hpo.resources import estimate_memory

time = torch.arange(600) * 0.05
development = torch.stack((time.sin(), time.cos()), dim=-1)[:500]

def build(params, seed):
    with torch.random.fork_rng():
        torch.manual_seed(seed)
        x = rd.reservoir_input(2)
        hidden = rd.ESNLayer(params["width"], feedback_size=2)(x)
        features = rd.Concatenate()(x, hidden)
        output = rd.AutoReadoutLayer(params["width"] + 2, 2, alpha=params["alpha"])(features)
        return rd.Model(inputs={"state": x}, outputs={"prediction": output}, washout=30)

def space(trial):
    return {
        "width": trial.suggest_int("width", 64, 512),
        "alpha": trial.suggest_float("alpha", 1e-8, 1e-3, log=True),
    }

def estimate(params, context):
    # This recipe retains the classic dense ESN structure.
    dense = replace(context, preset_options={"reservoir_size": params["width"]})
    return estimate_memory({"reservoir_size": params["width"]}, dense)

model = build({"width": 64, "alpha": 1e-6}, seed=7)
model.tune(
    development,
    search_space=space,
    factory=build,
    memory_estimator=estimate,
    memory_budget="8GiB",
    preset="quick",
    horizon=100,
)

For a different DAG, provide an estimate tailored to its layers. Include model copies, temporary activations, readout workspaces, transfers and the final fit on all development observations. A smaller screening run does not make that final fit smaller. You can also override the estimate for a fixed DAG with custom layers that allocate additional temporary storage.

The custom result cannot remove storage already known to exist. The tuner floors each account at its resident dataset/model bytes, retained prediction prefix and reserved replay history, without adding those bytes twice. Details record the requested totals, minimum totals and whether this floor was applied.

The advanced raw runner uses the same budget rules. Because its model factory is arbitrary, a budget always requires a custom estimator. Its context reserves the complete prediction prefix needed by arbitrary raw losses; that part grows with the forecast horizon. The common workflow's streaming built-in objective does not retain that output prefix; custom objectives receiving full predictions do. History replay can still retain growing input histories with the built-in objective.

docs.title: Composing models
docs.text: Build

docs.title: Composing models
docs.text: ResDAG treats reservoir architectures as directed acyclic graphs: reservoirs, augmentations, concatenations, and readouts, composed in whatever order the problem requires. Instead of monolithic model classes, the library provides individual layers and a functional API. You declare symbolic inputs, call layers on them, and wrap the resulting graph in ESNModel. Every page in this section builds on that pattern.

docs.title: Composition patterns
docs.text:
The five patterns below cover the most common architectures in the reservoir computing literature. All use the same imports and run as written:

from resdag import (
    CGReadoutLayer, Concatenate, ESNLayer, ESNModel,
    SelectiveExponentiation, reservoir_input,
)

Minimal ESN — the base architecture that the other patterns extend.

inp = reservoir_input(3)
states = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3)(inp)
out = CGReadoutLayer(200, 3, name="output")(states)
model = ESNModel(inp, out)          # (batch, time, 3) -> (batch, time, 3)

One reservoir, one readout.

Input-driven — the first input is always the feedback signal; further inputs are exogenous drivers.

feedback = reservoir_input(1)
driver = reservoir_input(5)
states = ESNLayer(150, feedback_size=1, input_size=5)(feedback, driver)
out = CGReadoutLayer(150, 1, name="output")(states)
model = ESNModel([feedback, driver], out)

Feedback plus a known exogenous series.

State augmentation, Ott-style — square the even-indexed states and let the readout see the raw input; this is what the ott_esn factory builds.

inp = reservoir_input(3)
states = ESNLayer(500, feedback_size=3)(inp)
augmented = SelectiveExponentiation(index=0, exponent=2.0)(states)
features = Concatenate()(inp, augmented)
out = CGReadoutLayer(3 + 500, 3, name="output")(features)
model = ESNModel(inp, out)

The ott_esn architecture, built layer by layer.

Parallel two-timescale reservoirs — a fast and a slow reservoir read the same signal; the readout mixes their features.

inp = reservoir_input(3)
fast = ESNLayer(120, feedback_size=3, leak_rate=1.0, spectral_radius=0.7)(inp)
slow = ESNLayer(120, feedback_size=3, leak_rate=0.2, spectral_radius=0.95)(inp)
merged = Concatenate()(fast, slow)
out = CGReadoutLayer(240, 3, name="output")(merged)
model = ESNModel(inp, out)

Two timescales, one readout.

Multi-readout — one reservoir, two named heads, fitted together in a single ESNTrainer.fit call keyed by name.

inp = reservoir_input(3)
states = ESNLayer(300, feedback_size=3)(inp)
coords = CGReadoutLayer(300, 3, name="coords")(states)
energy = CGReadoutLayer(300, 1, name="energy")(states)
model = ESNModel(inp, outputs=[coords, energy])

Readout names become the keys of the targets dict.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
• Layers

    Reservoir layers such as ESNLayer and NGReservoir, their parameters, and the transform layers used to connect them.

  • Readouts

    Choose direct ridge, SVD/pseudoinverse, conjugate-gradient, streaming, online RLS, or sparse FISTA readouts. Fit algebraically or enable gradients for an ordinary PyTorch optimizer.

  • Architectures

    The premade model factories, the graph each one builds, and patterns for hand-built DAGs: stacked reservoirs, driving inputs, multiple readouts.

  • Initialization

    Weight initialization for reservoirs: graph topologies, input and feedback initializers, plain callables, torch.nn.init functions, and the registry system that resolves names. Includes a catalog of every registered topology and initializer.

docs.title: Architectures
docs.text: Build

docs.title: Architectures
docs.text:
The factories in resdag.models build common architectures. Each one is a short function that wires layers into a model the same way you would by hand, then returns it ready to train. The result is an ordinary PyTorch module: most return ESNModel, while spatial patching and coupled ensembles return ParallelESNModel and CoupledEnsembleESNModel. You can retrain it on your data, customize initialization when building it, embed it in a larger network, or read its source and use it as a template. The current factories are ESN-family, but the composition system is not limited to them; new architectures are written as ordinary factory functions.

When no premade fits, write your own. A custom factory is a function that wires a graph and returns a model, and it works in every workflow (training, forecasting, tuning) the same way the premades do:

import resdag as rd

def my_esn(n: int, dim: int) -> rd.ESNModel:
    inp = rd.reservoir_input(dim)
    states = rd.ESNLayer(n, feedback_size=dim)(inp)
    return rd.ESNModel(inp, rd.CGReadoutLayer(n, dim, name="output")(states))

  • classic_esn

    A classic Echo State Network with configurable readout features.

  • coupled_ensemble_esn

    N independently trained sub-models coupled through a shared aggregated feedback signal during autoregression, trained and run through a single fit/forecast interface.

  • headless_esn

    Reservoir-only feature extractor with no readout, returning raw state sequences for use inside a larger PyTorch model.

  • linear_esn

    Identity-activation reservoir with no readout — a linear dynamics probe for spectral analysis and memory-capacity studies.

  • ott_esn

    State-augmented ESN for chaotic systems — squares even-indexed states before the readout. Pathak et al., PRL 120, 024102 (2018).

  • power_augmented

    Generalized state augmentation — every reservoir state raised to a configurable exponent before the readout. A ResDAG generalization of the Pathak et al. augmentation.

Each architecture page shows the wiring diagram of the model its factory builds, along with the factory's parameters and a usage example.

docs.title: Classic esn
docs.text: Build · Architecture

docs.title: classic_esn
docs.text: The standard Echo State Network baseline. Choose whether its readout uses the reservoir states alone or also sees the current feedback input.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input → Reservoir → Concatenate(Input, States) → Readout

This is the default, input_to_readout=True. With input_to_readout=False, the wiring is Input → Reservoir → Readout and the head has reservoir_size features. Both choices use the same reservoir initialization for a given seed. Which predicts better depends on the data and other settings; the automatic tuning workflow tries both.

The feedback signal drives a tanh reservoir, then rejoins its own states at the concatenation, so the readout (a RidgeReadoutLayer) solves ridge regression over feedback_size + reservoir_size features. The linear part of the input–output map reaches the readout unfiltered; the reservoir only has to supply what linearity cannot.

Model graph: the input feeds both the reservoir and the concatenation.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
import torch
from resdag.models import classic_esn
from resdag.training import ESNTrainer

t = torch.arange(1401) * 0.05
series = torch.stack((t.sin(), t.cos(), (2 * t).sin()), dim=-1).unsqueeze(0)

model = classic_esn(reservoir_size=300, feedback_size=3, output_size=3, seed=7)
ESNTrainer(model).fit(
    warmup_inputs=(series[:, :200],),
    train_inputs=(series[:, 200:1200],),
    targets={"output": series[:, 201:1201]},              # next-step targets
)
model.eval()
preds = model.forecast(series[:, 1001:1201], horizon=200)  # (1, 200, 3)
truth = series[:, 1201:1401]                             # held-out continuation

Choosing a baseline

Use classic_esn as the baseline against which augmented variants are compared. For chaotic attractor reconstruction, start from ott_esn instead.

docs.title: Coupled ensemble
docs.text: Build · Architecture

docs.title: coupled_ensemble_esn
docs.text: N independently trained ESN models that forecast jointly: at every autoregressive step, each sub-model receives the same aggregated output (the ensemble mean, by default) as its next feedback input. The sub-models differ only in their random initializations; the shared feedback signal keeps their trajectories synchronized during forecasting.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
The architecture is N replicas of a sub-model plus an aggregator. The shared feedback loop exists only at forecast time:

              ┌─→ sub-model 1 ─┐
feedback ──→──┼─→     ...     ─┼─→ aggregate ─→ ŷ_t
     ▲        └─→ sub-model N ─┘       │
     └─────────────────────────────────┘
        ŷ_t is every sub-model's next feedback

The factory builds the sub-models by calling model_factory(**model_kwargs) N times (default factory: ott_esn) and returns a CoupledEnsembleESNModel. It is not an ESNModel, but its fit and forecast follow the same conventions: warmup/train tuples, a targets dict keyed by readout name, forecast(warmup, horizon=...). It also provides save, load, warmup, and reset_reservoirs, applied across all sub-models.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
import torch
import resdag as rd

series = torch.cumsum(0.1 * torch.randn(1, 1401, 3), dim=1)

ensemble = rd.coupled_ensemble_esn(
    n_models=5, seed=42,
    reservoir_size=300, feedback_size=3, output_size=3,   # → each ott_esn
)
ensemble.fit(
    (series[:, :200],), (series[:, 200:1200],),
    {"output": series[:, 201:1201]},
    n_workers=4,                       # independent readout fits, one per sub-model
)
preds = ensemble.forecast(series[:, 1200:1400], horizon=100)   # (1, 100, 3)

preds, runs = ensemble.forecast(                # per-sub-model trajectories
    series[:, 1200:1400], horizon=100, return_individuals=True,
)

Sub-models train independently on the same data; coupling exists only in the forecast loop. seed makes construction deterministic: sub-model i is built under torch.manual_seed(seed + i), and seed + i is forwarded to the factory when it accepts a seed argument.

docs.title: Aggregators
docs.text:
aggregate takes "mean", "median", or any nn.Module mapping a stacked (N, batch, time, features) tensor to (batch, time, features). OutliersFilteredMean drops members whose output norm is an outlier (Z-score or IQR) before averaging — useful when one diverging sub-model would otherwise drag the shared feedback off the attractor:

ensemble = rd.coupled_ensemble_esn(
    n_models=10, reservoir_size=300, feedback_size=3, output_size=3,
    aggregate=rd.OutliersFilteredMean(method="z_score", threshold=2.0),
)

Non-finite predictions are excluded from both robust statistics and the average. If every member is invalid at a batch/timestep position, the aggregator raises ValueError identifying that position instead of feeding an invalid or fabricated value back into the models. If finite members all fail the outlier threshold, their finite-only mean is the fallback.

Members must have the same input widths, device and precision. These are checked at construction. A custom aggregator must return a tensor with the same (batch, time, features) shape as one member's output.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Notes n_models required ensemble size model_factory ott_esn any callable returning an ESNModel — premade or your own aggregate "mean" "mean", "median", or an nn.Module over (N, batch, time, features) seed None per-sub-model torch.manual_seed(seed + i); forwarded when the factory takes seed **model_kwargs — forwarded verbatim to every model_factory call

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: The design is related to the parallel-reservoirs scheme of J. Pathak et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 024102 (2018), in which multiple reservoirs jointly forecast one system through shared signals. This factory couples complete models through one aggregated feedback signal rather than through spatially overlapping reservoirs; it is not an implementation of that paper.

docs.title: Headless esn
docs.text: Build · Architecture

docs.title: headless_esn
docs.text: A reservoir with nothing after it: the model returns the raw state sequence (batch, time, reservoir_size). Use it as a frozen, randomly-initialized feature extractor inside any PyTorch model you are already training with gradients.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input → Reservoir

The same nonlinear reservoir as classic_esn (tanh activation, scaled spectrum, random bias) without the readout. The factory accepts no readout arguments; any head applied to the states is defined in the surrounding model.

Model graph: the input drives a single reservoir whose states are the output.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
The reservoir is an nn.Module like any other, so it embeds directly. Its weights are frozen by default (trainable=False); the optimizer only ever sees the head's parameters:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import resdag as rd

class Classifier(nn.Module):
    """Frozen reservoir features, gradient-trained head."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.features = rd.headless_esn(reservoir_size=300, feedback_size=3)
        self.head = nn.Linear(300, 10)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        states = self.features(x)          # (batch, time, 300)
        return self.head(states[:, -1])    # classify on the last state

clf = Classifier()
opt = torch.optim.Adam(clf.head.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

The full SGD-head pattern — training loop, state resets between sequences, GPU placement — is worked through in the deploy workflow.

The reservoir is stateful

States carry over between forward calls. Call model.reset_reservoirs() between independent sequences, or each batch starts where the last one left off.

docs.title: Linear esn
docs.text: Build · Architecture

docs.title: linear_esn
docs.text: A reservoir with the nonlinearity removed and no readout attached: the model's output is the state sequence of a linear dynamical system. This is an analysis instrument, not a forecaster.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input → Reservoir(activation="identity")

With identity activation the update reduces to a driven linear recurrence,

\[x_t = (1-a)\,x_{t-1} + a\,\bigl(W x_{t-1} + W_{\text{fb}}\,u_t + b\bigr),\]

so the eigenvalues of \(W\) determine the dynamics: spectral_radius and the topology spec act on the linear spectrum directly, with no saturation involved. The factory forces activation="identity" and accepts no readout arguments; passing readout_alpha or output_size raises TypeError.

Model graph: the input drives a single identity-activation reservoir whose states are the output.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
import torch
from resdag.models import linear_esn

model = linear_esn(reservoir_size=200, feedback_size=1)
states = model(torch.randn(1, 500, 1))    # (1, 500, 200) — states are the output

# Effective dimensionality of the linear response
S = torch.linalg.svdvals(states[0])
participation = (S.sum() ** 2 / (S**2).sum()).item()

Use cases:

  • Spectral analysis. Measure the effect of a topology and spectral radius on the state dynamics without tanh saturation: compare the state spectrum across topology specs with the nonlinearity removed.
  • Memory-capacity studies. Linear reservoirs are the reference case in short-term-memory analysis; drive with white noise and regress delayed inputs from states to trace the capacity curve.
  • Ablation baseline. Any gain a nonlinear ESN shows over this model on the same topology is attributable to the nonlinearity, not the recurrence.

docs.title: Ott esn
docs.text: Build · Architecture

docs.title: ott_esn
docs.text: A classic ESN with one additional transform that squares half the reservoir states before the readout, introduced by Pathak et al. (2018) for forecasting chaotic systems.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input → Reservoir → SelectiveExponentiation → Concatenate(Input, Augmented) → Readout

SelectiveExponentiation(index=0, exponent=2.0) squares the even-indexed state units and passes the odd-indexed ones through untouched. With zero bias, tanh's odd symmetry can limit the even-order features available to a linear readout. Squaring half the units supplies those features explicitly; nonzero biases also break the exact odd symmetry. The concatenation keeps the raw input available as in classic_esn. The default readout is RidgeReadoutLayer, using a direct Cholesky ridge solve. Other readout solvers remain configurable.

Computation graph of ott_esn.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
import torch
from resdag.models import ott_esn
from resdag.training import ESNTrainer

t = torch.arange(1401) * 0.05
series = torch.stack((t.sin(), t.cos(), (2 * t).sin()), dim=-1).unsqueeze(0)

model = ott_esn(
    reservoir_size=500, feedback_size=3, output_size=3,
    topology=("watts_strogatz", {"k": 6, "p": 0.3}),
    spectral_radius=0.95, seed=7,
)
ESNTrainer(model).fit(
    warmup_inputs=(series[:, :200],),
    train_inputs=(series[:, 200:1200],),
    targets={"output": series[:, 201:1201]},
)
model.eval()
preds = model.forecast(series[:, 1001:1201], horizon=200)  # (1, 200, 3)
truth = series[:, 1201:1401]                             # held-out continuation

docs.title: Power augmented
docs.text: Build · Architecture

docs.title: power_augmented
docs.text: The quadratic augmentation of ott_esn, generalized: every reservoir state is raised to a configurable exponent before the readout, and the exponent becomes a hyperparameter you can sweep.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input → Reservoir → Power(exponent) → Concatenate(Input, Augmented) → Readout

Two differences from ott_esn: the exponent is free rather than fixed at 2, and Power transforms every state unit rather than every other one. At exponent=2.0 the readout sees only squared states plus the raw input, where ott_esn interleaves squared and raw units. Whether full or alternating augmentation works better is system-dependent and worth comparing empirically on each problem.

Computation graph of the assembled model.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
import torch
from resdag.models import power_augmented
from resdag.training import ESNTrainer

t = torch.arange(1401) * 0.05
series = torch.stack((t.sin(), t.cos(), (2 * t).sin()), dim=-1).unsqueeze(0)

model = power_augmented(
    reservoir_size=500, feedback_size=3, output_size=3,
    exponent=3.0, seed=7,               # odd exponents preserve state signs
)
ESNTrainer(model).fit(
    warmup_inputs=(series[:, :200],),
    train_inputs=(series[:, 200:1200],),
    targets={"output": series[:, 201:1201]},
)
model.eval()
preds = model.forecast(series[:, 1001:1201], horizon=200)  # (1, 200, 3)
truth = series[:, 1201:1401]                             # held-out continuation

Because exponent is continuous, the factory works directly as a model_creator for hyperparameter tuning; sweep exponent alongside spectral_radius.

Choose the exponent for signed states

tanh reservoir states span [-1, 1], negatives and zeros included. Even integers (2.0) and odd integers (3.0, the default) are always safe. A non-integer exponent (0.5, 1.5) on a negative state returns nan, and a negative exponent (-1.0) on a zero state returns inf — silently, since this factory uses the default torch.pow. If you need a non-integer exponent on signed states, wire the model by hand with Power(exponent, sign_preserving=True), which applies sign(x) * abs(x) ** exponent. Nonnegative exponents avoid the negative-state issue; negative exponents still need care at zero.
