docs.title: Initialization
docs.text: Build

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text:
Every weight matrix in a reservoir is built by a function you can swap: the recurrent matrix with recurrent_initializer=, and the input/feedback matrices with their corresponding initializer hooks. topology= remains a supported alias for recurrent initialization. One spec grammar covers both:

Spec Example Resolves to None — Library default: dense uniform(-1, 1) "name" "erdos_renyi" Registry entry with its registered defaults (name, params) ("watts_strogatz", {"k": 6}) Registry entry with overrides callable my_fn, torch.nn.init.orthogonal_ Wrapped automatically (callable, params) (my_fn, {"blocks": 2}) Wrapper with bound kwargs object get_topology("ring_chord") Used as-is

A topology callable is fn(n, **kw) returning an (n, n) tensor, ndarray, or NetworkX graph; an initializer callable is fn(rows, cols, **kw) returning the rectangular matrix. In-place mutators — the torch.nn.init.*_ convention — are detected and handled.

Start with recurrent weight choices to compare matrix families, custom registration to define your own, or calibration to adapt activity using training data.

docs.title: From the registry
docs.text:
A name uses the registered defaults — show_topologies() and show_input_initializers() print what is available — a (name, params) tuple overrides them, and a configured object from get_topology() is built once and reused across layers. The same grammar drives the rectangular matrices:

from resdag import ESNLayer

layer = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, topology="erdos_renyi", spectral_radius=0.9)
layer = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9,
                 topology=("watts_strogatz", {"k": 6, "p": 0.3, "seed": 42}))
layer = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, input_size=5,
                 feedback_initializer="chebyshev",
                 input_initializer=("random", {"input_scaling": 0.5}))

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
For built-in initializers, a single seed on ESNLayer fixes the entire reservoir — the recurrent (topology) matrix, the feedback and input weights, and the random bias — so two layers built with the same seed are identical down to the last entry. It covers the registry/callable specs and the default uniform(-1, 1) draws used when no spec is given, and it is independent of the global RNG state. A custom callback must accept and use seed or generator to provide the same guarantee:

import torch

a = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, topology="erdos_renyi", seed=42)
b = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, topology="erdos_renyi", seed=42)
assert torch.equal(a.weight_hh, b.weight_hh)
assert torch.equal(a.weight_feedback, b.weight_feedback)
assert torch.equal(a.bias_h, b.bias_h)

seed accepts a plain int or a torch.Generator — the latter is convenient for threading a per-trial generator (e.g. seed + trial.number) through an HPO model_creator so every trial draws an identical reservoir run-to-run. An explicit seed inside a tuple/object spec always wins over the layer-level one. Pass seed=None (the default) and the reservoir still tracks torch.manual_seed, because built-in NumPy and Torch draws derive their generators from Torch's global RNG. Configured custom objects retain their own seed policy. See custom reproducibility.

docs.title: Any function is a topology
docs.text:
A bare callable is a valid spec; no registration is required.

import torch
from resdag import ESNLayer

def block_diagonal(n: int, blocks: int = 4) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Independent sub-reservoirs along the diagonal."""
    w = torch.zeros(n, n)
    size = n // blocks
    for b in range(blocks):
        s = b * size
        w[s : s + size, s : s + size] = torch.randn(size, size)
    return w

layer = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, topology=block_diagonal, spectral_radius=0.9)
layer = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9,
                 topology=(block_diagonal, {"blocks": 2}))
layer = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=1.0,
                 topology=torch.nn.init.orthogonal_)

Scale is separate from structure

However the matrix is built — graph, registry, bare callable, torch.nn.init — spectral_radius normally rescales the result afterwards. Builders marked prescaled=True keep their own scale. An explicit initializer object can override either policy; see scaling control.

docs.title: The input_scaling contract
docs.text:
input_scaling is the one knob that controls input-injection magnitude — among the most performance-critical ESN hyperparameters. Every input/feedback initializer honors the same contract, defined once on InputFeedbackInitializer:

  • input_scaling=None (the default for most initializers) applies no scaling — the matrix keeps its natural range.
  • input_scaling=s applies a single, uniform W <- s * W as the documented final transform, so the matrix's magnitude statistic scales linearly with s. Concretely, input_scaling=0.5 halves it and input_scaling=2.0 doubles it.

The "magnitude statistic" is max|W| for the elementwise initializers and the per-channel L2 norm for the two structured ring initializers (whose value is the scaling target). What input_scaling=0.5 does, per initializer:

Initializer Natural range / statistic Effect of input_scaling=0.5 random entries in [-1, 1] entries in [-0.5, 0.5]; max\|W\| → 0.5 random_binary entries in {-1, +1} entries in {-0.5, +0.5} normal Normal(loc, scale) entries every entry × 0.5 uniform Uniform(low, high) entries every entry × 0.5 bernoulli entries in {-1, +1} (+1 w.p. p) entries in {-0.5, +0.5} chessboard entries in {-1, +1} entries in {-0.5, +0.5} chebyshev Chebyshev map values every entry × 0.5 pseudo_diagonal structured [-1, 1] every entry × 0.5 binary_balanced balanced {-1, +1} every entry × 0.5 dendrocycle_input U[-draw_width, draw_width] on core every drawn entry × 0.5 (see below) opposite_anchors per-channel L2 norm = input_scaling per-channel L2 norm = 0.5 ring_window per-channel L2 norm = input_scaling per-channel L2 norm = 0.5

gain is now input_scaling

opposite_anchors and ring_window previously named this knob gain. gain is now a deprecated alias for input_scaling (identical meaning — the per-channel L2 norm); passing it emits a DeprecationWarning, and passing both raises.

dendrocycle_input: draw width vs. scaling

dendrocycle_input historically overloaded input_scaling to mean the draw half-width of U[-s, s]. That role is now the separate draw_width parameter (default 1.0); input_scaling is the uniform final multiply shared with every other initializer (default None). To reproduce the old dendrocycle_input(input_scaling=s) draw, pass draw_width=s.

# Same magnitude regime regardless of which initializer you swap in:
layer = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, feedback_initializer=("random", {"input_scaling": 0.5}))
layer = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, feedback_initializer=("opposite_anchors", {"input_scaling": 0.5}))

An optional connectivity knob (a fraction in (0, 1]) lives on the same base class: it keeps that fraction of nonzero entries per input channel — exactly round(connectivity * reservoir_size) per column, at least one. The distribution initializers normal, uniform, and bernoulli honor it directly (connectivity=0.1 → a 10%-dense input matrix); structured initializers that already define their own connectivity pattern (only the core ring receives input, a fixed window per channel) document whether they honor it.

docs.title: Coming from reservoirpy
docs.text:
The bread-and-butter input-matrix recipes have one-to-one equivalents, so a reservoirpy mat_gen call maps directly onto a resdag initializer name. The shared connectivity and input_scaling knobs carry the same meaning:

reservoirpy mat_gen resdag initializer Notes normal(loc=, scale=, connectivity=) ("normal", {"loc": …, "scale": …, "connectivity": …}) Gaussian entries; same connectivity density. uniform(low=, high=, connectivity=) ("uniform", {"low": …, "high": …, "connectivity": …}) Bounded uniform; configurable bounds. bernoulli(p=, connectivity=) ("bernoulli", {"p": …, "connectivity": …}) ±1 signs, +1 with probability p. random_sparse(dist="normal"/"uniform", …) normal / uniform with connectivity The sparse variants are just connectivity < 1. 
# reservoirpy: Win = bernoulli(N, dim_in, connectivity=0.1, input_scaling=0.5)
layer = ESNLayer(
    reservoir_size=200, feedback_size=3,
    feedback_initializer=("bernoulli", {"connectivity": 0.1, "input_scaling": 0.5}),
)

    Every registered recurrent-matrix builder, with its connectivity portrait and parameters.

  • Initializer catalog

    Every registered input/feedback initializer, with a portrait of the matrix it draws and its parameters.

docs.title: Registering your own
docs.text:
Registration makes a builder usable by name in every layer and factory, and therefore sweepable by name in an HPO study. Matrix builders return the matrix directly (the built-in "orthogonal" Haar-random matrix is one); graph builders return a NetworkX graph whose edge weights become matrix entries (unweighted edges count as 1):

import networkx as nx
from resdag.init.topology import register_graph_topology, register_matrix_topology

@register_matrix_topology("two_blocks", blocks=2)
def two_blocks(n: int, blocks: int = 2) -> torch.Tensor:
    return block_diagonal(n, blocks=blocks)

@register_graph_topology("double_ring", offset=2)
def double_ring(n: int, offset: int = 2) -> nx.DiGraph:
    g = nx.DiGraph()
    g.add_edges_from((i, (i + 1) % n, {"weight": 1.0}) for i in range(n))
    g.add_edges_from((i, (i + offset) % n, {"weight": 0.5}) for i in range(n))
    return g

Input/feedback initializers register the same way — a plain fn(rows, cols, **kw) is enough; register_input_feedback also accepts an InputFeedbackInitializer subclass when the initializer needs state or validation:

from resdag.init.input_feedback import register_input_feedback

@register_input_feedback("first_neuron", scale=1.0)
def first_neuron(rows: int, cols: int, scale: float = 1.0) -> torch.Tensor:
    w = torch.zeros(rows, cols)
    w[0, :] = scale
    return w

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Reservoir dynamics — why structure and spectral radius shape what a reservoir remembers.
  • Tune — sweeping topologies and initializers by name inside an HPO study.

docs.title: Customize initialization
docs.text: Start with a function. Register it when you want to select it by name in configuration files, model factories or tuning studies. Registration is local to the current Python process: import your registration module before using a name in another process.

docs.title: Recurrent matrices
docs.text:
A builder receives the reservoir size and returns an (n, n) tensor, NumPy array, or graph. An in-place torch.nn.init function works too.

import torch
from resdag import ESNLayer
from resdag.init import register_recurrent_initializer

@register_recurrent_initializer("my_cycle", prescaled=True, gain=0.9)
def my_cycle(n, gain=0.9, seed=None, *, device=None, dtype=None):
    # This matrix has an exact radius of abs(gain), so it owns its scale.
    return gain * torch.eye(n, device=device, dtype=dtype).roll(1, dims=0)

layer = ESNLayer(64, feedback_size=2, recurrent_initializer="my_cycle")
layer = ESNLayer(
    64, feedback_size=2,
    recurrent_initializer=("my_cycle", {"gain": 0.7}),
)

The same function can be passed directly without registration: recurrent_initializer=my_cycle or (my_cycle, {"gain": 0.7}). register_graph_topology and register_matrix_topology continue to work; they share the registry used by the new recurrent API. Unknown names and conflicting topology / recurrent_initializer specs raise errors.

For random builders, accept seed and use a local generator on the requested device. A layer seed is forwarded when your function accepts it; an explicitly bound seed wins. Your builder must return the requested shape with finite values. A function that ignores its seed cannot be made reproducible by the registry. Returning an already normalized matrix is optional: choose prescaled=True when its native scale is meaningful, or let the layer apply spectral_radius afterward.

docs.title: Input, feedback, bias and reset state
docs.text:
Rectangular builders receive (rows, cols). They can also be registered:

from resdag.init.input_feedback import register_input_feedback

@register_input_feedback("my_constant", value=0.1)
def my_constant(rows, cols, value=0.1, *, device=None, dtype=None):
    return torch.full((rows, cols), value, device=device, dtype=dtype)

layer = ESNLayer(
    64, feedback_size=2, input_size=1,
    feedback_initializer=("normal", {"scale": 0.2}),
    input_initializer="my_constant",
    bias_initializer=("my_constant", {"value": 0.0}),
    initial_state_initializer=("my_constant", {"value": 0.05}),
    seed=4,
)

bias_initializer sees a (1, reservoir_size) view of the bias. initial_state_initializer sees (1, state_size) once at construction. The resulting reset template is saved as a buffer and repeated independently for each batch item whenever a fresh state is needed. The default is zero. A sampled template stays identical across resets and changing batch sizes. Explicit supplied states still take precedence. bias=False rejects a bias initializer instead of silently ignoring it. For packed multi-component states, initialize the full packed width and respect the cell's documented component order.

In-place callables such as torch.nn.init.zeros_ and (torch.nn.init.normal_, {"std": 0.02}) use the same grammar. A configured InputFeedbackInitializer object is accepted as-is. Its own seed and state remain its responsibility.

docs.title: Separate gate parameters
docs.text:
The light-gated layer shares its input projection by default. Supply a gate initializer to make that projection independent, and control the gate's recurrence and bias separately:

from resdag import GatedReservoirLayer

gated = GatedReservoirLayer(
    64, feedback_size=2,
    recurrent_initializer=("signed_permutation", {"gain": 0.8}),
    gate_recurrent_initializer=("signed_permutation", {"gain": 0.1}),
    gate_feedback_initializer=("normal", {"scale": 0.05}),
    gate_bias_initializer=("my_constant", {"value": 2.0}),
    bias_initializer=torch.nn.init.zeros_,
    seed=9,
)

gate_input_initializer controls the optional driver's gate projection. An omitted gate projection reuses its candidate counterpart. gate_spectral_radius controls only the gate recurrence and obeys that initializer's scaling policy. These controls are independent of the candidate's spectral_radius. New parameters appear in state_dict only when configured, so rebuild the same configuration before loading weights.

docs.title: Save and share custom configurations
docs.text:
Weight checkpoints need the same architecture when loaded. Full-model checkpoints additionally pickle the initializer configuration; keep custom classes/functions at importable module scope. Import registration modules on workers before reconstructing architectures from names. Avoid anonymous or nested functions if you need full-model serialization.

See the input/feedback catalog for existing recipes, recurrent choices for spectral control, and API reference for subclass contracts.

docs.title: Reproducibility and numerical precision
docs.text:
Direct callbacks, (callback, kwargs) tuples and registered names use the same seed rules. A callback accepting seed= receives the layer seed unless you explicitly bind one. In-place Torch functions accepting generator= get a local generator on the destination device. A bound generator takes precedence and advances on each call; reuse a fresh generator with the same seed when you want to reproduce its first draw. Configured initializer objects keep their own seed policy and are used as supplied.

from resdag.init import get_recurrent_initializer
from resdag.init.input_feedback import get_input_feedback

# Explicit initializer seeds take precedence over the layer seed.
recurrent = get_recurrent_initializer(
    "orthogonal", seed=11, rescale=False,
)
feedback = get_input_feedback("normal", scale=0.2, seed=12)
layer = ESNLayer(64, feedback_size=2, recurrent_initializer=recurrent,
                 feedback_initializer=feedback, seed=99)

For built-in NumPy-backed initializers, omitting a seed draws from a generator derived from Torch's global RNG, so resetting torch.manual_seed(...) reproduces the draw. Custom callbacks that ignore both seed and generator remain responsible for their own randomness. Graph or NumPy float64 outputs retain their precision when copied into float64 reservoir weights; constructing float32 values first and converting them later cannot recover the lost digits.

Some structured initializers need options or dimensions that cannot be inferred from the layer. For example, supply ("dendrocycle_input", {"c": 0.5}) or ("ring_window", {"c": 0.5, "window": 5}). These tuple forms work the same way as configuring an initializer object explicitly. Each catalog page includes a complete example with suitable dimensions and required parameters, and the examples are executed in the test suite.

docs.title: Choose recurrent weights
docs.text:
recurrent_initializer= builds the square matrix that carries information between timesteps. It accepts graph builders, direct matrix builders, your own functions, and registered names. topology= remains an equivalent spelling; pass one or the other.

import torch
from resdag import ESNLayer

reservoir = ESNLayer(
    128, feedback_size=3,
    recurrent_initializer=("signed_permutation", {"gain": 0.9}),
    feedback_initializer=("normal", {"scale": 0.2}),
    seed=7, dtype=torch.float64,
)

docs.title: Pick a family
docs.text:
Family Choose it when Main control Graph connectivity Connections have a meaningful structure Existing graph catalog Delay line / cycle You want simple, interpretable memory Connection weights Haar orthogonal You want random rotations with uniform singular values gain signed_permutation You want a cheap, sparse orthogonal matrix gain householder_orthogonal You want orthogonal mixing without a QR decomposition Reflector count and gain singular_spectrum You want to control amplification in each direction Prescribed singular values eigen_spectrum You want prescribed real modes and oscillatory pairs Prescribed eigenvalues fast_spectral_initialization You want approximate radius initialization without eigenvalue computation Native spectral_radius, explicit rescale=False

A singular value controls how much one update can amplify a direction. An eigenvalue describes a repeated linear mode. They answer different questions: a non-normal matrix can transiently amplify inputs even with all eigenvalues inside the unit circle. Neither statistic alone guarantees useful nonlinear reservoir dynamics or accurate autonomous forecasts.

The structured builders return ordinary dense tensors. Their construction can be cheaper than QR; dense recurrence still costs a matrix multiplication at each timestep. signed_permutation does not automatically install a specialized permutation kernel. On ESNLayer, sparse=True explicitly selects the existing frozen CSR recurrence.

docs.title: Decide who controls scaling
docs.text:
Most historical builders are rescaled by the layer's spectral_radius= after construction. Builders registered with prescaled=True own their scale; the layer leaves their prescribed spectrum or gain intact and warns if its radius would otherwise be ignored.

For an explicit policy, configure the initializer object:

from resdag.init import get_recurrent_initializer

native = get_recurrent_initializer(
    "fast_spectral_initialization", spectral_radius=0.8, rescale=False, seed=7,
)
reservoir = ESNLayer(128, feedback_size=3, recurrent_initializer=native, seed=7)

# Explicitly permit an outer rescale, including a prescaled builder.
scaled = get_recurrent_initializer("orthogonal", gain=1.0, rescale=True, seed=7)
reservoir = ESNLayer(
    128, feedback_size=3, recurrent_initializer=scaled, spectral_radius=0.8,
)

rescale=False avoids the outer eigenvalue calculation. FSI's radius is an asymptotic random-matrix approximation, not an exact finite-size guarantee. rescale=True applies the layer's radius when supplied; it changes the absolute values of a prescribed spectrum. Leaving the policy as None keeps historical behavior. This explicit object form also avoids reserving a new keyword in arbitrary custom builder tuples.

docs.title: Precision and placement
docs.text:
Pass dtype= and device= when constructing a reservoir to initialize its parameters in the requested precision and location. Direct matrix builders accept these arguments too. A builder used through the registry receives the target tensor's dtype/device when it supports them. Explicit values bound in a spec take precedence.

from resdag.init.matrices import orthogonal_matrix

matrix = orthogonal_matrix(64, seed=4, dtype=torch.float64, device="cpu")

Graph construction and third-party callables may still run on the CPU or in their own precision, then copy to the target. Converting an already initialized float32 layer with .double() does not recover the precision lost during its original draws. Reproducibility is per device/backend; do not assume CPU and GPU random draws are identical.

Continue with custom registration, the complete builder catalog, or training-data calibration.

docs.title: Spectral measurement and initialization cost
docs.text:
Automatic scaling measures dense matrices with torch.linalg.eigvals. For large matrices with at most 10% nonzero entries it uses SciPy's sparse Arnoldi solver on CPU, with a dense fallback if that solve fails. Arnoldi is a numerical approximation; requesting several leading eigenvalues reduces sensitivity to clustered spectra. MPS measurements also use CPU. Dense eigendecomposition can make construction expensive for a large reservoir; it does not run at every forecast step.

A power estimate that stops changing can still have missed the dominant mode. It is therefore insufficient to validate the radius used for scaling. When construction cost matters, prefer a builder whose spectrum is known by design and explicitly keep its native scale with prescaled=True or rescale=False. Benchmark both construction time and subsequent forecasting for your workload.

docs.title: Migration: corrected graph weights and degree
docs.text:
Two graph builders now follow their stated mathematical definitions. Reservoirs using them can produce different weights and forecasts with the same old seed; retrain readouts and reevaluate previously selected hyperparameters.

  • regular now connects each node to exactly k distinct neighbours, excluding optional self-loops. Previously odd k silently produced k - 1 neighbours. Odd k uses an antipodal matching, so n must be even. Valid configurations satisfy 0 <= k < n and n * k even. Directed mode has k incoming and k outgoing neighbours. To preserve the old odd-degree connectivity, request k - 1; matching an old random realization exactly requires saved weights.
  • simple_cycle_jumps now adds the cycle and jump contributions on shared edges. With jump_length=1, forward edges have weight r_c + r_l and reverse edges have weight r_l. Previously jumps overwrote the cycle weight, so changing r_c could have no effect. Each bidirectional jump pair is counted once. Saved weights are the reliable way to retain an existing realization.
  • spectral_cascade(..., spectral_radius=0) now produces zero clique weights; it previously retained nonzero weights.
# True degree three, including one opposite neighbour on an even ring.
reservoir = ESNLayer(
    128, feedback_size=3,
    recurrent_initializer=("regular", {"k": 3}), seed=7,
)

# Cycle and jump contributions are both preserved where their edges overlap.
reservoir = ESNLayer(
    128, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=None,
    recurrent_initializer=("simple_cycle_jumps", {
        "jump_length": 1, "r_c": 0.6, "r_l": 0.1,
    }), seed=7,
)

docs.title: Layers
docs.text: Build

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Every architecture in the library is built from three kinds of component, all of which operate on (batch, time, features) tensors. Reservoirs hold the stateful dynamics; every reservoir family splits the work the same way: a cell that owns the single-step update and its parameters, and a layer that owns the sequence loop and the full state-management API. Readouts are the trainable maps from features to predictions, fitted algebraically in one solve or by gradient descent when unfrozen. Transforms are parameterless feature operations that connect everything else into a DAG.

Choose among leaky ESNs, gated reservoirs, continuous and spiking dynamics, oscillators, Legendre memory, native PyTorch GRU/LSTM adapters, and next-generation delay features. All use the same cell/layer contract. New families fit that contract without changes downstream. A readout is independent of the dynamics that produced the features it reads, and a transform operates only on the feature axis, so new implementations in any category compose with the existing ones.

  • ESNLayer

    The echo-state reservoir layer — the leaky update equation, its constructor parameters, the state API, and the projected fast path.

  • Legendre delay memory

    A fixed Legendre delay network that represents recent signal history with a linear state-space memory.

  • NGReservoir

    NG-RC reservoir layer with deterministic dynamics built from delay taps and polynomial monomials. Covers the k, s, p parameters, the feature-count formula, and warmup requirements.

  • Oscillator reservoir

    Coupled oscillator dynamics with separate position and velocity, using the standard reservoir training interface.

  • Reuse a PyTorch GRU or LSTM

    Reuse native PyTorch GRUCell and LSTMCell weights inside reservoir graphs, with frozen or trainable parameters.

  • Transforms

    Parameterless feature operations — concatenation, augmentation powers, deterministic dropout, and feature partitioning — with the augmentation pattern as a worked example.

docs.title: Changing a built layer
docs.text:
Live settings are forwarded to the cell: changing layer.leak_rate or layer.noise changes the next update. EuSN exposes its integration interval through both layer.epsilon and layer.dt. For LIF, changing layer.dt, layer.tau_mem or layer.tau_syn recomputes both exponential decays; changing layer.v_threshold changes the firing threshold. Time intervals/constants must be positive and finite. A failed assignment leaves the old settings intact. An explicit LIF alpha/beta override remains possible; another time-setting assignment recomputes them from the time constants.

Sizes, spectral radius and discretized Legendre settings are fixed when the weights are built. Rebuild the layer to change those settings. A rejected assignment raises instead of silently creating an ineffective attribute.

For dense recurrent weights, use ordinary PyTorch updates such as with torch.no_grad(): cell.weight_hh.copy_(new_weights). Supported frozen reservoirs built with sparse=True store only compressed indices and values; edit existing connections through cell.weight_hh.values() under torch.no_grad(). That view shares the stored values. Call cell.weight_hh.to_dense() when an inspection copy is needed. Setting cell.trainable = True expands compressed weights into a dense Parameter; create the optimizer after that change. Avoid .data edits, which bypass PyTorch's mutation tracking. See the sparse reservoir guide for device, initialization and memory details.

docs.title: Adding a layer
docs.text:
A new reservoir family is one ReservoirCell implementation wrapped in a BaseReservoirLayer subclass, which inherits the sequence loop and state API. The cell contract, in full:

class MyCell(ReservoirCell):
    state_size: int    # shape contract for the state
    output_size: int   # trailing dim of the per-step output

    def init_state(self, batch_size, device, dtype): ...
    def forward(self, inputs, state): ...   # -> (output, new_state)

docs.title: Esn layer
docs.text: Build · Layers

docs.title: ESNLayer
docs.text:
The echo-state family's layer: a recurrent reservoir whose weights are drawn once and frozen. Per timestep it applies the leaky-ESN update

\[ h_t = (1-\alpha)\,h_{t-1} + \alpha\, f\!\left(W_{fb}\,x_t + W_{in}\,u_t + W\,h_{t-1} + b\right) \]

and returns the full state trajectory (batch, time, reservoir_size). Every parameter is set in the constructor:

from resdag import ESNLayer

reservoir = ESNLayer(
    reservoir_size=500,         # units; output is (batch, time, 500)
    feedback_size=3,            # dim of the first input (required)
    input_size=None,            # dim of exogenous drivers, if any
    spectral_radius=None,       # target rho(W); None leaves W unscaled
    bias=True,                  # random bias b ~ U(-beta, beta)
    bias_scaling=1.0,           # beta; 0.0 restores the pre-0.5 zero bias
    activation="tanh",          # "tanh" | "relu" | "identity" | "sigmoid"
    leak_rate=1.0,              # alpha in [0, 1]; < 1 slows the dynamics
    trainable=False,            # True unfreezes all weights for backprop
    feedback_initializer=None,  # builder for W_fb
    input_initializer=None,     # builder for W_in
    topology=None,              # structure of W — see Initialization
)

docs.title: Key parameters
docs.text:
spectral_radius rescales W to a target largest eigenvalue — the bare layer defaults to None (unscaled), while every premade factory passes 0.9. leak_rate below 1 produces slow dynamics for slow signals. trainable=False freezes every parameter, which is what makes an ESN an ESN; flip it only when you intend to backpropagate through the dynamics. The three structural arguments — topology, feedback_initializer, input_initializer — accept the full spec grammar from Initialization: registry names, (name, params) tuples, bare callables, or configured objects.

Changed in 0.5

bias=True now draws a random bias from uniform(-bias_scaling, bias_scaling). The bias breaks the odd symmetry of tanh dynamics — without it, negated inputs produce exactly negated states. Set bias_scaling=0.0 to reproduce pre-0.5 runs, where the bias was zero-initialized and therefore a silent no-op.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
seed is the single knob that fixes the entire reservoir — the recurrent (topology) matrix, the feedback and input weights, and the random bias — including the default uniform(-1, 1) draws used when no explicit initializer or topology is given. Two layers built with the same seed are byte-identical down to the last entry; no global torch.manual_seed is needed. This is the canonical reproducible-layer recipe:

import torch
from resdag.layers import ESNLayer

a = ESNLayer(500, feedback_size=3, input_size=2, spectral_radius=0.9, seed=42)
b = ESNLayer(500, feedback_size=3, input_size=2, spectral_radius=0.9, seed=42)

assert torch.equal(a.weight_hh, b.weight_hh)
assert torch.equal(a.weight_feedback, b.weight_feedback)
assert torch.equal(a.weight_input, b.weight_input)
assert torch.equal(a.bias_h, b.bias_h)

seed accepts a plain int or a torch.Generator (handy for threading a per-trial generator from an HPO loop); a generator is reduced to its initial_seed(), so seed=7 and seed=torch.Generator().manual_seed(7) agree without advancing that generator or Torch's global RNG. Feedback, input, recurrent, bias and reset-state initialization use separate local streams: changing an optional input or one initializer does not shift the other roles. An explicit seed inside a (name, {"seed": ...}) spec always wins over the layer seed; custom initializer-owned RNGs keep their own policy. With seed=None (the default), the cell draws one master seed from Torch's CPU global RNG, then derives every local role from that value. torch.manual_seed therefore reproduces construction. Newly seeded weights changed when these streams were separated; see the migration notes.

Device-native draws

The torch-native weight draws (the default uniform(-1, 1) path and the random/random_binary initializers) happen directly on the layer's device — no CPU build and copy — so a seeded reservoir built on CUDA is reproducible on CUDA. Because torch's CPU and CUDA RNG streams differ, the same seed yields a different matrix on each backend; each backend is reproducible on its own.

docs.title: State
docs.text:
The state persists across forward calls. It re-initializes from the configured initial state (zeros by default) when the incoming batch size, device, or dtype changes, and it is detached between calls, so gradients never cross a forward-call boundary. The full contract is described in the concepts page; the API in brief:

reservoir.reset_state()              # forget; lazily re-initialized next forward
reservoir.reset_state(batch_size=4)  # configured initial state for four examples
reservoir.get_state()                # clone of (batch, reservoir_size), or None
reservoir.set_state(saved)           # restore a checkpoint
reservoir.set_random_state()         # standard-normal state

docs.title: Cell, layer, and the fast path
docs.text: Like every reservoir family, ESNLayer splits the work in two: an ESNCell owns the weights and the single-step update, while the layer owns the sequence loop and the state. The loop's fast path calls project_inputs once to precompute \(W_{fb}x + W_{in}u + b\) for every timestep, then evaluates the recurrent update at each step. This avoids repeating the input projections inside the loop. Kernel counts and performance depend on the backend, compilation settings and workload. Attribute access delegates to the cell, so reservoir.weight_hh and reservoir.spectral_radius work directly.

docs.title: Legendre delay memory
docs.text:
LegendreDelayLayer compresses recent signal history into Legendre polynomial coefficients. Its memory dynamics are fixed and linear; you can fit an ordinary readout on top or combine it with a nonlinear reservoir.

from resdag import LegendreDelayLayer

memory = LegendreDelayLayer(order=8, feedback_size=2, theta=50.0, dt=1.0)
# Input: (batch, time, 2). Output: (batch, time, 16).

order controls coefficients per channel, not total layer width. By default, every feedback/driver feature gets its own memory channel. In the example, two channels times eight coefficients gives 16 features. memory_channels= instead chooses a projected channel count; use feedback_initializer and input_initializer to customize the input encoders.

theta is the nominal history window in the same units as dt. With samples one second apart, theta=50, dt=1 targets roughly 50 seconds of history. Increasing order improves the representation within that window at the cost of a larger state. A finite-order delay network approximates a sliding history; it does not store every past sample exactly.

The continuous Legendre matrices are discretized with an augmented matrix exponential under a zero-order-held input. They are registered buffers, move with .to(), and are saved with state_dict(). Their native spectrum is part of the memory definition, so there is no arbitrary spectral_radius knob. trainable=True allows input encoders to train while leaving the analytical memory dynamics fixed.

The state and output share width order * memory_channels. Coefficients are packed channel by channel. Both standard and explicit-state sequence paths work, as do downstream readout fitting and checkpointing.

This is the fixed Legendre delay-network memory described in the Legendre Memory Unit paper. It implements the memory component; a learned nonlinear hidden unit is a separate component you can compose around it.

See layer composition, training, and API reference.

docs.title: Ng reservoir
docs.text: Build · Layers

docs.title: NGReservoir
docs.text:
NGReservoir implements the next-generation reservoir computing family (Gauthier et al. 2021): a reservoir with designed rather than random dynamics. It has no recurrent weights and no randomness. Features are built from time-delayed inputs and their polynomial products, so two constructions with the same k, s, p produce identical features.

NG-RC occupies the same DAG position as any other reservoir. 
from resdag import NGReservoir

layer = NGReservoir(
    input_dim=3,            # dimensionality of each input vector
    k=2,                    # delay taps, including the current input
    s=1,                    # spacing between taps, in timesteps
    p=2,                    # polynomial degree of the monomials
    include_constant=True,  # prepend a constant 1.0 feature
    include_linear=True,    # keep the delay-embedded inputs themselves
)

features = layer(x)         # x: (batch, time, 3) -> (batch, time, 28)
layer.feature_dim           # 28
layer.warmup_length         # (k-1)*s = 1

docs.title: What k, s, p control
docs.text:
k taps spaced s steps apart give the layer a memory window of (k-1)*s + 1 timesteps; p sets the degree of the monomials formed from everything in that window. With \(D = \text{input\_dim} \cdot k\) linear features, the output dimension is

\[ \text{feature\_dim} = \mathbb{1}[\text{constant}] + \mathbb{1}[\text{linear}]\,D + \binom{D+p-1}{p} \]

The three terms are the constant 1, the delay-embedded inputs, and every monomial of exactly degree p; include_constant and include_linear toggle the first two.

Exact degree, not degree-up-to-p (default)

By default the nonlinear block holds monomials of exactly degree p — lower-order cross terms (degrees 2, …, p-1) are excluded. So NGReservoir(p=3, include_linear=True) emits constant + linear + cubic with no quadratic terms. This matches Gauthier et al. (2021), whose Lorenz63 and double-scroll bases each use a single polynomial degree. Many NVAR / NG-RC implementations instead use the cumulative "degree up to p" basis — see below.

docs.title: Cumulative degree (cumulative=True)
docs.text:
Pass cumulative=True to emit every monomial of degree up to p (the full polynomial basis), rather than only the top degree:

layer = NGReservoir(input_dim=3, k=2, p=3, cumulative=True)

With D = input_dim · k linear features, the nonlinear block then spans degrees 2 … p when include_linear=True (degree-1 monomials are dropped — they would duplicate the linear block), or 1 … p when include_linear=False:

\[ \text{feature\_dim} = \mathbb{1}[\text{constant}] + \mathbb{1}[\text{linear}]\,D + \sum_{g=d_{\text{lo}}}^{p} \binom{D+g-1}{g}, \quad d_{\text{lo}} = \begin{cases} 2 & \text{include\_linear} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

The default (cumulative=False) is unchanged and stays bit-for-bit identical to previous releases; reach for the cumulative basis when porting configs that expect "degree up to p".

Degree 1 (p=1)

With p=1 the degree-1 monomials are the linear features themselves. To avoid two identical blocks (which would make the readout design matrix rank-deficient), the monomial block is dropped when p=1 and include_linear=True. With p=1 and include_linear=False the degree-1 monomials are kept, since they are then the only delay-embedded features.

Combinatorial growth

The binomial term grows fast in k, p, and input_dim; the layer warns when feature_dim exceeds 10,000. If the warning fires, reduce k, p, or the input dimension before training.

docs.title: State and warmup
docs.text: The state is not a hidden vector but a FIFO delay buffer of shape (batch, (k-1)*s, input_dim). The standard state API applies, with set_state validating that 3-D layout. The buffer needs (k-1)*s steps to fill, and outputs before that contain zeros from empty slots: discard the first warmup_length steps when accuracy matters. The full warmup is those (k-1)*s steps, compared to the hundreds an echo-state reservoir typically needs to wash out its initial condition.

docs.title: When to prefer it
docs.text: This family suits short datasets, where the (k-1)*s-step warmup consumes little data; systems that are low-dimensional with smooth polynomial structure; and settings that require exact reproducibility, since the construction is deterministic and needs no seed. The hyperparameters are three small integers that can be grid-searched exhaustively, with no spectral radius, leak rate, or topology to tune. The trade-off is the formula above: feature_dim grows combinatorially with input_dim, so high-dimensional signals favor reservoirs that compress into a fixed-size state. The layer has no learnable parameters, and gradients flow through it to upstream modules.

docs.title: Oscillator reservoir
docs.text:
CoRNNLayer carries position and velocity for each unit. The readout sees position; velocity remains part of the recurrent memory. This gives you a different temporal response from a leaky ESN while keeping the same model, trainer, explicit-state and forecast interfaces.

from resdag import CoRNNLayer

reservoir = CoRNNLayer(
    64, feedback_size=2,
    dt=0.05, gamma=1.0, epsilon=1.0,
    recurrent_initializer=("signed_permutation", {"gain": 0.5}),
    velocity_initializer=("signed_permutation", {"gain": 0.1}),
    seed=3,
)

One step uses the previous position h, velocity v, and projected input u:

v_new = v + dt * (tanh(W_h h + W_v v + u + b) - gamma*h - epsilon*v)
h_new = h + dt * v_new

gamma supplies restoring force, epsilon damping, and dt the integration step. velocity_initializer initializes the matrix multiplying velocity; it is not a reset-state initializer. The feedback and optional driver have independent initializer specs. trainable=False freezes all weights by default; True enables gradients through the oscillator parameters.

The internal state packs [position | velocity], shaped (batch, 2*N). Outputs have width N. Sequence processing preprojects the input stream once, then advances the oscillator at each timestep. forward_stateless and model as_module() work as for other reservoirs; explicitly returned states include both position and velocity.

Small dt and nonnegative damping are useful starting points, but arbitrary random weights do not inherit an unconditional stability guarantee. Evaluate long rollouts and held-out prediction quality for your chosen parameters. The implementation follows the explicit-damping discretization in the original coRNN paper.

See composition and training, initializers, and the cell/layer API reference.

docs.title: Reuse a PyTorch GRU or LSTM
Reuse a PyTorch GRU or LSTM
docs.text:
Wrap an existing torch.nn.GRUCell or torch.nn.LSTMCell to use it in a ResDAG graph. Its weights and gate equations are preserved; the wrapper adds the normal sequence, state, training and forecasting interfaces.

from torch import nn
from resdag import TorchRecurrentLayer

native = nn.LSTMCell(input_size=3, hidden_size=32)
reservoir = TorchRecurrentLayer(native, feedback_size=2, input_size=1)
# reservoir(feedback, driver): (batch, time, 32)

The native cell's input size must equal feedback_size + input_size. Feedback comes first in the concatenated input. input_size=None means feedback only. The wrapper copies the supplied cell so freezing it does not unexpectedly freeze the caller's original module. It inherits the original dtype/device.

Weights are frozen by default, making this useful for readout experiments on existing recurrent features. Pass trainable=True to train the recurrent weights with a PyTorch optimizer. Freezing a random GRU/LSTM does not guarantee a useful reservoir; compare its validation performance with a plain ESN.

GRU state has width hidden_size. LSTM state packs [hidden | cell] with width 2 * hidden_size; the readout sees only the hidden part. If you use explicit states, keep that packed width. The input projection is computed over the full sequence before the recurrence loop, and the gate updates match the native PyTorch cells.

import torch

feedback = torch.randn(4, 20, 2)
driver = torch.randn(4, 20, 1)
initial = reservoir.cell.init_state(4, feedback.device, feedback.dtype)
features, state = reservoir.forward_stateless([feedback, driver], initial)

Use the standard composition workflow to attach readouts and embed the complete trained graph in a larger model. See the API reference for state methods and the official GRUCell and LSTMCell documentation for native gate definitions.

docs.title: Transforms
docs.text: Build · Layers

docs.title: Transforms
docs.text:
Transforms are the parameterless feature operations that wire reservoirs, readouts, and the layers between them into a DAG. They act only on the feature axis of (batch, time, features), so they compose with the outputs of any reservoir family, and with each other, regardless of what produced the tensor.

Layer Signature What it does Concatenate Concatenate() Joins inputs along the feature dimension Power (exponent, sign_preserving=False) Raises every feature to exponent; the power_augmented augmentation SelectiveExponentiation (index, exponent) Raises even- or odd-indexed features (parity of index) to exponent; the Ott augmentation SelectiveDropout (mask) Zeros a fixed boolean mask of features — deterministic, for ablations FeaturePartitioner (partitions, overlap) Splits features into overlapping circular slices, returns a list — feeds parallel reservoirs

All five import from resdag directly. Two details: Concatenate takes any number of inputs that agree on every dimension but the last, and FeaturePartitioner requires the feature count to divide evenly by partitions, returning slices of width features // partitions + 2 * overlap with circular wrapping at the boundaries.

docs.title: The augmentation pattern
docs.text:
The most common composition: enrich a reservoir's states with a nonlinear copy, then let the readout see both the raw input and the augmented features. The ott_esn factory wires this pattern, squaring the even-indexed states, but any reservoir can take the middle position:

from resdag import (
    CGReadoutLayer, Concatenate, ESNLayer, ESNModel,
    SelectiveExponentiation, reservoir_input,
)

inp = reservoir_input(3)
states = ESNLayer(500, feedback_size=3)(inp)    # any reservoir slots in here
augmented = SelectiveExponentiation(index=0, exponent=2.0)(states)
features = Concatenate()(inp, augmented)        # readout sees input + states
out = CGReadoutLayer(3 + 500, 3, name="output")(features)
model = ESNModel(inp, out)

Swap SelectiveExponentiation for Power(2.0) and the result is power_augmented; drop the Concatenate and the readout sees only the augmented states. One thing to track is the readout's in_features: concatenation adds feature dimensions, and the readout must be constructed with the sum.

Both Power and SelectiveExponentiation exponentiate signed reservoir states. tanh states live in [-1, 1], so a non-integer exponent on a negative base returns nan under the default torch.pow, and a negative exponent on a zero base returns inf — silently, with no diagnostic. Even integers (2.0, the default) and odd integers (3.0) are always safe. For a non-integer exponent on signed states, pass sign_preserving=True, which applies sign(x) * abs(x) ** exponent and stays finite for negative bases:

Power(0.5, sign_preserving=True)        # sqrt(|x|), signed; finite on [-1, 1]

These five layers are not a closed set. Any nn.Module that maps (batch, time, features) to the same layout composes the same way; these are the ones the premade factories use.

docs.title: Readouts
docs.text: Build

docs.title: Readouts
docs.text:
A readout maps collected reservoir states to outputs. Every readout is an ordinary linear layer underneath, so any reservoir family's states can feed any readout, and both training paths remain available: a one-pass algebraic solve, or gradient descent with any PyTorch optimizer.

The solver is a pluggable contract: a new readout implements solve(states, targets) and inherits shape handling, validation, and parameter copy-back from the ReadoutLayer base class. Several solvers ship with the library — rd.ESN defaults to AutoReadoutLayer, checking numerical suitability while preserving the L2 objective and requested penalty. Lower-level model factories retain RidgeReadoutLayer, a direct Cholesky solve; CGReadoutLayer solves the ridge problem iteratively by conjugate gradient; and SVDReadoutLayer, PinvReadoutLayer, and IncrementalRidgeReadoutLayer cover rank-deficient, pseudo-inverse, and streaming cases. Theory · Readout solvers tabulates which to reach for.

Start with the practical solver guide for automatic fitting, diagnostics, explicit algorithms and MPS device policies.

  • CGReadoutLayer

    Family-agnostic trainable maps — the name contract, ridge regression by conjugate gradient, bias and precision semantics, and the solve hook for custom solvers.

docs.title: Choose and configure a readout
docs.text:
All readout-bearing factories accept readout and readout_kwargs separately from reservoir options:

import resdag as rd

model = rd.classic_esn(
    reservoir_size=300, feedback_size=3, output_size=3,
    readout="svd", readout_alpha=1e-6,
    readout_kwargs={"rcond": 1e-12, "trainable": True},
)

Names are auto, ridge, cholesky, cg, lsmr, svd, pinv, incremental, rls, and fista; a ReadoutLayer subclass also works. readout_kwargs passes additional constructor options and can override alpha, bias, and name. Input/output widths are fixed by the architecture. The pseudoinverse solver has no ridge penalty, so readout_alpha does not apply to pinv.

With readout="auto", readout_kwargs accepts solver, solve_dtype, rcond and cpu_fallback as well as the common readout options. Its solver choices are "auto", "primal", "dual", "qr" and "svd". The use_float64 and gram_dtype arguments below belong to other readout classes, not Auto.

trainable=True enables gradient updates to the same readout after an algebraic fit. Reservoir trainability is controlled independently by the factory's trainable argument. For streaming fits, choose readout="incremental" and call ESNTrainer.fit_stream.

SVD and pseudoinverse solves operate directly on the design matrix; they do not allocate an unused feature-by-feature Gram matrix. Direct ridge and incremental ridge form their Gram in the solve dtype (float64 by default) on every device. Setting gram_dtype=torch.float32 explicitly can speed up a well-conditioned CUDA fit, but can lose accuracy for correlated states. CG's automatic Gram dtype remains input precision on CUDA and solve precision on CPU.

For an explicit iterative fit without a feature-by-feature Gram matrix, choose readout="lsmr". It uses SciPy on CPU in float64, preserves the ridge penalty and unpenalized intercept, and reports per-output convergence. Accelerator inputs use a warned CPU bridge. It retains the feature matrix, so this is distinct from streaming over a long sequence.

docs.title: Stable fits and streaming checkpoints
docs.text:
With an intercept, batch solvers center features and targets before forming products. Incremental ridge merges centered chunk covariances and running means; it avoids subtracting large raw moments. Chunking preserves the same ridge objective, with ordinary floating-point differences.

use_float64=True keeps incremental accumulators and RLS inverse-correlation state in float64 even when model parameters are converted with .float() or .to(dtype=torch.float32). With use_float64=False, working buffers follow the parameter dtype. MPS cannot store float64 statistics: keep those readouts on CPU, or explicitly opt out for operations supported by your installed PyTorch. Ordinary ridge models fitted on CPU still support float32 MPS inference.

Incremental checkpoints now carry a statistics-format version. Legacy raw-moment checkpoints load and upgrade with a warning when data was accumulated. Already lost precision cannot be recovered: reset accumulators and refit highly offset or ill-conditioned streams before continuing. New checkpoints retain only one feature-by-feature Gram buffer; centered statistics do not double that storage.

Fresh RLS partial_fit starts from the same zero coefficient prior as fit_online; delta controls its strength. FISTA's optional power estimate is checked with backtracking before accepting a proximal update, including when the initial power vector misses a nonzero eigenspace.

docs.title: Cg readout
docs.text: Build · Readouts

docs.title: CGReadoutLayer
docs.text:
A readout is the trainable map from features to predictions, and it is deliberately family-agnostic: it sees (batch, time, features) and never asks which reservoir produced them. Any reservoir's states — or any transform of them — feed any readout.

ReadoutLayer is the base class: an nn.Linear applied independently per timestep (3-D input is flattened to (batch*time, features) and back), carrying a name for multi-readout DAGs, frozen by default, and exposing a fit(states, targets) interface for algebraic training. CGReadoutLayer performs ridge regression by conjugate gradient on the normal equations rather than gradient descent:

from resdag import CGReadoutLayer

readout = CGReadoutLayer(
    in_features=500,   # feature dim of whatever feeds it
    out_features=3,
    name="output",     # the key you pass in targets={...} when fitting
    alpha=1e-6,        # ridge strength; tune on a log scale
    bias=True,         # False solves the raw, uncentered problem
    max_iter=100,      # CG iteration cap
    tol=1e-5,          # CG convergence tolerance
)

In practice alpha has the largest effect on fit quality of any training parameter; sweep it logarithmically (1e-8 to 1e-2) before tuning anything else. ESNTrainer.fit(targets={"output": y}) matches targets to readouts by name: the key in the targets dict must equal the layer's name.

docs.title: Bias semantics
docs.text:
With bias=True the solver centers states and targets and recovers an unpenalized intercept afterwards — the standard ridge-with-intercept formulation. With bias=False it solves the raw, uncentered normal equations, because centering without an intercept at predict time would shift every prediction.

CG forms a full feature-by-feature Gram matrix: this is an iterative solve, not a matrix-free one. Centering happens before the products to avoid subtracting large nearly equal raw moments.

docs.title: Precision
docs.text: Two parameters control numerical precision. use_float64=True (the default) runs the CG iterations in float64. gram_dtype controls the Gram-matrix products, which dominate the cost: it defaults to float64 on CPU and to the input dtype on CUDA, because consumer GPUs execute float64 at a fraction of float32 throughput — forcing full precision there can make ESN training slower on GPU than on CPU. Pass gram_dtype=torch.float64 to force float64 everywhere; the numerics are covered in Readout solvers.

docs.title: Custom solvers
docs.text:
fit() owns the bookkeeping — flattening, sample-count and shape validation, copy-back into the nn.Linear parameters — and delegates the algebra to solve. A new solver overrides one method:

import torch
from resdag import ReadoutLayer

class LstsqReadout(ReadoutLayer):
    def solve(self, states, targets):
        # already flattened: states (N, in_features), targets (N, out_features)
        if self.bias is None:
            return torch.linalg.lstsq(states, targets).solution, None
        mean_x = states.mean(0, keepdim=True)
        mean_y = targets.mean(0, keepdim=True)
        coefs = torch.linalg.lstsq(states - mean_x, targets - mean_y).solution
        intercept = (mean_y - mean_x @ coefs).squeeze(0)
        return coefs, intercept

Return a coefficient matrix of shape (in_features, out_features) and an intercept when bias=True (or None with bias=False); the base class transposes into the (out, in) layout nn.Linear expects and sets is_fitted. Because every readout is an ordinary nn.Linear underneath, gradient training remains available: pass trainable=True and fit it with any optimizer instead.

docs.text:

  • Architectures — multi-readout DAGs keyed by name
  • Layers reference — full signatures

docs.title: Choose and inspect a readout
docs.text:
A readout learns how to turn reservoir features into predictions. Start with the automatic readout: rd.ESN uses it by default. You can choose every algorithm and precision setting explicitly when an experiment needs them.

When a feature-by-feature matrix would be too large, the optional readout="lsmr" route performs an iterative CPU float64 fit without forming a Gram matrix. Select it explicitly; automatic selection below remains unchanged. Its convergence controls and device bridge are documented separately.

docs.title: Start with an automatic fit
docs.text:
import torch
import resdag as rd

t = torch.arange(400, dtype=torch.float64) * 0.05
train = torch.stack((t.sin(), t.cos()), dim=-1)

model = rd.ESN(
    reservoir_size=32, input_size=2, washout=30,
    alpha=1e-5, seed=7, dtype=torch.float64,
)
model.fit(train)
prediction = model.forecast(horizon=40)
assert prediction.shape == (40, 2)
assert torch.isfinite(prediction).all()

Scaling is learned from the training data, and forecasts return in the original units. Numerical solver selection does not tune alpha or other model settings. Use held-out autonomous forecasts to choose those settings.

docs.title: What automatic selection does
docs.text:
All automatic paths solve the same L2 problem:

\[ \min_{W,b}\;\lVert XW+b-Y\rVert_F^2+\alpha\lVert W\rVert_F^2. \]

With bias=True, features and targets are centered and an unpenalized intercept is recovered. With bias=False, the solver uses the original matrices and no intercept. alpha is the penalty on the sum of squared errors; the solver does not divide that sum by the number of samples.

Path When automatic fitting tries it Primal Cholesky At least as many samples as features; solves a feature-by-feature system Dual Cholesky More features than samples and alpha > 0; solves a sample-by-sample system Augmented QR A tall normal-equations fit fails its numerical checks Design-matrix SVD A wide unregularized fit, or when a previous path is unsuitable

The Cholesky checks include full inverse-norm conditioning, estimated product roundoff and a relative optimality residual. A diagonal ratio or a small residual alone can miss bad conditioning. QR also checks its triangular factor and the relative scale of the data and regularization blocks. Unsafe matrix products that can erase small but representable coefficients are rejected.

Automatic recovery keeps the requested alpha. It never adds rescue jitter, never truncates positive-ridge singular values and never substitutes a sparse or online-learning objective. These guards reduce numerical failure; they do not guarantee the best forecast or universally accurate coefficients.

docs.title: See what actually happened
docs.text:
Readout layers are ordinary PyTorch modules, so inspect the fitted graph:

readout = next(
    layer for layer in model.graph.modules()
    if isinstance(layer, rd.AutoReadoutLayer)
)
report = readout.last_solve
assert report is not None
print(report.solver, report.solve_device, report.solve_dtype)
print(report.alpha, report.relative_optimality_residual)

For a custom graph with several readouts, inspect each one separately.

Report field Meaning requested_solver, solver Requested policy and the algorithm that completed the solve alpha Requested, unchanged L2 penalty input_device, input_dtype Placement and precision of the feature tensor received by this readout solve_device, solve_dtype Placement and precision actually used for fitting n_samples, n_features Flattened training matrix dimensions condition_estimate Estimated conditioning of the regularized normal system; methods use different norm estimates roundoff_estimate Estimated normal-equations roundoff; None for the final QR/SVD path relative_optimality_residual Scale-relative error in the ridge first-order equations relative_prediction_residual Training prediction error divided by the centered target norm when fitting an intercept, otherwise the raw target norm fallback_reasons Reasons previous paths were rejected or a CPU bridge was needed precision_warning Explanation when the final positive-ridge decomposition remains severely ill-conditioned, otherwise None

Residuals describe the working-precision solution before it is cast back to the input and parameter dtype. They use the features/targets seen by the readout, including workflow preprocessing and centering for an intercept. They are not forecast errors measured in the original physical units. Strong regularization can legitimately produce a large prediction residual. A tiny optimality residual does not prove that the coefficients, or an autonomous forecast, are accurate.

last_solve starts as None and records the last successful algebraic solve. It is immutable Python metadata and is not included in state_dict(). Loading weights into a fresh layer restores its fitted flag, but does not manufacture a past solve report. Moving a layer leaves the report describing its past solve.

docs.title: Force an algorithm
docs.text:
Choose "primal", "dual", "qr" or "svd" through solver:

forced = rd.ESN(
    reservoir_size=32, input_size=2, washout=30,
    alpha=1e-5, seed=7, dtype=torch.float64,
    readout_kwargs={"solver": "svd", "solve_dtype": torch.float64},
)
forced.fit(train)
assert torch.isfinite(forced.forecast(horizon=10)).all()

A forced algorithm stays selected. Unsafe normal equations warn when they can be computed; unrepresentable products or failed factorizations raise instead. Forced QR raises when rank, conditioning or data scale makes that path unreliable. Unregularized wide QR is unsupported: use SVD for that minimum-norm problem. If a device bridge is allowed, it preserves the forced algorithm.

Keeping Auto and setting readout_kwargs={"solver": "svd"} retains Auto's diagnostics and device policy. Selecting readout="svd" instead constructs the standalone SVDReadoutLayer, with its own precision options and no Auto CPU bridge. Fit that explicit class on a supported device, or fit on CPU and move the fitted model for inference.

For a preset graph from a lower-level factory, request automatic selection explicitly. Those factories retain their "ridge" default:

graph = rd.classic_esn(
    reservoir_size=32, feedback_size=2, output_size=2,
    readout="auto", readout_alpha=1e-5,
    readout_kwargs={"solver": "svd"}, seed=7, dtype=torch.float64,
)
custom = rd.Model(graph=graph, washout=30)
custom.fit(train)
assert custom.forecast(horizon=10).shape == (10, 2)

In a functional DAG, attach rd.AutoReadoutLayer(features, outputs, alpha=...) with the same layer(x) syntax as other readouts. Set trainable=True when you want an optimizer to refine the fitted linear parameters. Algebraic fit does not differentiate through the solve; subsequent forward calls preserve ordinary PyTorch gradients and fitting preserves the parameter objects.

docs.title: Precision and Apple MPS
docs.text:
AutoReadoutLayer defaults to float64 fitting on CPU and CUDA. On MPS it first tries native float32 normal equations. Cholesky substitution uses native triangular solves rather than assuming every PyTorch Cholesky helper is available. The fitted weights stay on their model device and keep their dtype.

If MPS needs QR/SVD, or an accelerator lacks a required operation, the default policy explicitly fits on CPU in float64. It emits a RuntimeWarning, records the reason and actual solve device/dtype, and returns coefficients to the input device. MPS cannot store float64 tensors, so requesting float64 fitting there also requires this bridge. Operation availability depends on the installed PyTorch version.

Disable the bridge when an experiment must remain on its chosen device:

no_bridge = rd.ESN(
    reservoir_size=32, input_size=2, washout=30,
    alpha=1e-5, seed=7, dtype=torch.float32,
    readout_kwargs={"cpu_fallback": False},
)

Move the whole model and training tensors to the same device as usual. Fitting raises with an explanation if the selected device needs a disabled CPU bridge. Set solve_dtype=torch.float32 or torch.float64 to choose working precision explicitly. Precision options do not change the model's parameter dtype. Measure runtime and held-out forecasts for your actual shapes and device; there is no universal solver speed ranking.

docs.title: Very small penalties and SVD limits
docs.text:
For SVD, a positive penalty uses the filter s / (s² + alpha). The implementation evaluates it in scaled form, avoiding overflow when squaring large finite singular values, while preserving the penalty. When alpha is a normal representable working-dtype scalar, small singular values are divided directly by alpha to avoid magnifying subnormal rounding through repeated division by sqrt(alpha).

That filter improvement does not remove finite-precision limits in centering, decomposition, projection or parameter storage. With nearly dependent features and a very small positive alpha, large opposing coefficients can cancel on the training data. Both SVD and augmented least squares can then have inaccurate coefficients despite small training and optimality residuals. Automatic fitting warns and records precision_warning when its final conditioning check detects this risk. Rescale features, explicitly choose a stronger penalty or use higher working precision; validate autonomous forecasts independently.

For alpha=0, SVD returns a minimum-norm least-squares fit after dropping singular values at or below rcond * s_max. Auto defaults rcond to working epsilon times max(n_samples, n_features); the explicit SVDReadoutLayer defaults to 1e-15. rcond=0 retains every nonzero computed singular value, which can amplify noise or require coefficients outside the parameter dtype. The cutoff does not apply to positive-ridge SVD. alpha and an explicit rcond must be finite and nonnegative; invalid live settings are rejected when solving.

docs.title: Updating solver settings from the previous preset default
docs.text:
readout_kwargs belongs to the selected readout class. Auto uses solve_dtype, not the older direct solver's use_float64/gram_dtype pair. Its solver names also differ: "primal" means primal Cholesky, while the explicit ridge solver's "solve" means LU.

# Automatic selection with an explicitly chosen working dtype.
automatic = rd.ESN(
    reservoir_size=32, input_size=2,
    readout_kwargs={"solve_dtype": torch.float32},
)

# Select the direct ridge class when you require its LU algorithm/options.
direct = rd.ESN(
    reservoir_size=32, input_size=2, readout="ridge",
    readout_kwargs={
        "solver": "solve", "use_float64": False, "gram_dtype": torch.float32,
    },
)

Passing use_float64 or gram_dtype to Auto raises an unexpected-keyword error; there is no silent translation or discarded setting. Explicit readout choices such as "svd", "cg" and "ridge" retain their own constructor options.

Continue with the solver mathematics, readout API reference, or custom solver extension.
