docs.title: Citing the methods
docs.text:
ResDAG implements published methods. Alongside the software entry, cite the original papers for the methods your work uses.

You used Cite Echo State Networks (ESNLayer, any premade model) Jaeger, The "echo state" approach to analysing and training recurrent neural networks, GMD Report 148 (2001) ESN design and tuning practice Lukoševičius, A Practical Guide to Applying Echo State Networks, in Neural Networks: Tricks of the Trade, Springer (2012) State-augmented chaos architecture (ott_esn, power_augmented) Pathak, Hunt, Girvan, Lu & Ott, Model-Free Prediction of Large Spatiotemporally Chaotic Systems from Data: A Reservoir Computing Approach, Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 024102 (2018) Next-generation reservoir computing (NGReservoir, NGCell) Gauthier, Bollt, Griffith & Barbosa, Next generation reservoir computing, Nat. Commun. 12, 5564 (2021)

Attribution

The squared-state architecture is colloquially called the "Ott ESN" — the citable source is Pathak et al. (2018), where Ott is the senior author, not a paper by Ott alone.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Project

docs.title: Contributing to ResDAG
docs.text:
ResDAG is a PyTorch-native reservoir computing library. Contributions are welcome — components, fixes, docs, benchmarks. This guide covers the mechanics; the design rationale lives in the documentation.

Looking for something to work on? Start with the roadmap, the canonical Pending/WIP/Done tracker. Update its task status and verification evidence in the implementation PR. Related issues can still use the type:epic, pillar:* and status:ready labels for discussion and dependency tracking.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/El3ssar/ResDAG && cd ResDAG
uv sync --locked --extra dev # lint/format/test toolchain from the committed lock
uv run pytest --no-cov -q    # full suite, including golden forecast regressions

pip install -e ".[dev]" works too if you don't use uv. Add hpo (Optuna) or docs (MkDocs + the figure pipeline) as needed — e.g. uv sync --locked --extra dev --extra docs or pip install -e ".[dev,docs]".

Rendered diagram checks also need the Graphviz system executable: install it with brew install graphviz on macOS or sudo apt-get install graphviz on Debian/Ubuntu, then verify dot -V. The development extra supplies its Python package. Local tests skip only checks that require rendering when these tools are unavailable; DOT export and error checks still run. CI provisions Graphviz and treats missing rendering tools as a failure.

docs.title: Quality gate
docs.text:
Run before pushing:

uv run ruff check src/ tests/ tools/ci_environment.py
uv run black --check src/ tests/ tools/ci_environment.py
uv run mypy src/resdag/
uv run pytest --no-cov -q          # full suite

docs.title: Type checking
docs.text:
CI type-checks the whole package — mypy src/resdag/, not a single file — and the tree is kept at zero errors. There is deliberately no per-module baseline and no disable_error_code escape hatch in pyproject.toml: new and changed code is gated immediately, so a typing error is a failing build, not a warning. The only standing allowance is ignore_missing_imports (for untyped third-party libraries such as pytorch_symbolic).

If your change surfaces a type error — even one that looks pre-existing — fix it in your PR with a real annotation/narrowing rather than suppressing it. Reach for cast/assert only when a runtime invariant genuinely guarantees the narrowing (and say so in a short comment); never use them, or a blanket # type: ignore, to paper over a possible-None/wrong-type bug. If you must ignore, use a specific # type: ignore[code] with a one-line justification.

docs.title: Fast local iteration — run only the affected tests
docs.text:
The full suite takes a few minutes. While iterating, run only the tests that your change can affect, computed from a static first-party import graph:

# What would run for your branch vs. main, and why:
uv run python tools/affected_tests.py --explain

# Run exactly that subset:
uv run pytest --no-cov -q $(uv run python tools/affected_tests.py --format args)

The selector errs toward running more tests, never fewer (broad-impact changes such as pyproject.toml, conftest.py, or a package __init__ fan out to the whole suite). Still do one full pytest run before you push.

docs.title: Selective CI
docs.text: Pull-request CI runs the same selector and tests only the affected subset, so a typical single-module PR finishes in seconds instead of minutes. The full suite is the safety net and still runs on every merge to main and on a nightly schedule. To force a full run on a PR, add the ci-full label.

docs.title: Reproducible environments and dependency updates
docs.text:
Pull-request, nightly, release, benchmark, and documentation gates install the versions in uv.lock, including development tools and the editable-build backend. CI checks that the lock matches pyproject.toml before installing. CPU jobs use the matching PyTorch CPU wheel and omit its CUDA-only dependency tree. Python 3.11 through 3.14 all run against this baseline.

To reproduce that environment in a fresh virtual environment:

python -m pip install uv==0.13.3
python tools/ci_environment.py --mode locked --extras dev,hpo

Use --extras docs for the documentation environment; development tools are always included. The installer prints the resolved packages and runs pip check to catch missing or conflicting dependencies.

The separate Latest dependency compatibility workflow runs the full test matrix and a strict documentation build every Wednesday and on manual dispatch. It resolves current packages within the declared dependency ranges, retaining the CPU PyTorch wheel. Its failures reveal upstream compatibility changes without silently changing the normal PR baseline. Reproduce it with python tools/ci_environment.py --mode latest --extras dev,hpo. The existing CI and Documentation workflows also accept a dependency-mode choice on manual dispatch, so either environment can be verified on a branch before merge. Pull requests always use the locked baseline.

When changing dependencies, update pyproject.toml, run uv lock, and commit both files. For an intentional upgrade, prefer uv lock --upgrade-package NAME and review the resulting lock diff. Run the full suite and strict docs build before proposing the new baseline.

docs.title: Test markers and GPU checks
docs.text:
The test suite mirrors src/resdag/. Markers:

  • gpu — CUDA variants, auto-skip on machines without a GPU
  • benchmark — performance assertions, deselected by default (pytest -m benchmark to run; they assert the GPU beats the CPU at scale)

The weekly GPU workflow requires a self-hosted runner carrying the gpu label. After provisioning it, set the repository Actions variable RESDAG_GPU_RUNNER_ENABLED=true to enable scheduled GPU runs. Manual dispatch works independently of that variable. A skipped schedule is not CUDA verification; only a completed run on a CUDA runner provides that evidence.

docs.title: Golden-forecast regression fixtures
docs.text:
tests/test_models/test_golden_forecast.py pins the behaviour of ESNModel.forecast for each premade model against committed golden trajectories under tests/fixtures/golden_forecast/ — a fully-seeded warmup → forecast on Lorenz-63, in CPU float64. It fails on any drift in the forecast path. If you change that path — or the canonical lorenz / prepare_esn_data generators it builds on — regenerate the fixtures and review the diff before committing:

uv run python tools/regen_golden_forecasts.py --check   # verify only (drift check, non-zero exit on drift)
uv run python tools/regen_golden_forecasts.py --all      # regenerate every fixture

The model specs, data splits, metric, and tolerances live in tests/test_models/golden_forecast.py, shared by the test and the tool so they can never disagree.

docs.title: Commit messages and releases
docs.text:
Releases are live. Every push to main whose commits since the last tag warrant a release publishes automatically (version bump, tag, GitHub release, PyPI via trusted publishing). Never rename release.yml — PyPI trusted publishing is bound to that filename. The mechanics below describe what runs.

Releases are fully automated from conventional commits — there are no manual tags or version edits. On every push to main, python-semantic-release parses the commits since the last release:

prefix effect feat: ... minor release (0.5.0 → 0.6.0) fix: ..., perf: ... patch release (0.5.0 → 0.5.1) feat!: ... or BREAKING CHANGE: footer major (including 0.x → 1.0; major_on_zero=true) docs:, chore:, ci:, refactor:, test:, style:, build: no release

A release rewrites __version__ in src/resdag/__init__.py and the mirrored version field in CITATION.cff (both are listed in version_variables, so they stay in lock-step automatically), tags vX.Y.Z, publishes a GitHub release with generated notes, and uploads to PyPI. Documentation deploys on the same push, and version strings in the docs substitute automatically.

Pull requests are squash-merged, and the PR title becomes the commit that decides the bump — so PR titles must be conventional (feat: add Rössler topology). CI checks the title format on every PR. Inside your branch, commit however you like; only the squash title counts.

docs.title: Recovering a failed package publication
docs.text: Treat test results, the GitHub release, and PyPI publication as separate outcomes. If PyPI reports that a filename belonged to a deleted upload, that version cannot be reused: leave the existing GitHub tag and artifacts intact and advance to a fresh patch version through a fix(release): ... commit. Rerunning the unchanged release cannot resolve the collision. In particular, the first 1.x PyPI publication must skip 1.0.0, whose filenames are reserved by a deleted historical upload.

docs.title: Adding components
docs.text:
Every component type is an open set with one extension point:

component how docs page Topology (graph) @register_graph_topology("name", **defaults) on a NetworkX generator generated automatically from the registry Topology (matrix) @register_matrix_topology("name", **defaults) on an fn(n) -> matrix generated automatically Input/feedback initializer @register_input_feedback("name") on a function or InputFeedbackInitializer subclass generated automatically Readout subclass ReadoutLayer, implement public solve(states, targets) one file in docs/build/readouts/ Reservoir family implement the ReservoirCell contract, wrap in a BaseReservoirLayer subclass one file in docs/build/layers/ Premade architecture factory function returning a model, in src/resdag/models/ one file in docs/build/architectures/

Registered topologies and initializers document themselves: their docs pages (figure, parameters, usage) are generated from the registry at build time. For the other component types, drop a Markdown file in the listed folder — navigation and index cards pick it up automatically.

New components need tests (place them in the mirror location under tests/) and, for anything with tunable structure, a figure — see below.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
uv run mkdocs serve            # live preview at 127.0.0.1:8000/ResDAG/
uv run mkdocs build --strict   # link-checking build, run before pushing
  • Colors and fonts for the entire site and every figure live in docs/_tooling/theme.json. After editing: uv run python docs/_tooling/apply_theme.py --figures
  • Figures are generated by the per-category scripts in docs/_tooling/figures/ — never edit images in docs/assets/figures/ by hand.
  • The token block in docs/css/notebook.css between the ===== TOKENS ===== markers is generated; edit theme.json instead.
  • The landing page is a single file: docs/overrides/home.html.

docs.title: Pull request checklist
docs.text:
• Conventional PR title (it becomes the release-deciding commit)
  • ruff check, black --check, and pytest pass locally
  • New code has tests; new components have docs (see table above)
  • mkdocs build --strict passes if you touched docs
  • Figures regenerated via the scripts if you changed visuals

docs.title: Ecosystem
docs.text: Project

docs.title: pytorch_symbolic
docs.text: ResDAG's composition layer is built on pytorch_symbolic by Szymon Mikler. It provides the symbolic tracing that turns layer calls on placeholder tensors into executable model graphs — the mechanism behind Input, the functional API, and the model class. Without it, the central premise of this library — reservoir models composed as arbitrary DAGs — would not exist in its current form. Credit where it is due.

docs.title: TSDynamics
docs.text:
TSDynamics is a companion library of dynamical systems by the same author: a catalog of chaotic ODEs, maps, and delay systems with a uniform integration interface, plus Lyapunov analysis utilities.

TSDynamics generates trajectories and ResDAG learns to forecast them. Install pip install "resdag[dynamics]" for the tested optional integration. The example below uses TSDynamics 6's systems and analysis namespaces. No TSDynamics import is required for the rest of ResDAG.

docs.title: Generate, train and forecast
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import torch
import tsdynamics as ts
import resdag as rd
from resdag.metrics import largest_lyapunov, valid_prediction_time
from resdag.utils import prepare_esn_data

system = ts.systems.Lorenz()
trajectory = system.run(final_time=140.0, dt=0.02, ic=[1.0, 1.0, 1.0]).after(20.0)
# Keep the recorded time axis: dt is the output sample spacing.
spacing = np.diff(trajectory.t)
assert np.allclose(spacing, spacing[0])
dt = float(spacing[0])
series = torch.tensor(trajectory.y, dtype=torch.float64).unsqueeze(0)

warmup_steps, train_steps, val_steps = 500, 4000, 1000
history = series[:, :warmup_steps + train_steps + 1]
mean = history.mean(dim=(0, 1), keepdim=True)
scale = history.std(dim=(0, 1), keepdim=True, correction=0).clamp_min(1e-8)
normalized = (series - mean) / scale  # training statistics apply to future data too
warmup, train, target, forecast_warmup, truth = prepare_esn_data(
    normalized, warmup_steps=warmup_steps, train_steps=train_steps,
    val_steps=val_steps,
)
model = rd.classic_esn(
    reservoir_size=200, feedback_size=3, output_size=3,
    seed=7, dtype=torch.float64,
)
rd.ESNTrainer(model).fit((warmup,), (train,), {"output": target})
prediction = model.forecast(forecast_warmup, horizon=truth.shape[1])
# First forecast sample and first truth sample describe the same next timestep.
score = valid_prediction_time(
    prediction, truth, units="lyapunov", dt=dt,
    lambda_max=largest_lyapunov("lorenz"),
)
physical_prediction = prediction * scale + mean
print(f"Valid prediction time: {score:.2f} Lyapunov times")

The canonical Lorenz exponent above assumes the default Lorenz parameters. For a customized continuous system, compute its exponent explicitly:

lambda_max = largest_lyapunov(system, dt=dt, final_time=500.0)
# Internally this calls ts.analysis.lyapunov_spectrum(system, ...).

Increase integration/averaging time and check convergence when interpreting that estimate. Data-based exponents are also available through largest_lyapunov(series, dt=dt, from_="data"); they are noisy diagnostics.

ResDAG currently consumes the trajectory's numeric samples through this explicit conversion. It does not automatically carry the time axis or system metadata through training. Preserve trajectory.t, its parameters and preprocessing statistics with experiment results. Resample irregularly spaced observations before using a fixed-step reservoir; the dt used for Lyapunov conversion must match the observations, including any stride or downsampling.

docs.text:

  • Contributing — development setup

docs.title: ESN workflow migration
docs.text:
rd.ESN now uses the same nn.Module workflow as a custom rd.Model. The previous facade is replaced directly. There is no compatibility class.

Previous behavior Current workflow NumPy input produced NumPy forecasts Supply floating Torch tensors; forecasts are Torch tensors. Trajectories use the optional dynamics integration. A batch of size one was squeezed The input layout is preserved: (1, T, D) forecasts stay (1, H, D). esn.forecast(100) supplied a positional horizon Use esn.forecast(horizon=100). The optional first argument is observation history. .model exposed the raw graph Use .graph; .workflow is the registered common Model child. .feature_size was inferred on fitting .input_size is known after construction with a width, build(width) or successful fitting. The facade had its own conversion and fitting logic Training-only scaling, explicit targets and forecasts all use Model's implementation.

Convert external arrays explicitly at the boundary:

import numpy as np
import torch
import resdag as rd

external_array = np.sin(np.linspace(0, 6, 100))[:, None]
series = torch.as_tensor(external_array, dtype=torch.float64)
esn = rd.ESN(reservoir_size=16, washout=5, seed=5).fit(series)
forecast = esn.forecast(horizon=10)
array_for_plotting = forecast.detach().cpu().numpy()
assert forecast.shape == (10, 1)

Automatic standardization is now the default. Fit uses training samples after washout and returns predictions in the original units. Set preprocessing=None when supplying your own transformed data. Washout may be zero.

Build before attaching an optimizer so it sees every parameter:

trainable = rd.ESN(
    reservoir_size=12, input_size=1, washout=5,
    dtype=torch.float64, readout_kwargs={"trainable": True}, seed=6,
)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(trainable.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
trainable.fit(series)
parameter_ids = [id(parameter) for parameter in trainable.parameters()]
trainable.build(1)  # Same-width calls preserve the existing parameters.
assert parameter_ids == [id(parameter) for parameter in trainable.parameters()]

Without a width, first fitting stages a candidate and attaches it after success. A failed first fit leaves the preset unbuilt. Refitting preserves the existing workflow, parameters and streaming state when fitting fails.

Ordinary esn(x) is differentiable and carries state between calls. Reset it when switching independent sequences, or thread explicit states with forward_stateless. Forecasting resynchronizes on supplied history or the cached training tail and begins at the immediate unseen sample.

Use .to(...), .float() and .double() for standard module conversion. A conversion before lazy fitting fixes the current placement; subsequent data must match. There are no facade-specific .device or .dtype shadow fields. A fixed seed initializes the whole preset, including unfitted readout weights, while restoring the surrounding Torch CPU/available accelerator RNG streams. Unseeded construction follows ordinary Torch random-state behavior.

A state_dict includes the fitted workflow and width. Recreate the same preset architecture/settings before loading; device and dtype may differ. Metadata checks cannot verify the full behavior of arbitrary custom Python functions. Use model.save("run.pt") and rd.load("run.pt") to restore the complete architecture and fitted state without reconstructing the DAG; see model artifacts.

The current ESN and Model checkpoint metadata version is 2. Custom preprocessing and named trajectory clocks are explicit parts of that schema. Older common-workflow checkpoints are rejected with a reconstruction/refit message; no compatibility loader or automatic converter is provided.

Custom input_transforms={"input": module} and output_transforms={"output": module} follow the same reversible preprocessing protocol as Model. Their original modules remain registered before a lazy build and remain the fitted workflow's modules afterward. See custom preprocessing and named trajectories.

docs.title: Public boundaries and checkpoint safety
docs.text:
The API sweep keeps the existing package organization and supported extension interfaces. Use rd.hpo.run_hpo, rd.hpo.LOSSES and rd.hpo.get_study_summary for advanced tuning; duplicate top-level aliases are removed. Internal tuning context builders and step validators are private. Custom memory estimators still receive MemoryContext, and estimate_memory remains a supported extension helper.

Ordinary raw graph/parallel/ensemble checkpoints now use restricted Torch loading. Their metadata and custom extra state must use supported tensors and primitive containers; save-time validation rejects executable Python objects. Full Python files require explicit load_full(path, trusted=True). Complete portable Model.save/rd.load remains the recommended workflow. Failed saves preserve an existing destination through an atomic replacement.

docs.title: Dataset generators return raw values
docs.text:
lorenz, rossler, henon and mackey_glass now default to normalize=None, matching NARMA, sine and Kuramoto–Sivashinsky. Previously, these four generators standardized the complete returned window before users split training and test data, letting held-out observations affect the training scale. Newly generated series therefore have different units unless normalization is explicit.

For the common workflow, pass the raw training prefix to model.fit; the model learns its scaling from training observations and forecasts in original units. For raw graph workflows, split first and use prepare_esn_data(..., normalize=True) or fit normalize_data statistics on the training prefix and reuse them for later observations.

normalize="standard" retains the previous transformation exactly for a fixed generator configuration and seed. It scales the full returned window, so use it only when that window belongs entirely to one training split or when reproducing an explicitly declared global-normalization experiment. Saved model weights and already materialized data are unchanged. See data and datasets.

docs.title: Graph tooling and PyTorch integration
docs.text: ResDAG keeps layer(input) functional construction. The common rd.Model owns the original graph once, so optimizers, device moves, hooks and state dictionaries see ordinary PyTorch modules. Users do not need private graph attributes to build, fit or run a model.

docs.title: Which tool does which job?
docs.text:
Tool Useful role Current boundary pytorch_symbolic Declare branches, shared nodes and named model boundaries with layer(input) syntax. Retained construction backend. ResDAG validates its execution plans internally. PyTorch nn.Module Own layers, parameters and buffers; compose trained models inside larger networks. Supported by rd.Model, with carried recurrent state and original-unit predictions. PyTorch FX Capture or transform the surrounding network while keeping the reservoir as one module call. Use a leaf tracer, shown below. Direct tracing through the entire workflow is unsupported. torch.export Produce a tensor computation graph for deployment when a module satisfies export's constraints. No general ResDAG export guarantee. A stateful workflow, its fitting logic and its Python metadata are not a deployment graph contract. Graphviz/DOT Render the declared architecture. Unified Model.save/ESN.save exports SVG/PNG/PDF/DOT with named ports, preprocessing and delayed feedback; inspection executes no layers.

Replacing functional construction with FX would require tracing a computation before recovering the reservoir-specific ports, fitting stages and state rules. That would add a second interpretation of the same model. Keep the current constructor and use standard tools at the boundaries where they already work.

This is a scoped implementation decision, not a claim that the existing backend is permanent. A future replacement must preserve functional syntax, shared-module ownership, multiple heads, fitting order, checkpoint behavior and explicit recurrent state, with measured benefits.

docs.title: Trace a larger PyTorch pipeline
docs.text:
An FX leaf remains a call_module operation: FX records the call without executing or tracing into the reservoir. The captured network shares that same model instance. The same leaf rule supports the rd.ESN preset. Resetting either reference resets the same reservoir. The common model guide contains a complete executable example.

Regression tests verify tensor and named multi-head pipelines, unchanged state and hooks during capture, parameter identity, prediction/state parity, upstream gradients, chunked state carry and dtype moves. These checks run on the minimum supported Torch version as part of the regular suite. They do not establish compatibility with every third-party graph transformation.

Direct torch.fx.symbolic_trace(pipeline) currently reaches the workflow's concrete tensor validation and fails. A direct strict export probe of a fitted recurrent pipeline on Torch 2.10 also fails on a tensor with grad_fn. Neither failure justifies silently freezing state or removing validation. Deployment export needs its own explicit-state contract and acceptance tests.

See PyTorch's FX documentation for leaf tracing and control-flow limits, and its export programming model for graph capture and state constraints.

docs.title: Phase five: measure before optimizing
docs.text:
The goal is fast, accurate autonomous forecasts with the same customizable model interface. A faster fit does not establish an accurate forecast. Keep training speed, forecasting speed, numerical agreement and forecast skill as separate measurements.

Current measurements

The first-increment results below precede the correction to independent initialization streams. The continuation report records fresh tuning on the corrected streams, saved-model parity and measured execution costs. Newly seeded models can differ from the historical results on this page.

docs.title: Agreed accuracy target
docs.text:
The maintainer approved these choices on 23 October 2026:

  • Aim for a median 7–8 Lyapunov times over several reservoir seeds and previously unseen forecast starting points. Publish every observation and its spread; an unusually successful forecast does not establish success.
  • Count the uninterrupted prefix whose per-step normalized RMS error stays strictly below 0.3. Also publish the result at 0.5.
  • Estimate each component's variation from training observations only. Do not change the denominator when extending the forecast horizon.
  • Compute a horizon for each seed and starting point, then aggregate those horizons. Taking the first crossing of a median error curve can conceal failures in individual forecasts.

For a forecast prediction[t, j], reference truth[t, j] and fixed training standard deviations scale[j], the per-step error is sqrt(mean_j(((prediction - truth) / scale)**2)). The first invalid or nonfinite step ends the valid prefix. Convert its length to Lyapunov times with steps * actual_dt * lambda_max. Record the system parameters, integration method, time step and exponent source. If the whole evaluated horizon remains valid, report that result as a lower bound.

Seven or eight Lyapunov times is a target for the experiment program. The library does not guarantee that score for an arbitrary model or dataset.

docs.title: First increment: preparation and regression evidence
docs.text:
Repair the existing comparison harness before publishing new rankings:

  1. Generate one raw trajectory shared by the adapters. Fit scaling on the admitted training observations for each workload, never the entire series.
  2. Use inputs at indices 0..T-1 and next-sample targets at 1..T. Synchronize forecasting on observed history ending at T; the first unseen target is at T+1. Score only future observations.
  3. Check the first emitted sample with an independent time-index oracle. Every adapter must emit the same physical time, including its first step.
  4. Pass all declared hyperparameters through the adapters and honor requested timing repeats. Keep unavailable optional libraries as explicit skips; an execution failure in an available adapter must make the runner fail.
  5. Freeze classical and state-augmented model recipes. Compare the phase-three and phase-four implementations using the same raw data, initial weights, scaling, precision, solver, seeds, histories and forecast horizons.

The existing Lorenz golden tests cover short prefixes and limited quality floors. They remain useful regression tests, but do not prove the 7–8 target or Rössler performance. Do not regenerate fixtures to make a loss disappear.

The public valid_prediction_time currently normalizes using the supplied truth window and reduces batch errors before taking the first crossing. Keep that documented behavior available. The phase-five experiment protocol uses fixed training scales and individual horizons explicitly; changing the public metric requires a separate API decision.

docs.title: Frozen model regression results
docs.text:
On 23 October 2026, source-isolated runs compared phase three (00ca741) with merged phase four (0b546d6). All 36 complete forecasts and fitted tensor fingerprints matched. These are deterministic float64 CPU workloads, with no stochastic training noise. They do not establish unchanged results for every architecture or an earlier major version.

System / model Seeds × origins Median at 0.3 Range at 0.3 Median at 0.5 Lorenz / vanilla 3 × 3 3.659 0.561–5.379 3.713 Lorenz / OTT 3 × 3 3.151 0.561–5.252 3.622 Rössler / vanilla 6 × 3 5.855 3.396–8.376 5.891

Horizons are in Lyapunov times; none reached the ten-Lyapunov-time scoring limit. The starting points come from one held-out portion of each trajectory; some Rössler forecast windows overlap. The spread is descriptive, not a confidence interval for independent trajectories. These frozen recipes establish an implementation baseline, not the best achievable accuracy.

Reproduce the matched comparison from the repository with the HPO and dynamics extras installed on Python 3.12 or newer:

python benchmarks/accuracy_regression.py --before 00ca741 --after 0b546d6 --artifacts-dir /tmp/resdag-frozen-accuracy --output frozen-accuracy.json

Use a new artifact directory for each run. The committed measurements record data hashes, recipes, per-seed/origin scores, source import paths and artifact hashes. Fit/forecast wall times there are exploratory observations, not paired timing evidence.

docs.title: Then: improve models without tuning on the test set
docs.text:
Use chronological training, validation and final-test data. Select time step, reservoir size, initialization, leak, input/bias scales and readout settings with validation data only. Freeze the selected recipe before scoring the final test trajectories. Use the existing Optuna workflow, its seed/origin controls and its complete model artifacts rather than building a second tuning engine.

Distinguish these two questions:

  • Accuracy regression: did the same model and data lose skill after an implementation change? Match weights and settings; compare coefficients, states, full forecasts and per-origin horizons.
  • Best practical result: how good can each library get with the same search budget? Let each use its ordinary APIs, record actual time and full configurations, and evaluate the selected recipes on untouched data.

For implementation timing, use paired/interleaved runs on fixed workloads, record thread counts and synchronize accelerators. Report construction and compilation separately from fit and forecast. A setup cost must not disappear inside an untimed preparation step. Memory results must identify what was measured and whether inputs, solver workspaces and compilation are included.

docs.title: Historical first tuning measurements
docs.text:
Four bounded searches used the existing Model.tune workflow and Optuna TPE: vanilla and OTT models on both systems. Each attempted 24 configurations, using three initialization seeds and three validation starting points. Pruning was explicitly disabled. The successful/failed counts were 19/5, 24/0, 15/9 and 12/12, respectively; invalid candidates were never eligible to win. Every successful candidate completed all nine full validation forecasts.

The search varied width (300, 400, 600 or 1,000), spectral radius, leak, input/bias scale, ridge penalty and recurrent degree. All candidates used tanh, float64 CPU execution and an SVD readout. Lorenz used 10,001 training observations at dt=0.02; Rössler used 8,501 at dt=0.145. Both discarded 500 training inputs as washout. Validation and final-test periods each covered three nonoverlapping windows of at least ten Lyapunov times.

Winning settings were frozen before evaluating the reserved seeds 201–205. The first engineering smoke had used seed 101; its separate 101–105 bank is retained as a supplementary check. No test scores selected or changed the winning settings. This experiment uses explicit validation, so fits retain only the original training observations. Histories can include later observed values, but forecasts never receive future truth after their starting point.

docs.title: Test results at the 0.3 threshold
docs.text:
All numbers below are Lyapunov times. Each primary median uses five reserved seeds and three starting points. ≥ means the evaluated horizon ended before the forecast failed; it is a lower bound.

System / model Untuned median Tuned primary median Primary range Valid through the full window Pooled ten-seed median Lorenz / vanilla 5.252 9.110 3.351–≥10.016 7 / 15 ≥10.016 Lorenz / OTT 5.271 ≥10.016 8.440–≥10.016 8 / 15 ≥10.016 Rössler / vanilla 0.352 7.578 5.456–≥10.001 1 / 15 6.761 Rössler / OTT 0.362 ≥10.001 7.547–≥10.001 9 / 15 ≥10.001

The supplementary vanilla Rössler median was 6.326, so its pooled result is below the 7–8 target. That seed sensitivity remains work to improve, even though the primary bank reaches the target. These results describe one canonical trajectory per system, with several seeds and origins. They are not a guarantee across systems, sampling intervals, trajectories or hardware.

Replaying all selected settings and controls before and after phase four gave 150 matched cases (300 rollouts) with byte-identical full forecasts, fitted tensors and scores. Together with the frozen comparison, this provides measured nonregression evidence for the tested deterministic classical models. It does not establish an unchanged numerical trajectory for every earlier major release, stochastic fit or custom temporal operation.

The complete report includes both thresholds, all individual scores, the supplementary bank, failed-trial reasons, complete winning recipes and exact execution snapshots. The final reporting follow-up and original tuning execution have separately recorded source hashes. Its timings are not controlled speed comparisons.

These measurements used explicit model-building recipes and search spaces. They are not measurements of the automatic default search. The subsequent approved API increment brings input strength, bias and recurrent density into built-in vanilla and OTT tuning, while retaining the existing quick/balanced/thorough budgets and custom search controls. It preserves custom components and current workflow settings. Edited graphs keep fixed-DAG tuning until given an explicit rebuilding recipe. See the default ranges and component policies.

That increment also fixed sparse workflow staging: at that version, derived CSR weights were rebuilt from the copied dense parameter, avoiding a PyTorch sparse-storage deepcopy failure. The continuation replaces that duplicate representation with compressed-only storage. The recorded experiment recipes and their original execution hashes remain available separately.

Run the full bounded experiment with:

python benchmarks/tuned_accuracy.py --before 00ca741 --after 0b546d6 --artifacts-dir /tmp/resdag-tuned-accuracy --output tuned-accuracy.json

--quick --n-trials 1 is an interface smoke check with a separate seed bank; it does not reproduce the reported search budget. Saved winning .pt models are written to the artifact directory and can be loaded with rd.load. Supply observed history up to the desired test origin to reproduce that forecast; their cached training tail ends earlier.

docs.title: Decisions still requiring consultation
docs.text:
• Any change to public metrics or the model/state/solver contracts.
  • Sparse/dense selection policies or a new compilation default after profiling.
  • Changes to the approved cross-library budget or model family. The first comparison uses vanilla ESNs on both systems, 600 tuning seconds per library/system, then five reserved seeds and three starts. Different budgets or broader scale regimes need agreement before another long run. Neither equal candidate counts nor equal elapsed time proves universal superiority.

Use standard Torch/SciPy operators, Optuna and existing benchmark timing tools. The first increment makes no CUDA performance or cross-library ranking claim. See the tracker for status.

docs.title: Phase five measurements
docs.text: The continuation separates three questions: whether stored models keep their predictions, how well newly initialized models forecast, and what the execution changes cost or save. PR #465's implementation is released in v5.0.0. The roadmap tracks the CPU follow-up and remaining work; each measurement identifies its own source revision.

docs.title: Fresh vanilla recipe follow-up
docs.text: The separate validation and held-out study now completes 48 validation trials and 180 final forecasts. Lorenz retains its ≥10.016 LT trajectory-median result; the selected Rössler recipe improves from 3.013 to 6.750 LT at the main 0.3 threshold (7.154 LT at 0.5). Both winners retain the current input in their readout. All final predictions replay byte for byte after cleanup. The main Rössler target remains open, and this recipe study does not change the comparative CPU findings below.

docs.title: Current all-PyTorch closeout
docs.text:
The latest checks cover composition inside a trainable PyTorch network, parallel CPU forecasting, independent-trajectory accuracy and saved-experiment replay. Model execution stays entirely in PyTorch. CPU teacher-forced compilation and the private SciPy recurrence backend are not added.

An encoder → fitted reservoir → prediction head passes independent tensor and finite-difference gradient checks, repeated optimizer updates, explicit-state chunking and standard state-dictionary reload. Vanilla, OTT and named multi-head graphs also pass full-graph forward/backward capture with PyTorch's AOT eager backend. CPU and native MPS forward/backward checks reject host scalar reads and cross-device tensor operations in the tested hot path. These establish composition correctness; AOT eager capture and MPS checks do not measure CUDA throughput. CUDA is unavailable on this host.

The acceptance tests found integration defects. CPU autocast could request an unsupported low-precision CSR multiplication; that operation now uses the stored weight precision on the same device, preserving gradients through the surrounding mixed-precision network. Full-graph capture could fail while inspecting the stored state's grad_fn; the compile-aware guard now detaches only carried state under the existing default. Current-call gradients and explicit cross-call gradient retention remain covered. Hosted Torch 2.10 checks on Python 3.11–3.13 also exposed evaluation of a typing union inside the preprocessing getter. Quoting that typing-only argument preserves its eager identity operation and lets Dynamo capture the forward graph; all four compiled cases and the full pipeline selection pass in an isolated Python 3.13/Torch 2.10 reproduction.

The experiment guide now saves resolved settings, versions, split identities, artifact hashes and exact replay data. Its verification command loads the saved models and reproduces predictions and scores without integrating a system, tuning or fitting again. Recorded timings remain observations from the original run.

docs.title: Parallel CPU forecast
docs.text:
The adopted single-frame path removes redundant sequence-wrapper work during closed-loop forecasting in the built-in parallel model. It keeps the original projection and recurrent arithmetic, warmup and state semantics. Hooks, overridden methods, custom activations/readouts, autocast and non-CPU devices use the ordinary compatible path.

Two fresh-process ABBA blocks compare frozen source snapshots differing only in this parallel implementation. The four synthetic workloads use float64, 150 units per patch, 501 training observations, 100 washout/history observations and a 129-step forecast; patch core width is four and halo width six. Torch and native pools are verified at one thread. Construction is outside the clock; public fit and history-plus-forecast calls are inside it.

All 64 timed fit/forecast pairs and 32 discarded warmup pairs retain exact fitted tensors, fit states, complete predictions and final forecast states across variants. Each block contains four fresh processes in ABBA order, with one warmup and two timed repetitions per case/process. The ratios below divide the block's pooled baseline median by its candidate median; two blocks are descriptive process observations, not confidence intervals.

Batch / patches Forecast ratio, block 1 / block 2 Fit control ratio, block 1 / block 2 1 / 8 1.098 / 1.055 0.981 / 1.004 1 / 64 1.041 / 1.078 0.973 / 1.015 4 / 8 1.096 / 1.096 0.956 / 0.982 4 / 64 1.023 / 1.041 0.929 / 0.996

Forecast elapsed time falls by about 2–9% in these workloads. Fitting does not use the new path: its unchanged control varies from about 1.5% faster to 7.6% slower. Read these small forecast gains with that control variation in mind. This is bounded parallel-forecast evidence, not a universal training improvement or a cross-library speed ranking. All 96 workflows also preserve their exactness hashes from the earlier run before the typing-only compiler fix. The earlier parallel patch-scaling failure was not reproduced with the current benchmark recipe; its threshold is unchanged.

Download every sample, exactness hash, frozen source and replay script.

docs.title: Independent trajectories
docs.text:
Six previously selected recipes were frozen before generating ten new trajectories: five initial conditions for each system. Each recipe/system is refitted on each trajectory's own training prefix with three new reservoir seeds, then evaluated at three nonoverlapping forecast origins. There is no new hyperparameter search or winner selection. All 90 fits and 270 forecasts complete with finite predictions; no failed runs are excluded.

The four primary recipes come from the corrected-initialization capability study. At the main 0.3 normalized-error threshold, the preregistered aggregate is the median of the five trajectory medians; each trajectory median contains nine seed/origin forecasts. The independent unit is a trajectory, not each of the 45 nested forecasts. Full individual ranges include censored lower bounds. Each recipe retains its own selected size and settings; this is not an architecture ablation with matched hyperparameters.

Primary recipe Median at 0.3, Lyapunov times Individual range at 0.3 Forecasts reaching the test limit at 0.3 Median at 0.5 Lorenz, friendly vanilla 5.995 1.902–≥10.016 6 / 45 6.810 Lorenz, OTT ≥10.016 6.575–≥10.016 35 / 45 ≥10.016 Rössler, friendly vanilla 6.326 2.505–≥10.001 7 / 45 7.144 Rössler, OTT ≥10.001 4.193–≥10.001 25 / 45 ≥10.001

The two secondary state-only vanilla recipes from the common-family comparison reach the ten-Lyapunov-time median limit on both systems. They use different feature/solver policies and remain separate from the primary friendly recipes. This demonstrates sensitivity to the chosen recipe; it does not replace the negative friendly-vanilla results. The 7–8-time typical-performance target is still unmet for those two frozen friendly recipes. OTT meets the median target in this study, although individual forecasts can be shorter.

These are robustness checks of frozen recipes refitted on independent runs, not zero-shot transfer of one trained reservoir to a new initial condition. They do not compare competitor accuracy on this new bank or establish that an implementation change caused the vanilla shortfall. Previously inspected forecast banks remain distinct from these new observations.

A paired regression for the initial implementation separately repeats the same 90 fits and 270 forecasts on clean baseline eb70bf11, using the sealed observations and initial weights. Every fitted-tensor fingerprint, complete prediction, final state and score matches exactly. This second pass adds no tuning or test-based selection.

The preregistered runtime was frozen before the release-metadata rebase. Its version literal is 5.0.0. Subsequent changes update that literal to 5.0.1, tighten a parallel-only custom-readout guard unused by these six recipes, and quote the preprocessing getter's typing-only cast for older compiler support. The public record retains the original source and every subsequent source bridge; it does not relabel the frozen capture as a later checkout.

On the final corrected runtime, a separate replay loads all 90 original fitted checkpoints and reproduces all 270 forecasts exactly, including complete prediction bytes, final states and both scores. Every fitted tensor fingerprint also matches; the common graph's nonpersistent post-fit state is restored by the original teacher-forced input prefix. This replay performs no readout solve, fitting, integration or tuning. Two stopped restore-setup attempts are retained separately; neither found a forecast discrepancy or contributes to the original study's scores.

Download all 270 scores, lossless error traces, trajectory summaries, paired regression and reproduction inputs.

docs.title: Closeout verification
docs.text:
The implementation is in PR #467. The initial 3493889 checks identified the older-Python/Torch 2.10 graph-capture failure described above. Corrected runtime 941cd8bf passes all eight full locked/latest hosted suites, including the previously failing combinations. These package checks cover the corrected candidate source; its wheel retains the base version 5.0.1 and is not the previously published 5.0.1 artifact. The final tracker update changes prose only.

Check Result Complete corrected-source local suite 6,509 passed, 245 skipped, 13 benchmark cases deselected; 93.86% coverage against the unchanged 90% floor. Compiler acceptance cases isolate their caches rather than changing Torch's global recompile limit. Configured local CPU gates Four passed, four unavailable-device skips, one deselected; thresholds unchanged. Clean candidate package 110 installed-wheel checks passed, three unavailable-CUDA skips, plus all eight common-workflow guide blocks. All 205 runtime modules, the typing marker, 209 RECORD entries and actual installed import origins verify against the frozen source and sdist. Minimum optional dependency 13 experiment checks pass with an actual isolated TSDynamics 6.0.2 install, including fresh-process exact trajectory replay. Older Python / minimum Torch Python 3.13.16 / Torch 2.10.0 reproduces all four original graph-capture failures; the corrected source passes all 34 pipeline checks, including those four cases, with three unavailable-CUDA skips. Static and documentation Configured Ruff/Black checks and whole-package mypy (205 modules) pass. Strict MkDocs passes; all four changed pages were visually inspected, and all three new downloadable records match their served bytes. Hosted full compatibility Python 3.11–3.14 passes in both the locked run and latest-dependency run. Each of the eight full lanes passes 6,256 tests, with 498 skips and 13 benchmark cases deselected; coverage is 91.65–91.70% against the existing 90% floor. Hosted integrations and gates All six TSDynamics lanes pass 322 checks each, with seven intentional skips. CPU gates, 103 Python comparison/protocol checks, 18 real pinned Julia checks, static checks and strict documentation pass.

docs.title: CPU follow-up
docs.text:
PR #466 is merged as 3b34005 and released in v5.0.1. All four post-merge full suites, three TSDynamics lanes, the published-wheel fit/forecast/save/load replay and live documentation deployment pass.

The adopted CPU changes reuse AutoReadout residual diagnostics when its admitted Gram solution is unchanged, while recomputing them after a fallback replaces the coefficients. Sparse cycle normalization uses an analytic spectrum, fixing iterative eigensolver failures without dense allocation. The CSR fixes also handle complex value views and explicitly stored zero weights. Automatic storage, solver and compilation choices retain their established settings.

The experimental timestep-view and driver-slicing rewrites in dc695a6 were rejected: the measurements did not establish a CPU benefit. The original sequence-loop and driver slicing are retained. Records against dc695a6 below remain historical candidate evidence; they do not measure the final adopted implementation's whole-workflow speed.

docs.title: Retained-runtime accuracy regression
docs.text:
All 30 previously scored ResDAG forecasts from the equal-time comparison were replayed on the final retained runtime after restoring the original slicing. Every complete Lorenz/Rössler forecast is byte-identical, using the same frozen winners, five seeds and three origins. The public record identifies the source as final-runtime-manifest and includes exact hashes for all 205 runtime modules, plus the manifest hash. This preserves those measured scores. It is regression evidence from an already inspected bank; no new tuning, timing or independent-trajectory claim is made.

Download the complete replay.

docs.title: Rejected-candidate public workflow timing
docs.text:
Two fresh-process ABBA blocks compare 18f78c83 with dc695a6 on this Apple M5 with 24 GiB RAM, Torch 2.10 and float64 CPU tensors. Each revision explicitly loads the same saved weights and synthetic observations. Torch and native thread policies are verified at one. Seven workflow/batch cases and six dense/CSR cases each retain seven timed repetitions per process after warmup: 728 timed executions of each operation (fit, history plus forecast and reservoir forward), plus 104 discarded warmups of each operation. Every fitted-model, complete-prediction and final-state hash agrees exactly between revisions within its case.

The overall workflow speed effect is inconclusive. During the first matrix, latency increased sharply within a candidate process, then remained high in the following baseline process. Dependency versions, source/import identities and observed thread settings remained the same. The cause of this change in execution conditions was not recorded. Every run remains included; medians alone cannot establish a small implementation speedup or slowdown here.

Ratios below are before/after process-median times. Brackets retain the full range of four nearest AB/BA ratios; these are descriptive observations, not confidence intervals.

Workflow Fit ratio History + forecast ratio Dense classic, 400 / batch 1 1.091 [0.994–10.407] 1.001 [0.941–9.639] Dense OTT, 400 / batch 1 1.009 [0.992–9.301] 0.955 [0.904–8.200] Sparse cycle, 400 / batch 1 0.998 [0.948–6.209] 0.971 [0.800–8.451] Sparse ER, 400 / batch 1 1.041 [0.935–8.671] 1.086 [0.896–7.735] Dense classic, 1,000 / batch 1 1.040 [0.758–24.056] 1.015 [0.815–25.358] Dense classic, 1,000 / batch 4 1.006 [0.808–1.133] 0.982 [0.743–0.999] Dense classic, 1,000 / batch 16 1.029 [1.014–1.594] 1.000 [0.921–1.570]

The storage profile uses the same ER matrices in dense and CSR form at 400/1,000/2,000 units, expected degree six and batch one. Both representations remain exact across revisions; their cross-storage complete forecasts differ by at most 5.14e-10 on these synthetic observations. Storage timings also show variability, and pairs run in declared order rather than a separately balanced crossover experiment. They do not justify a new automatic storage rule.

Two earlier attempts stopped during the first baseline worker, before a complete comparison: one repeated normalization of placeholder weights that would be replaced, and another compared dense negative-zero bits with omitted CSR zeros. The harness now loads saved weights before checking their logical identity, normalizing zero signs only for that initial recurrent comparison. Fitted weights, predictions, states and stored artifact bytes retain exact checks. The aborted attempts remain in the audit archive and contribute no timings to the complete diagnostic reports.

Download all workflow samples and hashes, storage samples and hashes. The CPU protocol documents the reusable command, all dimensions, preprocessing, untimed work and process-level statistics.

docs.title: Within-process loop attribution
docs.text:
A separate diagnostic interleaves the original and candidate teacher-forced loop functions inside each of two fresh processes using one common runtime (6b3b108). It changes only BaseReservoirLayer.forward_stateless; it does not compare isolated revisions or separately measure the driver-slicing rewrite. Each case/process includes one warmup per function, then seven ABBA rounds. All fitted-model, complete-prediction and final-state hashes match.

The following medians and full ranges use all 28 within-process paired ratios per case across both processes. These repeated pairs share their process environment and are not independent process observations or confidence intervals.

Workflow Fit ratio History + forecast ratio Dense classic, 400 / batch 1 1.032 [0.390–1.451] 0.893 [0.490–1.882] Dense classic, 1,000 / batch 4 1.003 [0.445–1.730] 0.945 [0.313–1.511] Dense ER, 2,000 / batch 1 0.996 [0.793–1.642] 1.014 [0.671–1.365]

The variation remains broad and does not establish a consistent loop speedup. Torch 2.10's ATen/TensorIndexing.h already returns the existing tensor for full-axis slices during ordinary eager multidimensional indexing. The rewrite can reduce index parsing, but its proposed removal of extra full-axis tensor views does not describe that eager path. Both experimental slicing rewrites were therefore rejected; their complete measurements remain available.

Download the within-process diagnostic.

docs.title: Adopted readout reuse and exploratory compilation
docs.text:
A bounded AutoReadout probe fits two well-conditioned Gaussian problems with 5,000 samples, 128/400 features, three outputs, intercept and penalty 10. Two fresh-process ABBA blocks, seven timed fits after warmup, gave paired median ratios 1.154 [1.025–1.514] and 1.193 [1.128–1.389]. All coefficients, intercepts and complete diagnostic reports match. This measures the admitted primal path's duplicate-diagnostic removal; it does not measure a complete forecast or fallback QR/SVD speed. The probed AutoReadout code is byte-identical to the retained implementation. The public workflow matrix above uses Ridge.

An exploratory 400-unit float64 classic CPU compile probe observed a 45.54 s first compiled request. Warm 257-step forecasts took 37.99 ms versus 44.79 ms eager; 1,025-step forecasts took 106.82 ms versus 157.40 ms. Both complete predictions matched exactly. The second horizon reused the same 64-step compiled chunk cache; it is not a second cold start. One cold process and these synthetic signals do not establish a general compiler policy or chaotic-forecast accuracy. CPU teacher-forced sequences remain eager.

These two probes have narrower provenance than the archived workflow harness. The readout probe isolates unchanged readout dependencies. Compilation used the then-live candidate checkout before the slicing rewrites were restored, without an isolated overall source manifest. Its timings remain historical candidate observations and do not establish final adopted-runtime speed. Compilation remains opt-in. Readout records and compile records retain their raw samples, diagnostics, native settings and warnings.

docs.title: CPU recurrence investigation
docs.text:
After merging PR #466 as 3b34005, we profiled the complete public fit and history-plus-forecast workflows before choosing the next optimization. These experiments use fresh synthetic development data and fixed saved weights; they are neither another accuracy search nor a new comparison with competitors.

On this Apple M5, recurrence is the main cost. In a separate instrumented 1,000-unit, batch-one dense fit, recurrent multiplication accounts for 54.7% of Torch self CPU time and tanh for 20.1%. The successful Ridge solve costs about 26 ms, versus about 25 ms for a direct SciPy diagnostic without ResDAG's guards. Transactional model copying accounts for roughly 1–1.6 ms in cProfile. Removing numerical guards or failed-fit isolation would miss the main cost. Profiler times identify work; the latency measurements below come from uninstrumented public calls.

docs.title: Optional sparse CPU execution candidate
docs.text:
A private prototype substitutes SciPy CSR multiplication for Torch CSR multiplication, leaving projection, activation, leak, scaling, training and forecast commands unchanged. Both processes use the same 1,000-unit matrix with 6,070 stored connections, float64, batch one, 10,001 observations, 500 washout/history steps and a 553-step forecast. The fixed readout is Ridge, not AutoReadout. Construction is outside the clock; fit includes preprocessing, the complete training prefix and transactional commit. Forecast includes history replay. Lazy SciPy operator construction and every Tensor/NumPy bridge are inside the measured calls.

Each fresh process runs four ABBA rounds after one discarded warmup per mode. The ratios use the eight nearest AB/BA pairs within that process. Brackets show their full observed range, not confidence intervals.

Process Sparse fit, Torch → SciPy Paired fit ratio History + forecast, Torch → SciPy Paired forecast ratio 1 531.84 → 171.67 ms 3.108 [3.061–3.125] 60.01 → 21.23 ms 2.822 [2.776–2.885] 2 528.04 → 173.07 ms 3.053 [3.005–3.081] 59.21 → 21.38 ms 2.764 [2.138–2.873]

All 32 timed workflows have byte-identical fitted coefficients, complete predictions and final states across the two modes and processes. Warmups ran but were not fingerprinted separately. These are two processes on one host, not independent machines or evidence about Lorenz/Rössler forecast skill. Native thread limits are verified at one; power/thermal and process CPU/wall receipts are retained. API thread limits do not measure operating-system thread occupancy or CPU frequency.

This backend was not adopted. The maintainer chose to keep model execution entirely in PyTorch. The private diagnostic remains useful cost attribution; it does not establish production cache ownership, live weight/index updates, serialization, device changes, gradients, PyTorch transforms, autocast or compilation behavior. The current storage and execution defaults remain unchanged.

docs.title: Dense batch candidate and rejected alternatives
docs.text:
At batch four, replacing one matrix multiplication with four matrix-vector multiplications improves public fit by 1.775×/1.798× and forecast by 1.929×/1.956× in the two processes. However, the changed reduction order produces substantially different fitted coefficients and closed-loop predictions on this poorly conditioned synthetic fixture. This candidate is not adopted. Those differences do not score physical-system accuracy, but they preclude calling the change numerically identical.

At batch one, matrix-vector multiplication and transposing the dense equation provide no measured primitive benefit. Reusing tanh output storage also gives no meaningful gain in the bounded allocation probe. Torch CSR is slower than dense in the initial 1,000-unit public profile; compressed storage alone is not a speed guarantee. Sequential profile rows are not a paired storage comparison.

Download raw timings, hashes, source manifests and diagnostic scripts. The earlier cross-library CPU gap remains open until an adopted implementation is measured on the same comparison protocol. Extending CPU teacher-forced compilation is deferred: its startup and maintenance costs are not justified by established workflow gains. The next work prioritizes standard PyTorch fit/forecast performance and composition inside larger GPU models, preserving gradients and device placement. CPU measurements do not establish GPU throughput.

docs.title: Forecast accuracy after independent initialization
docs.text:
Correcting the initialization streams intentionally changes new models built with old seeds. We ran four fresh tuning studies on the corrected implementation (dcedbba; runtime unchanged in 1dc8cfb). Each attempted 24 configurations, using three initialization seeds and three validation starts. All four winners were frozen before evaluation on reserved seeds 401–405, with three starts per seed. No tuning followed those test results.

The table reports the median and full range of 15 individual forecasts. The primary limit is per-step normalized RMS error 0.3, using training-only component standard deviations; 0.5 is also reported. Horizons are in Lyapunov times. ≥ means the forecast reached the scoring limit, so its true valid horizon can be longer.

System / family Median at 0.3 Range at 0.3 Reached limit Median at 0.5 Lorenz / vanilla ≥10.016 4.474–≥10.016 9/15 ≥10.016 Lorenz / OTT ≥10.016 ≥10.016 throughout 15/15 ≥10.016 Rössler / vanilla 4.203 0.445–6.346 0/15 4.234 Rössler / OTT ≥10.001 8.438–≥10.001 9/15 ≥10.001

Vanilla Rössler does not meet the 7–8 target in this experiment. Its winning configuration was the predeclared known recipe: validation gave 7.485, while reserved testing gave 4.203. Relaxing the error limit to 0.5 does not resolve that shortfall. The unoptimized baseline gave 0.259. More robust validation and further model/search work remain necessary; we did not choose another winner after seeing the test results.

The 15 forecasts share reservoir seeds and one trajectory per system. They are not 15 independent dynamical-system runs. For example, the Lorenz vanilla winner's five per-seed medians range from 7.535 to ≥10.016, and their median is 8.857; its pooled median above is ≥10.016. Raw trajectories and chronological origins were historically known, while the reserved initialization bank was fresh. These results do not establish generalization across independent trajectories or superiority of default tuning.

Study Complete configurations Failed configurations Attempts Lorenz / vanilla 21 3 24 Lorenz / OTT 23 1 24 Rössler / vanilla 15 9 24 Rössler / OTT 11 13 24

Every complete configuration received all nine full validation forecasts. Failures remain recorded; there was no pruning or replacement budget. This capability check uses explicit classic/OTT factories, including their direct input features and readout intercept, with a float64 CPU SVD readout. Its elapsed time includes concurrent correctness testing and cannot support a speed comparison. See the design for the scoring equations and chronological windows.

Download all capability scores, settings and provenance.

docs.title: Run the capability protocol yourself
docs.text:
From a repository checkout, install the optional dependencies and run the single-revision command. Generating TSDynamics observations requires Python 3.12 or newer:

python -m pip install -e ".[hpo,dynamics]"
python -m pip install -r benchmarks/requirements.txt
python benchmarks/tuned_accuracy.py --mode capability --after HEAD \
  --test-seeds 401 402 403 404 405 --n-trials 24 \
  --artifacts-dir /tmp/resdag-capability --output capability.json

It archives the committed source, generates the observations, records their versions and hashes, and freezes all four winners before evaluation. Use fresh output paths. To reuse saved observations exactly, add --data-dir /path/to/saved-data; that directory contains data.json, lorenz.npy and rossler.npy. For a bounded plumbing check, use --quick --n-trials 1 and omit --test-seeds; quick mode uses the separate smoke seed 101.

This command repeats the protocol. Reusing seeds 401–405 reproduces an existing bank; it does not create a fresh test. A new scientific experiment needs a previously unused bank chosen before tuning. The measurements above used an archived external wrapper and its frozen workers; this later supported command was not their original driver. Backend and dependency differences can change numerical results.

docs.title: Stored models and regression anchors
docs.text:
Four trained 4.1.0 checkpoints were loaded in both the published implementation and the corrected runtime. All 12 history-conditioned forecasts and their fitted tensor fingerprints were byte-identical. This checks materialized model behavior; it does not imply that newly constructed models keep the old draws. Current-memory and RNG round trips are also covered by the artifact test suite.

Two existing CI quality tests had implicitly identified their reservoir weights only by a seed. Their strict bounds failed after those seeds generated different weights. The tests now use explicit public initializer callbacks to reproduce their historical weights. All 18 reservoir tensors match the pinned old implementation byte for byte. Seeds, target data and accuracy limits are unchanged; the FORCE suite and parallel forecast floor pass. Fresh-default skill is measured separately above.

docs.title: Compact storage and paired CPU execution
docs.text:
For a fixed 400-unit model, compressed-only storage reduced the sparse cycle's retained tensor storage from 1,321,042 to 37,842 bytes, and the sparse random example from 1,351,978 to 58,466 bytes. These counts deduplicate tensor storage; they are not peak process-memory measurements. Read memory and sparse models for temporary initialization, feature-history, solver and device boundaries.

Two independent fresh-process ABBA runs compared merged 041db61 with 1dc8cfb, explicitly loading the same baseline weights into both versions. Each used 1,501 synthetic training samples, washout 100 and 256 forecast steps. Each setting retains four processes and 28 timed repetitions per version after warmup. Every prediction digest matched across all processes. The second run was prompted by one apparent 10% slowdown; both runs remain in the pooled result.

Ratios below are baseline time divided by new time. Above 1 is faster; below 1 is slower. These are workload-specific medians, not a universal speed guarantee.

Model Torch threads Fit ratio Forecast ratio Dense vanilla 1 0.987× 0.969× Dense OTT 1 0.989× 0.950× Sparse cycle 1 1.112× 1.139× Sparse random 1 0.978× 0.997× Dense vanilla 4 1.017× 1.007× Dense OTT 4 1.025× 1.011× Sparse cycle 4 1.133× 1.142× Sparse random 4 1.028× 1.018×

The one-thread dense forecast medians are roughly 3–5% slower in this sample. The configured CPU gates pass with unchanged thresholds, but that does not erase these measured costs. Broader batching and compilation profiling remain open. The paired experiment controls Torch threads; native Accelerate uses its default policy in both versions. It is separate from the verified single-thread equal-budget protocol below. Initialization is excluded from fit/forecast timing.

docs.title: Equal tuning time across libraries
docs.text:
The first full comparison completed on 23 October 2026, using source 1dc8cfb. ResDAG, ReservoirPy and ReservoirComputing.jl each received 600 tuning seconds per system, followed by the same reserved seeds 301–305 and three starts. All six winners froze before final evaluation. Independent audits checked every forecast, scale, cutoff and winning trial. All 90 final forecasts completed without API errors or nonfinite predictions.

Each row summarizes 15 forecasts at the primary 0.3 limit. ≥ marks the scoring ceiling; it is not an exact prediction limit.

System / library Median LT Full range LT Reached limit Lorenz / ResDAG ≥10.016 8.893–≥10.016 14/15 Lorenz / ReservoirPy ≥10.016 8.911–≥10.016 14/15 Lorenz / ReservoirComputing.jl ≥10.016 8.422–≥10.016 10/15 Rössler / ResDAG 9.628 7.609–≥10.001 6/15 Rössler / ReservoirPy 9.639 7.599–≥10.001 7/15 Rössler / ReservoirComputing.jl 9.701 7.609–≥10.001 7/15

All six medians reach the scoring ceiling at the secondary 0.5 limit. ResDAG meets the 7–8 target in this common vanilla experiment, with accuracy close to both other libraries. The classic input-skip/SVD experiment above still has its separate Rössler shortfall. Different families, initialization distributions, settings and history windows prevent attributing the difference to one feature.

All selected reservoirs have 1,000 units, with independently tuned settings. The following medians describe those selected models on this Apple M5, 24 GiB, macOS 27.0.1 CPU. They are not matched-weight repeated timing trials.

System / library Build + fit seconds Synchronize + forecast + score seconds Lorenz / ResDAG 1.7965 0.1280 Lorenz / ReservoirPy 0.3839 0.0390 Lorenz / ReservoirComputing.jl 2.0427 0.0392 Rössler / ResDAG 1.1705 0.1321 Rössler / ReservoirPy 0.2690 0.0412 Rössler / ReservoirComputing.jl 0.9860 0.0262

ResDAG is slower in these selected CPU workflows. Its comparable accuracy does not establish a speed advantage. Batching, compiled execution and the single-sequence hot path remain profiling priorities.

The native thread APIs reported one for Torch, BLAS and Julia, with fresh CLI environment controls. This verifies the requested API settings, not operating system thread occupancy. The fixed synthetic Julia storage pilot selected CSC before accuracy tuning. Python model-memory fields count tensors/arrays; Julia's parameter-tree counts have a different scope. Process peak RSS includes startup and earlier work, so these fields do not support a common memory ranking.

Each track's final attempted configuration crossed the cutoff and was excluded; eligible validation work completed within 600 seconds. Actual track durations were 600.024–601.188 seconds, and the partially completed fits/forecasts remain recorded. There were no other trial failures or automatic retries. Eligible complete counts were 300 / 801 / 207 on Lorenz and 310 / 881 / 351 on Rössler, in ResDAG / ReservoirPy / Julia order. Different sampled configurations make these counts unsuitable as standalone throughput ratios.

Native solver safeguards also matter: ResDAG recovery can project the Gram matrix or increase effective regularization. Logged final evaluation includes one recovery that explicitly kept its requested penalty, plus condition diagnostics; ReservoirPy also reports ill-conditioning warnings. Warnings are deduplicated and do not provide complete per-fit effective-penalty accounting. The same requested search range does not imply identical numerical objectives.

Download all 90 scores, selected settings, timings and provenance.

The protocol describes native mask/RNG/solver differences, one-worker float64 execution, actual native thread controls, deadlines, failures, startup and memory accounting. This common state-only vanilla family is distinct from the classic/OTT capability check above. An equal-time study compares selected models; matched-weight execution checks measure implementation costs separately. This is one timed study on one historically known trajectory per system, not evidence of universal superiority or generalization to independent trajectories.
