def esp_index(
    model: "ESNModel",
    feedback_seq: torch.Tensor,
    *driving_seqs: torch.Tensor,
    history: bool = False,
    iterations: int = 10,
    transient: int = 0,
    window: int | None = None,
    relative: bool = False,
    chunk_size: int | None = None,
    verbose: bool = True,
) -> Union[
    dict[str, list[torch.Tensor]],
    Tuple[dict[str, list[torch.Tensor]], dict[str, list[torch.Tensor]]],
]:
    """
    Compute the Echo State Property (ESP) index for reservoir layers.

    The ESP index measures how quickly trajectories from different initial
    states converge when driven by the same input.  All
    `resdag.layers.reservoirs.base_reservoir.BaseReservoirLayer`
    reservoirs are discovered automatically, so the diagnostic applies equally
    to ESN, NG-RC, and any future custom-cell reservoir.

    Random restarts are drawn through each reservoir's public
    `resdag.layers.reservoirs.base_reservoir.BaseReservoirLayer.set_random_state`,
    which samples a **standard-normal** state — the same convention as
    `resdag.core.ESNModel.set_random_reservoir_states`.  The index is
    therefore directly comparable to states produced elsewhere in the library.

    Parameters
    ----------
    model : ESNModel
        Model containing reservoir layers.
    feedback_seq : torch.Tensor
        Feedback sequence, shape `(batch, timesteps, features)`.
    *driving_seqs : torch.Tensor
        Optional driving sequences in model input order.
    history : bool, default=False
        If True, return full distance history over time.
    iterations : int, default=10
        Number of random initial states to average over.
    transient : int, default=0
        Timesteps to discard from sequence start.
    window : int or None, default=None
        Length of the trailing window over which the index is averaged.  By
        default (`None`) the index is the mean over *every* post-transient
        timestep, which for a healthy reservoir is dominated by the early
        convergence transient rather than the asymptotic distance.  Setting
        `window=k` averages only the **last** `k` post-transient steps, so
        the index reflects the asymptotic regime — a far more diagnostic
        statistic.  Must be a positive integer no larger than the number of
        post-transient timesteps.  Does not affect the returned `history`
        tensors, which always span the full post-transient sequence.
    relative : bool, default=False
        If True, normalise each per-step distance by the corresponding
        base-state norm, `||base - rand|| / (||base|| + eps)`, yielding a
        scale-free relative distance that is comparable across reservoir sizes
        and spectral radii.  If False (default), the raw absolute distance is
        used.  The normalisation is applied to both the returned index and the
        `history` tensors.
    chunk_size : int or None, default=None
        Maximum number of random restarts run together in a single batched
        forward pass.  All restarts are statistically independent and differ
        only in their initial state, so they are folded into the batch
        dimension and evaluated in one forward pass instead of `iterations`
        sequential passes (typically a ~3x speed-up).  A large
        `reservoir_size * iterations` product can exhaust device memory,
        however; set `chunk_size` to cap the per-pass batch at
        `batch * chunk_size` and process the restarts in chunks.  `None`
        (default) runs all `iterations` restarts in one pass, transparently
        falling back to chunking (halving the chunk each time) if a CUDA
        out-of-memory error is raised.
    verbose : bool, default=True
        Print progress and skip messages.

    Returns
    -------
    dict or tuple
        If `history=False`: dict mapping layer names to single-element
        lists containing the ESP index scalar tensor.
        If `history=True`: tuple of (ESP indices dict, history dict).
        History tensors have shape `(iterations, timesteps, batch)` and span
        the full post-transient sequence regardless of `window`.

        Reservoirs whose ESP is undefined (no randomisable state) are omitted
        from both dictionaries.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `transient` is not smaller than the number of timesteps, if
        `window` is not a positive integer no larger than the number of
        post-transient timesteps, if the model contains no reservoir layers,
        or if no reservoir has a well-defined ESP.

    Notes
    -----
    For LINEAR systems (identity activation), input does NOT affect ESP
    because the input contribution cancels out in the state difference.
    This is mathematically correct behavior.

    State is never mutated by direct assignment.  The zero base orbit is set
    via `res.reset_state(batch_size=...)` and the random restarts via
    `res.set_random_state()`, so each cell's own shape contract (2-D for
    ESN, 3-D delay buffer for NG-RC) is honoured and validated by the public
    state-management API.

    The caller's reservoir states are saved before the computation and
    restored afterwards (even on error), so calling `esp_index` never leaves
    the model's reservoirs in a mutated (random) state.

    **Batched restarts.**  The `iterations` random restarts are statistically
    independent and differ only in their initial state, so they are folded into
    the batch dimension: the feedback (and any drivers) are tiled `iterations`
    times, one random initial state is composed per restart into a single
    `(batch * iterations, ...)` state, and the whole ensemble is evaluated in
    **one** forward pass rather than `iterations` sequential passes.  The
    random restarts are drawn in exactly the same order as the sequential loop
    (outer over restarts, inner over reservoirs), so the *initial states* are
    bit-identical to the sequential computation.  The reservoir *outputs* — and
    hence the returned index — match the sequential value to floating-point
    rounding (typically `< 1e-6` relative), the only difference being the
    reassociation of a wider batched matmul; the result is fully deterministic
    under a fixed seed.  (If a reservoir cell injects per-step state noise in
    training mode, `noise > 0`, the batched noise draws differ from the
    sequential ones; the index remains a valid, seed-deterministic stochastic
    diagnostic but is no longer numerically identical.  Run the model in eval
    mode to disable noise entirely.)

    Examples
    --------
    Score only the asymptotic regime with a scale-free statistic:

    ```python
    idx = esp_index(model, feedback, window=50, relative=True)
    ```

    See Also
    --------
    resdag.core.ESNModel.set_random_reservoir_states :
        Source of the standard-normal restart convention used here.
    """
    from resdag.data.prepare import _validate_step_count
    from resdag.layers.reservoirs.base_reservoir import BaseReservoirLayer

    iterations = _validate_step_count("iterations", iterations)
    transient = _validate_step_count("transient", transient, allow_zero=True)
    if window is not None:
        window = _validate_step_count("window", window)
    if chunk_size is not None:
        chunk_size = _validate_step_count("chunk_size", chunk_size)

    device = feedback_seq.device
    dtype = feedback_seq.dtype
    batch_size, total_timesteps, _ = feedback_seq.shape

    if transient >= total_timesteps:
        raise ValueError(f"transient ({transient}) >= timesteps ({total_timesteps})")

    timesteps = total_timesteps - transient

    if window is not None and not (0 < window <= timesteps):
        raise ValueError(
            f"window ({window}) must be a positive integer no larger than the "
            f"number of post-transient timesteps ({timesteps})."
        )

    if chunk_size is not None and chunk_size <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"chunk_size ({chunk_size}) must be a positive integer or None.")

    inputs = (feedback_seq,) + driving_seqs

    # Save the caller's reservoir states *before* any probing/mutation so they
    # can be restored on the way out (including on error).  ``esp_index`` is a
    # read-only diagnostic; it must not leave the model's reservoirs in the
    # random state it uses internally.  ``_has_well_defined_esp`` and the base
    # orbit below both mutate state, so the snapshot has to be taken here first.
    # ``get_reservoir_states`` omits reservoirs whose state is ``None`` (never
    # warmed up), so those names are tracked separately and reset back to
    # ``None`` on restore instead of being left holding an internal state.
    saved_states = model.get_reservoir_states()
    reservoirs_with_none_state = [
        module
        for module in model.modules()
        if isinstance(module, BaseReservoirLayer) and module.state is None
    ]

    try:
        # Discover every reservoir layer (cell-agnostic): any
        # BaseReservoirLayer, not just ESNLayer.  This includes NGReservoirLayer and
        # any custom-cell layer.
        all_reservoirs: list[tuple[str, "BaseReservoirLayer"]] = []
        for name, module in model.named_modules():
            if isinstance(module, BaseReservoirLayer):
                all_reservoirs.append((name, module))

        if not all_reservoirs:
            raise ValueError("No reservoir layers found in model.")

        # Partition reservoirs into those with a well-defined ESP (a non-empty,
        # randomisable state) and those without.  A reservoir with no per-sample
        # state — e.g. a ``k=1`` NG-RC delay buffer of size 0 — has no notion of
        # "different initial states converging", so its ESP is undefined.
        reservoirs: list[tuple[str, "BaseReservoirLayer"]] = []
        for name, res in all_reservoirs:
            if _has_well_defined_esp(res, batch_size):
                reservoirs.append((name, res))
            elif verbose:
                label = name or type(res).__name__
                print(
                    f"Skipping reservoir '{label}': ESP is undefined "
                    f"(reservoir carries no randomisable state)."
                )

        if not reservoirs:
            raise ValueError(
                "No reservoir with a well-defined ESP found in model "
                "(every reservoir carries an empty state)."
            )

        # Run base orbit from the zero initial state.  Routed through the
        # public, validating, cloning API instead of assigning ``res.state``.
        for _, res in reservoirs:
            res.reset_state(batch_size=batch_size)

        base_states = _run_and_collect(model, reservoirs, inputs)
        if transient > 0:
            base_states = {name: s[:, transient:, :] for name, s in base_states.items()}

        # Evaluate all random restarts.  They are statistically independent and
        # differ only in their initial state, so they fold into the batch
        # dimension and run in one (or a few chunked) forward passes instead of
        # ``iterations`` sequential ones.
        random_states_by_iter = _collect_random_restarts(
            model,
            reservoirs,
            inputs,
            batch_size=batch_size,
            iterations=iterations,
            transient=transient,
            device=device,
            dtype=dtype,
            chunk_size=chunk_size,
            verbose=verbose,
        )

        esp_sums = {name: torch.tensor(0.0, device=device, dtype=dtype) for name, _ in reservoirs}
        if history:
            esp_history = {
                name: torch.zeros(iterations, timesteps, batch_size, device=device, dtype=dtype)
                for name, _ in reservoirs
            }

        # Reduce per restart.  Splitting the batched outputs back into
        # per-restart blocks and reducing them one at a time reproduces the
        # sequential arithmetic exactly (same per-iteration mean, then mean over
        # iterations), so ``window`` / ``relative`` / ``history`` behave
        # identically to the sequential path.
        for i in range(iterations):
            random_states = random_states_by_iter[i]
            for name, base in base_states.items():
                rand = random_states[name]
                # Distance at each (batch, timestep): norm over the feature
                # dimension.  Works for any output rank the reservoir produces.
                dist = torch.norm(base - rand, dim=-1)  # (batch, timesteps)

                if relative:
                    # Scale-free relative distance: divide by the base-state
                    # norm so the index is comparable across sizes / radii.
                    base_norm = torch.norm(base, dim=-1)  # (batch, timesteps)
                    dist = dist / (base_norm + 1e-12)

                # Mean distance for this restart.  With ``window`` set, average
                # only over the trailing window (the asymptotic regime);
                # otherwise over every post-transient timestep.
                dist_for_index = dist[:, -window:] if window is not None else dist
                esp_sums[name] += dist_for_index.mean()

                if history:
                    # Store the full post-transient sequence regardless of
                    # window: (batch, timesteps) -> row i of
                    # (iterations, timesteps, batch).
                    esp_history[name][i] = dist.T  # Transpose to (timesteps, batch)

        # Average over iterations
        esp_indices = {name: [val / iterations] for name, val in esp_sums.items()}

        if history:
            # Wrap history values in lists for API consistency
            esp_history_out = {name: [h] for name, h in esp_history.items()}
            return esp_indices, esp_history_out

        return esp_indices
    finally:
        # Restore the caller's reservoir states, whatever happened above.  Use
        # ``strict=False`` because reservoirs skipped as ESP-undefined (or any
        # that had no state to begin with) are simply absent from the snapshot.
        model.set_reservoir_states(saved_states, strict=False)
        # Reservoirs that started with a ``None`` state (never warmed up) are
        # absent from the snapshot, so ``set_reservoir_states`` would leave them
        # holding an internal state.  Reset them back to ``None`` to fully
        # restore the caller's pre-call condition.
        for module in reservoirs_with_none_state:
            module.reset_state()

docs.title: The mental model
docs.text: Use rd.ESN(...).fit(training_data) for a preset, or connect layers and wrap them in rd.Model for a custom DAG. Both support the same fit, forecast, tune and save commands. The four ideas below explain what those commands do.

docs.title: 1 — The dynamics are designed, not learned
docs.text:
A reservoir is a recurrent network whose weights are chosen and then frozen: a connectivity structure (random, a graph, any matrix-building function), scaled to a target spectral radius, driven by your signal. It is a fixed nonlinear dynamical system that unfolds your input's history into hundreds of feature trajectories. Because nothing inside is learned, every structural choice is a hyperparameter; ResDAG therefore treats connectivity structure as a pluggable function rather than a fixed implementation detail.

Reservoir families are an open set. The same interface also holds reservoirs with no randomness at all: NGReservoir builds features from delayed inputs and polynomial combinations — next-generation reservoir computing.

docs.title: 2 — Reservoir layers are stateful
docs.text:
The hidden state persists across forward calls — each reservoir family defines its own shape, such as (batch, reservoir_size) for an ESNLayer. That persistence is what lets a warmup pass hand a synchronized reservoir to a forecast loop. The state-management API:

layer.reset_state()            # forget everything (lazy re-init)
layer.get_state()              # clone the live state
layer.set_state(saved)         # restore a checkpoint
layer.set_random_state(batch_size=4)
model.reset_state()            # every reservoir in an rd.Model or rd.ESN

By default, stored state is detached at forward-call boundaries, so consecutive batches do not accumulate autograd history. Set detach_state_between_calls=False deliberately, or use model.forward_stateless(..., states=...) to carry attached state explicitly. The raw graph's as_module() adapter can process independent batches without changing stored states. A configured reset initializer supplies the starting state; otherwise it is zero.

Explicit-state execution requires reservoirs to be separate functional graph nodes. If a reservoir is hidden inside nn.Sequential or another module, forward_stateless(), the default as_module() adapter and forecasting reject the graph before running its operations. This prevents stored state from changing outside the returned state dictionary. Ordinary stateful model(x) calls still support those containers, as does as_module(stateful=True). Containers with only pointwise layers, such as a linear readout followed by an activation, can remain grouped.

Moving a model with .to(...) preserves its stored state values. An ordinary batch-size change initializes a fresh state; a state explicitly restored with set_state instead raises on a mismatched batch size to avoid discarding it.

docs.title: 3 — Readout training is a closed-form solve
docs.text:
Readouts are fitted algebraically on collected states rather than trained by gradient descent. The friendly rd.ESN defaults to AutoReadoutLayer, a linear ridge readout that checks numerical safety before choosing Cholesky, augmented QR or SVD. It preserves the requested regularization and reports its choices. Lower-level factories retain their explicit Ridge/Cholesky default. These solves need no learning rate or epoch schedule. Other solvers plug into the same contract: CGReadoutLayer (iterative conjugate gradient) and SVD/pinv/streaming variants (see Theory · Readout solvers). ESNTrainer.fit resets once and advances one continuous warmup-plus-training prefix in dependency order. A readout's pre-hook fits its training suffix before the readout produces the complete prefix for downstream nodes. Multiple heads share upstream work; a later reservoir warms up on the fitted upstream mapping without replaying it. Expose these dependencies as separate functional graph nodes or standard torch.nn.Sequential containers. A custom module that hides both readouts and reservoirs must expose that order before algebraic fitting.

Because every readout is an ordinary nn.Linear underneath, gradient-based training remains available: freeze the reservoir and train a deep head with Adam, or set trainable=True and backpropagate through everything. The Train page covers all three approaches.

The pure-PyTorch quickstart

Prefer a normal optimizer loop? ReservoirFeatureExtractor wraps a reservoir as a plain nn.Module that drops into nn.Sequential ahead of any head, frozen by default — so you compute its features once under torch.no_grad() and train the head with Adam like any other model. The runnable snippet is Train · Path 2 — frozen reservoir, gradient head, and Scale & deploy embeds the same frozen backbone inside a classifier nn.Module.

docs.title: 4 — Forecasting is autoregressive feedback
docs.text:
A trained model maps signal now → signal one step ahead. Forecasting closes the loop: after a teacher-forced warmup, each prediction is fed back as the next input, horizon times. Exogenous drivers slot in alongside the feedback with a fixed timing convention: drivers for the forecast window start exactly where the warmup drivers ended.

For scikit-learn users

The common model interface separates fitting from autonomous rollout:

scikit-learn ResDAG est.fit(X, y) model.fit(data) learns training-only scaling, warms up the reservoir and fits the readout forecasting future values model.forecast(history=data, horizon=...) synchronizes on observations, then feeds predictions back into the model applying a trained model to supplied inputs model(x) returns predictions in original units and carries reservoir state

The ESN preset handles both phases in one PyTorch module: ESN(...).fit(series).forecast(horizon=...). It learns scaling only from training data and returns original-unit tensors:

import torch
from resdag import ESN

series = torch.randn(2000, 3).cumsum(0)              # (time, features)
prediction = ESN(reservoir_size=300).fit(series).forecast(horizon=200)

esn.graph exposes the raw graph. Build custom branches with the same workflow through rd.Model; put either directly inside nn.Sequential.

The Build section expands on idea 1 — layers, topologies, initializers, and architectures; the Workflows section covers ideas 2–4 in practice — training, forecasting, tuning, and deployment.

docs.title: Train it, forecast with it, reuse it
docs.text: A reservoir turns recent observations into a useful memory. The readout learns how to turn that memory into a prediction. Usually training needs one algebraic solve, rather than an epoch loop.

docs.title: 1. Keep training and test data separate
docs.text:
Install with pip install resdag. Start with a floating Torch tensor shaped (time, signals) or (batch, time, signals). Convert NumPy data explicitly with torch.as_tensor(array).

import torch
import resdag as rd

t = torch.arange(1400, dtype=torch.float64) * 0.05
series = torch.stack((t.sin(), t.cos()), dim=-1)
training, truth = series[:1200], series[1200:]
options = dict(reservoir_size=100, washout=100, seed=0, readout="svd", dtype=torch.float64)
model = rd.ESN(**options).fit(training)

fit infers the signal count, learns scaling from the supervised training inputs only, and fits the next-sample readout. Washout is the initial period used to synchronize the reservoir before solving. Test samples never enter that solve or the scaling statistics.

For a TSDynamics simulation, install resdag[dynamics] and pass its trajectory directly. The trajectory guide explains timestamps, signal names, resampling and trajectory forecasts.

docs.title: 2. Forecast and measure error
docs.text:
prediction = model.forecast(horizon=len(truth))
assert prediction.shape == truth.shape
rmse = (prediction - truth).square().mean().sqrt()
assert torch.isfinite(rmse)

The first prediction estimates the sample immediately after the observations. A horizon of 200 returns 200 future samples, in the original units. Supply history=new_observations to synchronize on a different observed sequence. Otherwise the model uses its saved training history.

Chaotic forecasts eventually diverge. Compare several starting points and seeds on validation data, then evaluate the final choice on an untouched test period. Automatic tuning handles the validation split, candidate comparison and final refit. Matched speed–accuracy comparisons remain in roadmap phase five.

docs.title: 3. Save and restore the complete model
docs.text:
model.save("trained.pt")
restored = rd.load("trained.pt", map_location="cpu")
restored_prediction = restored.forecast(horizon=len(truth))
torch.testing.assert_close(restored_prediction, prediction, rtol=0, atol=0)
model.save("model.svg")  # diagram; requires the optional visualization tools

The checkpoint includes the architecture, fitted weights, preprocessing, observed history and ordinary-forward reservoir memory. You do not reconstruct the DAG. Forecasts replay their supplied or saved history; a checkpoint does not resume an in-progress delayed rollout. See save and load for custom components, notebook bundles and diagram formats. Standard state_dict() remains available for larger PyTorch pipelines that already own the architecture.

docs.title: 4. Put it inside a larger PyTorch model
docs.text:
from torch import nn

pipeline = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(2, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    restored,
    nn.Linear(2, 1, dtype=torch.float64),
)
restored.reset_state()
batch = training[-20:].unsqueeze(0).detach().requires_grad_()
loss = pipeline(batch).square().mean()
loss.backward()
assert batch.grad is not None and torch.isfinite(batch.grad).all()

Frozen reservoir weights still pass gradients to the preceding encoder. Use ordinary Torch losses and optimizers. Fit or build(input_size=...) before attaching an optimizer, so it sees every parameter.

Calls carry reservoir state. Reset before unrelated windows; train() and eval() do not reset it. For explicit state across chunks:

first, state = restored.forward_stateless(training[:20])
second, state = restored.forward_stateless(training[20:40], states=state)
assert first.shape == second.shape == (20, 2)

These calls leave stored reservoir state unchanged. The returned states can retain gradients across chunks. Detach them yourself when intentionally truncating backpropagation.

docs.title: 5. Customize only what you need
docs.text:
Use readout and readout_kwargs to select or configure a solver. Supply custom initializers directly or register them by name. Use model.graph for raw, already-preprocessed graph execution.

For branches, drivers, multiple outputs or a different recurrent cell, build rd.Model(inputs={...}, outputs={...}). It uses the same fit, forecast, forward, state and checkpoint commands. Start with the common model guide, then the public component recipes. Use custom preprocessing to change the units of individual inputs or outputs while retaining automatic inverse conversion. Named trajectories align several timestamped inputs and targets for a custom graph.

docs.title: 6. Choose device and precision explicitly
docs.text:
Move both the model and tensor data with .to(device=..., dtype=...). Fitted statistics move with the model. An untouched lazy ESN adopts its first training tensor's dtype/device; explicit constructor placement or .to(...) fixes them.

On MPS, use float32. The default automatic readout uses supported native solves when its numerical checks pass, and reports/warns about any CPU float64 fallback. Set readout_kwargs={"cpu_fallback": False} to require native fitting, or explicitly choose a solver. See readout solvers.

Use compile=True only for supported fast execution, and measure first-time compilation separately. For custom operations that need the whole sequence, choose history execution. It trades extra computation and memory for complete-prefix semantics.

docs.title: Forecast targets and feedback connections
docs.text:
A forecast starts with the first unseen sample after your history. Two settings describe how a custom model gets there:

  • Prediction lead tells a head what to learn. Lead 2 pairs an input at time t with the observation at t + 2.
  • Feedback delay tells a connection when to reuse an output. Delay 2 feeds an output back into its input two model steps after that output was produced.

Both default to 1. For normal self-feedback, use the same lead and delay. Different values let you build deliberately lagged connections between parts of a model.

docs.title: Start with the default
docs.text:
import torch
import resdag as rd

x = rd.reservoir_input(1, dtype=torch.float64)
y = rd.RidgeReadoutLayer(1, 1, alpha=0.0).double()(x)
model = rd.Model(
    inputs={"state": x},
    outputs={"next_state": y},
    washout=0,
)
observed = torch.arange(8, dtype=torch.float64)[:, None]
model.fit(observed)
prediction = model.forecast(horizon=4)  # approximately 8, 9, 10, 11

fit(observed) prepares the shifted input/target pairs for you. The default feedback connection runs from the first output to the first input. Its delay automatically matches that output's prediction lead.

docs.title: Predict two steps ahead
docs.text:
x = rd.reservoir_input(1, dtype=torch.float64)
y = rd.RidgeReadoutLayer(1, 1, alpha=0.0).double()(x)
model = rd.Model(
    inputs={"state": x},
    outputs={"next_state": y},
    prediction_lead=2,
    feedback=[rd.Feedback(output="next_state", input="state", delay=2)],
    washout=0,
)
observed = torch.arange(5, dtype=torch.float64)[:, None]
model.fit(observed)
prediction = model.forecast(horizon=4)  # approximately 5, 6, 7, 8

The last two warmup outputs already estimate samples 5 and 6. Forecasting keeps both pending predictions, then generates 7 and 8. It does not skip sample 5. You can omit feedback here: the automatic connection also uses delay 2.

For a head trained to add 1, choosing lead 1 and delay 2 instead produces 5, 5, 6, 6 after the history 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. That repeated pattern is the declared lag, rather than an indexing correction.

docs.title: Route by public names
docs.text:
Each Feedback uses the names from the model's inputs and outputs mappings. Internal layer names and mapping insertion order do not select connections.

connections = [
    rd.Feedback(output="slow_prediction", input="slow_state", delay=2),
    rd.Feedback(output="fast_prediction", input="fast_state", delay=1),
]
leads = {"slow_prediction": 2, "fast_prediction": 1}

Pass these as feedback=connections, prediction_lead=leads when constructing your graph. A lead mapping can override selected heads; other heads use lead 1. An output can feed several inputs, but each input accepts at most one feedback connection. Connected widths must match. Add an explicit graph projection when you need a width conversion.

Inputs without a connection are external drivers. Supply them by name in forecast(..., future_inputs={"forcing": future_forcing}). Their first sample belongs immediately after the observed history. For ordinary next-step heads, a horizon of 100 needs 99 driver samples: warmup already provides the first prediction. More generally, the count is max(0, horizon - min(model.prediction_leads.values())).

Use feedback=[] when every input is externally driven. History must contain at least the largest lead and largest connection delay so every pending value can be initialized. Names, widths, history and driver lengths are checked before forecasting changes reservoir state or runs model hooks.

docs.title: Scaling and explicit targets
docs.text:
Feedback travels through original units: the source head's inverse transform is followed by the destination input's transform. Independently fitted target statistics therefore work without manual packing or scaling. All tensor operations stay on the model device; only an explicitly selected trajectory result converts to NumPy.

With fit(inputs, targets=...), target arrays are already aligned with their input rows. prediction_lead records the physical time that each target row represents; it does not shift explicit arrays a second time. For example, a lead-2 target supplied at input row t must already contain the desired value at physical time t + 2.

All returned heads share the same future physical timeline. With return_warmup=True, the shared historical prefix starts at the largest lead: for history length W and largest lead L, the result has W - L + horizon samples per head. Trajectory timestamps follow this same alignment.

docs.title: Custom temporal modules
docs.text:
Fast forecasting uses one input frame per step. Built-in pointwise transforms and explicit reservoir layers support this. A custom module can declare supports_framewise = True when its evaluation is independent across time, preserves batch/time dimensions, and has no hidden temporal state.

For a pure causal sequence transform such as a prefix sum, choose forecast(..., execution="history"). This recomputes the entire growing observed/generated input prefix from the configured reservoir reset on each step. It retains every prefix sample and costs more time and memory. Such graphs also fit their terminal heads from complete-prefix features before discarding washout rows, and retain their complete fitting history for cached forecasting. Ordinary fast models retain only their compact synchronization tail. History execution currently requires compile=False.

Custom temporal modules must be pure across evaluation calls. Expose mutable streaming state through a BaseReservoirLayer adapter; replay cannot discover or reset arbitrary buffers hidden in a custom module.

docs.title: State and checkpoints
docs.text:
Each forecast call starts a fresh rollout from its history, rebuilding delayed queues. get_state() and set_state() describe reservoir state for ordinary forward calls; those tensors do not include pending feedback or its clock and cannot resume a delayed forecast by themselves.

state_dict() includes prediction leads, connection names/delays, fitted scalers and cached history. Loading restores those settings after validating the graph's named ports. Complete model artifacts are covered by the model workflow guide.

docs.title: First forecast
docs.text: Start · First forecast

docs.title: First forecast
docs.text:
An ESN learns a map from the signal now to the next sample. Its reservoir weights stay fixed; fitting solves the linear prediction head. During an autonomous forecast, each prediction becomes the next input.

This example needs only the core installation. It separates training and unseen observations before fitting. Scaling is learned from training inputs and predictions are returned in the original units.

import torch
import resdag as rd

series = rd.datasets.lorenz(6001, normalize=None, seed=7)[0]
training, truth = series[:5001], series[5001:]

model = rd.ESN(reservoir_size=300, washout=200, seed=7)
model.fit(training)
prediction = model.forecast(horizon=len(truth))

assert prediction.shape == truth.shape == (1000, 3)
rmse = (prediction - truth).square().mean().sqrt()
print(f"Forecast RMSE: {rmse.item():.4g}")

washout=200 lets the reservoir synchronize before collecting supervised training rows. The last observed sample supplies the last shifted target. forecast() uses the saved training history and begins at the first unseen sample, truth[0]. It never needs truth to generate those predictions.

The default readout checks numerical safety while preserving the requested ridge penalty. Use readout_kwargs={"solver": "svd"} to force SVD, or choose another readout solver. CUDA placement uses ordinary .to("cuda") on both model and tensors; measure your workload using the deployment guide.

docs.title: Save and reuse the model
docs.text:
model.save("lorenz.pt")
restored = rd.load("lorenz.pt")
replayed = restored.forecast(horizon=len(truth))
torch.testing.assert_close(replayed, prediction, rtol=0, atol=0)

The artifact includes the graph, fitted scaling, readout weights, observed history and current recurrent memory. Loading does not require the original DAG-building code for built-in components. See save, load and diagrams for custom layers and image exports.

docs.title: Improve forecast accuracy
docs.text:
The small example above demonstrates the workflow; its parameters are not a claim of long-range chaotic prediction. Tune on observations reserved for validation and keep final test samples outside the tuning call:

# Optional: pip install "resdag[hpo]"
# model.tune(training, preset="quick")
# prediction = model.forecast(horizon=len(truth))

Tuning refits the winning configuration on the supplied training observations. Its built-in validation split never uses truth above. The balanced and thorough presets check more configurations, random initializations and forecast starting points. See tuning for custom search ranges and objectives.

A separate recorded Lorenz experiment, with its trajectory, reservoir seed and forecast start fixed before final evaluation. The full supplied window is shown in original units. The valid prefix stops at the first component-normalized RMS error of 0.3; training observations supply the scales. This image is not a benchmark of the small example above. The [study protocol and complete results](../project/phase-five-robustness.md) report all independent trajectories and both 0.3 and 0.5 thresholds.

For your own data, use the same fit/forecast calls with a (time, signals) or (batch, time, signals) tensor. TSDynamics trajectories carry timestamps and signal names automatically. Plot and animate a forecast adds a custom model diagram, component plots and an attractor movie.

docs.title: Run a forecast experiment
docs.text:
This example builds a network, draws its DAG, trains it and measures how long its autonomous prediction follows a Lorenz trajectory. The same commands work for a vanilla ESN, an OTT model and your own DAG.

Install on Python 3.12 or newer:

python -m pip install "resdag[hpo,dynamics,viz]"

SVG diagrams also need the Graphviz executable: brew install graphviz on macOS, or your system's Graphviz package. Saving .dot works without it.

docs.title: Generate data and keep the future separate
docs.text:
from time import perf_counter

import numpy as np
import torch
import tsdynamics as ts
import resdag as rd

trajectory = ts.systems.Lorenz().run(
    final_time=100, dt=0.02, transient=20,
    solver="dop853", rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-12,
)
training, truth = trajectory[:4000], trajectory[4000:4500]
washout = 200

training contains observed samples. truth is the future we will check after training. Neither the readout nor preprocessing sees truth during fit. The model learns scaling from training data and returns predictions in the original units.

docs.title: Choose a ready-made model
docs.text:
models = {
    "vanilla": rd.ESN(
        reservoir_size=192, input_size=3, washout=washout,
        readout="svd", seed=7, dtype=torch.float64,
    ),
    "ott": rd.Model(
        graph=rd.ott_esn(192, 3, 3, readout="svd", seed=7, dtype=torch.float64),
        washout=washout,
    ),
}

Both have 192 reservoir units and give the readout the observed input alongside the reservoir features. Vanilla uses the states unchanged; OTT squares every other state before concatenation, keeping the same feature count. These are starting settings, not tuned accuracy recipes.

docs.title: Or connect your own DAG
docs.text:
Two branches can remember the same signal at different rates. Concatenating their states with the original input gives the readout all three sources.

x = rd.reservoir_input(3, dtype=torch.float64)
fast = rd.ESNLayer(
    96, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9, leak_rate=1.0,
    seed=7, dtype=torch.float64,
)(x)
slow = rd.ESNLayer(
    96, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9, leak_rate=0.3,
    seed=8, dtype=torch.float64,
)(x)
features = rd.Concatenate()(x, fast, slow)  # 3 + 96 + 96 signals
y = rd.SVDReadoutLayer(195, 3, alpha=1e-6).double()(features)
models["custom"] = rd.Model(
    inputs={"state": x}, outputs={"prediction": y}, washout=washout,
)
models["custom"].save("custom.svg")

Open custom.svg to inspect the connections. In a notebook, models["custom"].plot_model() returns a displayable Graphviz diagram. Changing a layer, its initializer or solver changes the model you train; the surrounding fit/forecast workflow stays the same.

docs.title: Train, forecast and measure
docs.text:
For each future sample, compare the prediction with the true signals. Normalize each signal's error with the standard deviation of its training targets after washout. For next-sample training, those are training.y[washout + 1:]: the final observed sample is a known training label. This keeps the score's scale fixed before seeing the future.

The valid prediction horizon ends at the first error of 0.3 or higher. Converting it to Lyapunov times uses the actual sample interval and the canonical Lorenz exponent, approximately 0.9056 per unit of physical time.

scale = training.y[washout + 1:].std(axis=0)
scale = np.where(scale == 0, 1.0, scale)
dt = float(training.t[1] - training.t[0])
lambda_max = 0.9056
results = {}

for name, model in models.items():
    start = perf_counter()
    model.fit(training)
    fit_seconds = perf_counter() - start

    start = perf_counter()
    prediction = model.forecast(history=training[-500:], horizon=len(truth))
    forecast_seconds = perf_counter() - start
    np.testing.assert_allclose(prediction.t, truth.t, rtol=0, atol=1e-10)

    error = np.sqrt(np.mean(((prediction.y - truth.y) / scale) ** 2, axis=-1))
    valid = np.isfinite(error) & (error < 0.3)
    steps = len(valid) if valid.all() else int(np.argmax(~valid))
    secondary = np.isfinite(error) & (error < 0.5)
    secondary_steps = len(error) if secondary.all() else int(np.argmax(~secondary))
    results[name] = {
        "fit_seconds": fit_seconds,
        "forecast_seconds": forecast_seconds,
        "valid_steps": steps,
        "valid_lyapunov_times": steps * dt * lambda_max,
        "reached_horizon": bool(valid.all()),
        "secondary_valid_lyapunov_times_at_0_5": secondary_steps * dt * lambda_max,
        "secondary_reached_horizon": bool(secondary.all()),
    }
    print(name, results[name])

The forecast receives observed history to synchronize the reservoir. Its first prediction is the sample immediately after that history. After that, its own predictions feed the reservoir: it does not receive future truth.

If reached_horizon is true, the result is a lower bound: extend the test window before claiming that you measured the model's full limit. A single origin and seed do not establish general accuracy. These illustrative settings do not promise 7–8 Lyapunov times. Choose settings on separate validation data, then compare several seeds and starting points on an untouched test period. See automatic tuning.

The stricter 0.3 threshold is the main score; 0.5 is a secondary, more permissive score. The phase-five 7–8 Lyapunov-time target applies to the median across seeds and starting points at 0.3, with the full spread reported. A lucky single forecast is not enough.

These training-normalized scores have a different scale from resdag.metrics.valid_prediction_time, which uses the supplied truth window's standard deviation. State the normalization and threshold when comparing reported numbers. Do not compare horizons measured with different definitions.

docs.title: Tune without using the final test
docs.text:
Pass only training to tuning. It holds out the final 20% of that data for candidate selection, then refits the winner on all of training. The separate truth segment stays outside the call.

tuned = models["vanilla"]
tuned.tune(
    training, preset="balanced", threshold=0.3, horizon=200, seed=7,
    n_trials=2, seeds=[7], n_origins=1,  # small tutorial budget
)
tuned_prediction = tuned.forecast(horizon=len(truth))
np.testing.assert_allclose(tuned_prediction.t, truth.t, rtol=0, atol=1e-10)
tuned_error = np.sqrt(np.mean(((tuned_prediction.y - truth.y) / scale) ** 2, axis=-1))
tuned_valid = np.isfinite(tuned_error) & (tuned_error < 0.3)
tuned_steps = len(truth) if tuned_valid.all() else int(np.argmax(~tuned_valid))
print("Winning settings:", tuned.tuning_report.best_params)
print("Final-test Lyapunov times:", tuned_steps * dt * lambda_max)

The explicit overrides keep this tutorial short. Remove n_trials, seeds and n_origins for the full balanced budget: 24 configurations × 3 seeds × 3 forecast starting points. Increase the validation horizon when measuring longer predictions; it must fit completely within the held-out validation span. Two candidates over a short validation horizon are a workflow demonstration, not evidence of the 7–8 target. A final test that stays valid throughout remains a lower bound.

Built-in vanilla and OTT models now search input strength, bias and recurrent connection density as well as width, radius, leak and regularization. Use models["ott"].tune(training, ...) for the same automatic workflow. Supply search_space to fix settings or choose different ranges. These convenient defaults are separate from the explicitly configured phase-five accuracy experiments; reproducing their reported horizons requires their recorded recipes and evaluation protocol.

For a separate validation trajectory, supply validation=(validation_trajectory, None) while keeping the final test out of the call. For custom DAGs, provide a model-building recipe to search over layer widths, wiring and initializers. The winner stays in the same model object and is ready to forecast.

docs.title: Save the trained DAG and reload it
docs.text:
custom = models["custom"]
custom.save("custom.pt")
restored = rd.load("custom.pt")
expected = custom.forecast(history=training[-500:], horizon=len(truth))
actual = restored.forecast(history=training[-500:], horizon=len(truth))
np.testing.assert_allclose(actual.y, expected.y, rtol=0, atol=0)

The file contains the graph, fitted readout, preprocessing and current memory. You do not need to know or rebuild its DAG. See save and load for registered custom components, trusted notebook bundles and device mapping.

docs.title: Try Rössler or a larger reservoir
docs.text:
The runnable script generates data, evaluates all three models, saves their diagrams and portable checkpoints, and checks reload parity.

Run these commands from a ResDAG checkout. The complete script is examples/17_forecast_experiment.py.

python examples/17_forecast_experiment.py --system lorenz --output lorenz-run
python examples/17_forecast_experiment.py --system rossler --reservoir-size 400 --output rossler-run

Each run also writes experiment.json and replay-data.pt. The manifest records the resolved arguments, system and integration settings, dependency versions, actual data/split identities, metric definitions, model configurations and artifact hashes. The Torch data file retains the exact training observations, clocked history, future truth and original predictions. Use a separate output directory for each experiment.

Verify a saved run with:

python examples/17_forecast_experiment.py --verify lorenz-run/experiment.json

Verification checks the files and time alignment, reconstructs the saved TSDynamics history, loads the models, and compares complete forecasts and recomputed scores exactly. It performs no new integration, fitting or tuning. It needs the existing dynamics extra to reconstruct the clocked history; diagrams are checked as saved files without rendering them again. Original timings remain recorded observations; replay does not verify performance. Versions are recorded so numerical differences after changing software, precision or hardware can be investigated rather than hidden by a tolerance.

The script uses canonical Rössler parameters (a, b, c) = (0.2, 0.2, 5.7) and an approximate largest exponent of 0.0714. Its default evaluation window covers at least ten Lyapunov times for either system; that is the available scoring window, not a prediction-quality claim. Override --dt, --horizon, --seed, --washout or --history to make the experiment yours. Changing system parameters also requires a corresponding exponent; never reuse a canonical exponent for a different dynamical regime.

--diagram-format dot avoids visualization dependencies. The reported CPU wall times include the convenient workflow and are exploratory measurements, not a controlled speed comparison. Phase-five benchmarks define the reproducible comparison.

docs.title: On GPUs
docs.text:
Move the model and its floating inputs to CUDA with .to("cuda"). Forward calls preserve gradients and device placement inside larger Torch networks. Readout fitting may use a reported CPU fallback when the selected solver cannot complete a safe solve on the accelerator; configure its solver policy explicitly when that fallback is unsuitable.

Speed depends on reservoir width, batch size, sequence length, sparsity, precision and the surrounding network. Small sequential forecasts can spend more time launching kernels than multiplying matrices. Larger batches can amortize that overhead, but there is no universal reservoir-size crossover or guaranteed speedup. Run examples/11_gpu_benchmark.py on the target hardware, and measure both startup and repeated execution. CUDA throughput is not established by the current CPU/MPS correctness checks.

Scale & deploy covers device placement patterns in detail.

docs.title: The common model workflow
docs.text:
rd.Model adds training, scaling and forecasting around a functional graph. It is an ordinary PyTorch module. You keep control of the layers, their initializers and the readout solver.

Inputs are floating Torch tensors shaped (time, features) or (batch, time, features), on the same device and dtype as the graph. Named multi-input data uses a dictionary of those tensors. rd.ESN provides the same Torch workflow for a ready-made classic reservoir. Convert NumPy arrays with torch.as_tensor at the boundary. fit and forecast also accept TSDynamics trajectories, including named trajectories for several ports. Ordinary model(x) calls retain the tensor interface.

This is part of phase two. The common interface supports the ESN preset, symbolic, parallel and coupled graphs. Raw ESNModel and factories remain useful building blocks. Unified tuning is available for presets and custom DAGs. Complete model saves, automatic loading and diagram exports are available through the same interface.

docs.title: Build, fit and forecast
docs.text:
The inputs are named signals. The outputs are named predictions. Connect layers with layer(x), then give those connections to rd.Model.

import torch
import resdag as rd

# A small example with two signals in different physical units.
t = torch.arange(400, dtype=torch.float64) * 0.05
series = torch.stack((10 + 2 * t.sin(), -3 + 0.5 * t.cos()), dim=-1)
train, truth = series[:300], series[300:340]

x = rd.reservoir_input(2, dtype=torch.float64)
h = rd.ESNLayer(64, feedback_size=2, seed=7, dtype=torch.float64)(x)
y = rd.SVDReadoutLayer(64, 2, alpha=1e-6).double()(h)
model = rd.Model(inputs={"state": x}, outputs={"prediction": y}, washout=30)

model.fit(train)
prediction = model.forecast(history=train[-60:], horizon=40)
assert prediction.shape == truth.shape
assert torch.isfinite(prediction).all()

For one input and one output of the same width, fit(train) learns to predict the next sample. It uses the first washout samples to synchronize the reservoir, then fits the readout. Pass only training data to fit; keep validation and test samples separate.

Standard scaling is automatic. Its statistics come from the supervised training inputs, excluding washout and the final shifted target. Forecasts are returned in the signals' original units. The first forecast sample estimates the sample immediately after the supplied history.

Omit history to continue from the saved tail of the training data. Supplying history resynchronizes the reservoir on that history before forecasting. Choose preprocessing=None to handle scaling yourself, or choose an existing normalization method: "standard", "minmax", "noncentered" or "meanpreserving".

Override individual ports with input_transforms={"state": your_module} and output_transforms={"prediction": your_module}. Each module preserves the signals and provides a reversible change of units. Use a distinct instance for each port; torch.nn.Identity() disables preprocessing on one port. Explicit overrides still apply when the global policy is off. See custom preprocessing for a complete example, fitting rules and checkpoints. Operations that add features or memory belong inside the DAG as ordinary layers.

docs.title: Use a preset graph
docs.text:
For the ready-made vanilla model, choose its readout features explicitly:

state_only = rd.ESN(
    reservoir_size=64, input_size=2, input_to_readout=False,
    washout=30, readout="svd", seed=7, dtype=torch.float64,
).fit(train)
state_only_prediction = state_only.forecast(horizon=40)
assert state_only_prediction.shape == truth.shape

The default input_to_readout=True gives the head both reservoir memory and the current input. False gives it reservoir memory alone. model.tune() tries both for an unmodified vanilla recipe. A custom DAG can connect either set of features directly; OTT's augmented features keep their own wiring.

Wrap a factory-built graph with the same model interface:

graph = rd.classic_esn(
    reservoir_size=64, feedback_size=2, output_size=2,
    readout="svd", seed=7, dtype=torch.float64,
)
preset = rd.Model(graph=graph, washout=30)
preset.fit(train)
preset_prediction = preset.forecast(history=train[-60:], horizon=40)
assert preset_prediction.shape == truth.shape

model.graph gives access to the exact underlying graph and its parameters. It works in the graph's raw, preprocessed units. Use model(...) when your pipeline supplies and expects the original units.

docs.title: Parallel and coupled models
docs.text:
The same wrapper works for a spatial field split into overlapping patches:

parallel = rd.Model(
    graph=rd.parallel_esn(
        input_dim=2, core_width=1, halo=1, reservoir_size=32,
        readout="svd", seed=7, dtype=torch.float64,
    ),
    washout=30,
)
parallel.fit(train)
parallel_prediction = parallel.forecast(history=train[-60:], horizon=40)
assert parallel_prediction.shape == truth.shape

Inputs and returned predictions use the full field width. Scaling is learned per field component, before the backend gathers local patches. Each patch keeps its own recurrent state; reservoir and readout weights remain shared.

For an ensemble whose members share one aggregate feedback signal:

coupled = rd.Model(
    graph=rd.coupled_ensemble_esn(
        n_models=3, model_factory=rd.classic_esn,
        reservoir_size=32, feedback_size=2, output_size=2,
        readout="svd", seed=7, dtype=torch.float64,
    ),
    washout=30,
)
coupled.fit(train)
coupled_prediction = coupled.forecast(history=train[-60:], horizon=40)
assert coupled_prediction.shape == truth.shape

The coupled backend retains its existing single aggregate output. Each member fits its own head, even when internal readout names differ. Inspect individual member forecasts through coupled.graph; the common workflow returns the aggregate. Parallel and coupled forecast currently require compile=False. Unsupported compiled forecasts fail before running the graph.

Both families use the same original-unit forward calls, carried state, explicit-state calls, dtype/device moves and state dictionaries as symbolic graphs. Rebuild the same architecture before loading a state dictionary, including custom aggregator settings. Its schema checks structural facts, not arbitrary Python configuration. Use model.save("run.pt") and rd.load("run.pt") for complete architecture reconstruction; see save and load.

docs.title: Give several heads explicit targets
docs.text:
Name each output and pass matching targets. Explicit targets line up with the supplied input samples; fit does not shift them. Here we supply that shift ourselves and add a second quantity to predict:

state = rd.reservoir_input(2, dtype=torch.float64)
features = rd.ESNLayer(32, feedback_size=2, seed=11, dtype=torch.float64)(state)
position = rd.SVDReadoutLayer(32, 2, alpha=1e-6).double()(features)
energy = rd.SVDReadoutLayer(32, 1, alpha=1e-6).double()(features)
multi = rd.Model(
    inputs={"state": state},
    outputs={"position": position, "energy": energy},
    washout=30,
)
next_state = train[1:]
multi.fit(
    {"state": train[:-1]},
    targets={
        "position": next_state,
        "energy": next_state.square().sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True),
    },
)
named = multi({"state": train[-20:]})
assert named["position"].shape == (20, 2)
assert named["energy"].shape == (20, 1)

Each target gets its own training-only scaling. The user-facing output names do not need to match the graph's generated readout names. Feedback converts the selected prediction through original units before applying the receiving input's scaling. See feedback and timing for named connections, delays and predicting several samples ahead.

docs.title: Put the trained model inside PyTorch
docs.text:
model(x) returns a tensor for a single output, preserves gradients and carries reservoir state between calls. Reset before starting an unrelated sequence. train() and eval() do not reset that state.

from torch import nn

pipeline = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(2, 2, dtype=torch.float64),
    model,
    nn.Linear(2, 1, dtype=torch.float64),
)
model.reset_state()
batch = train[-20:].unsqueeze(0).detach().requires_grad_()
loss = pipeline(batch).square().mean()
loss.backward()
assert batch.grad is not None
assert torch.isfinite(batch.grad).all()

Frozen reservoir weights still pass gradients to the preceding layer. Stored reservoir state follows the layers' existing detach policy at call boundaries. For explicit streaming state and gradients across chunks, use prediction, state = model.forward_stateless(chunk, states=previous_state). That path leaves stored reservoir state unchanged.

Move the complete model with ordinary .to(device) or .double() calls; fitted scaling statistics move with it. Scaling and the graph are included in state_dict(). As with ordinary PyTorch checkpoints, loading a state dict still requires a compatible model architecture. Use model.save("run.pt") and rd.load("run.pt") to restore a complete model without rebuilding its graph; see save and load.

On Apple MPS, AutoReadoutLayer uses supported float32 operations when its numerical checks pass. Unsafe or unsupported decompositions use a reported, configurable CPU float64 bridge. You can also fit on CPU and move the model with model.float().to("mps"). See solver controls.

docs.title: Train the surrounding network
docs.text:
After fitting the RC block, ordinary Torch optimizers can train the encoder and prediction head. The reservoir and algebraically fitted readout stay frozen unless you explicitly make them trainable. Construct the optimizer after fitting or building the model, so every parameter is registered.

Reset the reservoir before unrelated training windows. Calls otherwise carry memory, with gradients detached at each ordinary call boundary. For gradients across chunks of one sequence, use forward_stateless(..., states=...) and carry the returned state yourself.

The following uses standard PyTorch mixed precision and gradient scaling:

import copy

amp_device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
amp_pipeline = copy.deepcopy(pipeline).to(device=amp_device, dtype=torch.float32)
amp_optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(amp_pipeline.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
amp_scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler("cuda", enabled=amp_device.type == "cuda")
amp_dtype = torch.float16 if amp_device.type == "cuda" else torch.bfloat16
amp_batch = train[-20:].unsqueeze(0).to(device=amp_device, dtype=torch.float32)
amp_target = amp_batch[..., :1]

for _ in range(2):
    amp_pipeline[1].reset_state()
    amp_optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    with torch.autocast(amp_device.type, dtype=amp_dtype):
        amp_prediction = amp_pipeline(amp_batch)
        amp_loss = torch.nn.functional.mse_loss(amp_prediction.float(), amp_target)
    amp_scaler.scale(amp_loss).backward()
    amp_scaler.step(amp_optimizer)
    amp_scaler.update()

CPU CSR multiplication has no low-precision kernel. Under CPU autocast, a sparse ESN therefore computes its recurrent multiplication and carried state in its stored weight precision; the surrounding encoder and head still use autocast. No tensor moves to another device for this operation. Explicitly stored low-precision CSR weights still require a matching supported Torch kernel.

Standard torch.compile(pipeline) is separate from the reservoir forecast's compile=True shortcut. The surrounding network's forward and backward can be captured together; ordinary calls still detach stored state between calls. The forecast shortcut remains inference-only. Full-graph capture and compiled backward are tested for the built-in vanilla, OTT and named custom DAG examples with the AOT eager backend. This checks compiler compatibility, not CUDA throughput. Measure cold setup and warm execution on your actual device and check forecast accuracy when changing precision.

docs.title: Capture the surrounding pipeline with FX
docs.text:
If a larger pipeline uses PyTorch FX, keep the reservoir as one module call. Use FX's standard leaf-module hook:

from torch import fx

class ReservoirTracer(fx.Tracer):
    def is_leaf_module(self, module, qualified_name):
        return isinstance(module, (rd.Model, rd.ESN)) or super().is_leaf_module(
            module, qualified_name
        )

captured = fx.GraphModule(pipeline, ReservoirTracer().trace(pipeline))
assert captured.get_submodule("1") is model
model.reset_state()
expected = pipeline(batch.detach())
model.reset_state()
actual = captured(batch.detach())
torch.testing.assert_close(actual, expected)

Capture preserves the same model, parameters and carried state. It does not execute the reservoir during tracing. Direct tracing through rd.Model and general deployment export are not supported; see the graph-tooling review for the evaluated boundaries.

docs.title: Current boundaries
docs.text:
• The common wrapper supports symbolic ESNModel, ParallelESNModel and CoupledEnsembleESNModel graphs. Their original low-level APIs remain available.
  • Automatic next-sample targets require one unambiguous input/output pair. Several heads need explicit named targets; their predictions are returned as a dictionary. Internal fitted readouts can stay hidden from predictions: provide their targets through fit(..., readout_targets={...}), as shown in training internal readouts.
  • Default feedback connects the first output to the first input. Custom named routes support fanout and explicit delays. Inputs without a feedback route need future driver values.
  • Reservoirs must be separate functional nodes for explicit-state and forecast execution. See state management.
  • Forecasting and explicit-state calls honor PyTorch execution hooks, including hooks on the model, reservoir, nested modules and global hook registrations. Input/output hooks on Model or ESN operate in the original signal units. Adding or removing hooks takes effect on the next call; hook-free models keep the lean flat forecast path. Hooks select an eager compatible path, with a warning when compile=True was requested.
  • Fast forecasting requires framewise operations or explicit reservoir nodes. Custom sequence operations can use history execution, which replays their full growing prefix. Delayed/named feedback uses explicit state; reservoir state alone cannot resume an in-progress delayed rollout.
  • Fitting stages a copy of the graph before committing trained weights. This preserves the existing model after a failed fit and keeps parameter objects intact, but requires memory for that temporary copy and the solver workspace.

See the core reference for signatures and the phase-two design note for agreed behavior and remaining decisions.

docs.title: Named trajectories
docs.text:
Use named TSDynamics trajectories when a model has several observed inputs or prediction heads. ResDAG aligns the observed inputs on one clock and uses each head's prediction_lead to find its target labels. You still call fit and forecast; you do not need to pack signals into one array.

Install resdag[dynamics] on Python 3.12 or newer. Every named input in one call must be a Trajectory; every explicit target must also be a trajectory. Mixed tensor and trajectory ports are rejected because tensors have no physical timestamps. The ordinary named tensor workflow remains available when you already prepared aligned arrays.

docs.title: Build a model with two prediction heads
docs.text:
Here position follows x[t+1] = x[t] + force[t]. One head predicts one sample ahead; another predicts two. The two-step head feeds position back after two graph steps. Their returned forecasts refer to the same physical dates.

import numpy as np
import torch
import tsdynamics as ts
import resdag as rd

def build_model():
    state = rd.reservoir_input(1, dtype=torch.float64)
    force = rd.reservoir_input(1, dtype=torch.float64)
    features = rd.Concatenate()(state, force)
    near = rd.RidgeReadoutLayer(2, 1, alpha=0.0).double()(features)
    far = rd.RidgeReadoutLayer(2, 1, alpha=0.0).double()(features)
    return rd.Model(
        inputs={"state": state, "force": force},
        outputs={"near": near, "far": far},
        prediction_lead={"near": 1, "far": 2},
        feedback=[rd.Feedback("far", "state", delay=2)],
        washout=2,
    )

def position(time):
    return time * (time + 1) / 2

state_times = np.arange(13, dtype=np.float64)
force_times = np.arange(0.25, 12.26, 0.5)
observations = {
    "force": ts.Trajectory(
        force_times, (force_times + 1)[:, None], variables=("forcing",)
    ),
    "state": ts.Trajectory(
        state_times, position(state_times)[:, None], variables=("position",)
    ),
}
# Labels may begin later than observations. Each target owns its component name.
near_times = np.arange(6, 17, dtype=np.float64)
far_times = np.arange(5, 17, dtype=np.float64)
targets = {
    "near": ts.Trajectory(
        near_times, position(near_times)[:, None], variables=("near_position",)
    ),
    "far": ts.Trajectory(
        far_times, position(far_times)[:, None], variables=("far_position",)
    ),
}
model = build_model().fit(observations, targets)

The default interval comes from the first declared model input, state, so it is one time unit here. Caller dictionary order does not change it. The shared grid stays inside both observed ranges and ends at their latest common endpoint: [1, 2, ..., 12]. Set resample_dt to choose another interval; resample_method accepts "linear", "pchip" or "cubic".

For each origin t, the near head uses the target at t + dt, and the far head uses the target at t + 2*dt. Both labels exist for origins 5..10. Only those origins and their actual labels fit the scaling and readouts. washout=2 excludes the first two shared input samples; it does not discard another two samples after the late labels begin. Earlier observations still warm the recurrent layers. The cached tail includes observations through time 12, even after the last supervised origin. Fast framewise models retain washout + required_history input samples; complete-history models retain the full aligned observations. Pass explicit history when you need a longer warmup window.

Target observations after the latest common input endpoint are held out. They do not enter interpolation coefficients, fitted statistics or weights. Keep validation/test data outside the fit call as usual. Input interpolation may use available source observations surrounding a shared-grid point within that input's observed range. Resampling never extrapolates and does not apply an anti-alias filter when increasing the interval.

docs.title: Forecast with future drivers
docs.text:
Position is fed back by the model, while force needs external future values. Drivers are sampled at the required fitted ticks after the history endpoint; their own endpoints do not move the model's clock. With this one-step/two-step pair, a horizon of four needs three future driver samples.

driver_times = np.array([13.0, 13.25, 14.5, 15.0])
future_force = ts.Trajectory(
    driver_times, (driver_times + 1)[:, None], variables=("forcing",)
)
prediction = model.forecast(horizon=4, future_inputs={"force": future_force})
assert list(prediction) == ["near", "far"]
for name, result in prediction.items():
    assert isinstance(result, ts.Trajectory)
    assert result.variables == (f"{name}_position",)
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(result.t, [13, 14, 15, 16])
    np.testing.assert_allclose(result.y[:, 0], position(result.t), atol=1e-10)

tensors = model.forecast(
    horizon=4, future_inputs={"force": future_force}, return_type="tensor"
)
for name in model.output_names:
    torch.testing.assert_close(tensors[name], torch.from_numpy(prediction[name].y))

with_history = model.forecast(
    observations, horizon=4, future_inputs={"force": future_force}, return_warmup=True
)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(with_history["near"].t, np.arange(3, 17))
np.testing.assert_array_equal(with_history["near"].t, with_history["far"].t)

The warmup portion starts at history index max(prediction_leads), so every head shares the same timeline. A horizon of one needs no future driver here. If exactly one driver sample is needed, a one-row trajectory is supported. Tensor drivers are also accepted and are treated as caller-aligned samples.

Pass history={input_name: trajectory, ...} to forecast from another observed window. History is resampled to the fitted interval and must keep each input's component names and order. A new tensor history has no absolute clock: request tensor results and use tensor drivers, or provide timestamped history.

Ordinary model(named_tensors) preserves Torch gradients. Tensor forecasts stay on the model's device and dtype. Only a trajectory result converts its predictions to NumPy on CPU; bfloat16 values become float32 at that boundary. One output returns a single trajectory. Several outputs return a dictionary in declared model order, each with its target component names and source metadata.

docs.title: Restore a matching graph
docs.text:
The state dictionary records the shared clock, ordered port metadata, target component names, scaling and the cached observed tail. Reconstruct the same graph and custom preprocessing before loading its state.

torch.save(model.state_dict(), "named-model.pt")
restored = build_model()
restored.load_state_dict(torch.load("named-model.pt", weights_only=True))
replayed = restored.forecast(horizon=4, future_inputs={"force": future_force})
for name in model.output_names:
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(replayed[name].t, prediction[name].t)
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(replayed[name].y, prediction[name].y)

The current trajectory checkpoint envelope is version 2 for both bare and named inputs. Older common-workflow trajectory checkpoints are rejected; reconstruct and refit those models before saving a current checkpoint. There is no automatic checkpoint converter. Live producing-system objects are kept only in memory; restored forecasts retain plain source metadata and have .system is None. Generic artifact loading without reconstructing the graph remains a separate roadmap phase.

For a single observed signal with implicit next-sample targets, start with the basic trajectory workflow. For custom reversible scaling, see custom preprocessing.

docs.title: Forecast a TSDynamics trajectory
docs.text:
rd.Model.fit(trajectory) reads a TSDynamics Trajectory directly. The model learns next-sample targets and training-only scaling, and forecast() returns a new trajectory in the original signal units, with component names and future timestamps. Ordinary model(tensor) calls still return differentiable tensors.

Install the optional dynamics extra on Python 3.12 or newer:

python -m pip install "resdag[dynamics]"

docs.title: Simulate, fit and forecast
docs.text:
Use TSDynamics' public run method to generate a trajectory. Split training and evaluation samples before fitting or resampling.

import numpy as np
import torch
import tsdynamics as ts
import resdag as rd

trajectory = ts.systems.Lorenz().run(final_time=2.0, dt=0.02)
training, truth = trajectory[:81], trajectory[81:91]
model = rd.Model(
    graph=rd.classic_esn(16, 3, 3, seed=7, dtype=torch.float64, readout="svd"),
    washout=10,
)
model.fit(training)
prediction = model.forecast(history=training[-20:], horizon=10)

assert isinstance(prediction, ts.Trajectory)
assert prediction.y.shape == truth.y.shape == (10, 3)
assert prediction.variables == ("x", "y", "z")
assert np.isfinite(prediction.y).all()
np.testing.assert_allclose(prediction.t, truth.t, rtol=0, atol=1e-12)

The trajectory stores times in .t, values in .y and component labels in .variables. The forecast starts one sample after the supplied history. Omitting history uses the training tail retained by fit.

The example checks the interface and sample alignment; its small reservoir does not establish a forecast-accuracy benchmark for Lorenz.

docs.title: Check the physical-time boundary
docs.text:
A measured signal needs no producing system. Here the observed position rises by one every 0.25 time units. A terminal linear readout learns that increment exactly, making the first unseen value and timestamp explicit.

def ramp_model(**options):
    x = rd.reservoir_input(1, dtype=torch.float64)
    y = rd.RidgeReadoutLayer(1, 1, alpha=0.0).double()(x)
    return rd.Model(inputs={"state": x}, outputs={"next": y}, washout=0, **options)

observed = ts.Trajectory(
    10.0 + 0.25 * np.arange(8),
    np.arange(8.0)[:, None],
    variables=("position",),
)
ramp = ramp_model().fit(observed)
future = ramp.forecast(horizon=4)
np.testing.assert_allclose(future.y, [[8.0], [9.0], [10.0], [11.0]], atol=1e-11)
np.testing.assert_allclose(future.t, [12.0, 12.25, 12.5, 12.75], rtol=0, atol=1e-12)

with_history = ramp.forecast(history=observed, horizon=4, return_warmup=True)
np.testing.assert_allclose(with_history.y, np.arange(1.0, 12.0)[:, None], atol=1e-11)
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    with_history.t, 10.0 + 0.25 * np.arange(1, 12), rtol=0, atol=1e-12
)

With return_warmup=True, each historical input contributes its next-sample prediction. Those dates are the history dates after the first observation, followed by the forecast dates. The boundary prediction appears once.

Scaling statistics use supervised training inputs after washout, excluding the final observation that supplies the shifted target. Validation and test samples never belong in that fit call. Forecasting leaves those statistics and the cached training tail unchanged.

docs.title: Choose a sampling grid
docs.text:
Valid irregular trajectories are resampled automatically. By default, the new grid preserves the first time, last time and sample count. Its interval is (last_time - first_time) / (n_samples - 1). Existing regular observations pass through. Sampling comes from the actual time axis, even if source metadata contains an older dt.

Set resample_dt to choose an interval. That grid ends at the final observation and stays inside the observed time range, so it can drop a fractional interval at the beginning. Interpolation never extrapolates. resample_method accepts "linear" (default), "pchip" or "cubic". Interpolation does not apply an anti-alias filter when choosing a larger interval; apply any required filtering before supplying the training data.

irregular_times = np.array([2.0, 2.2, 2.9, 4.0])
irregular = ts.Trajectory(
    irregular_times,
    (3 * irregular_times + 10)[:, None],
    variables=("position",),
)
automatic = ramp_model().fit(irregular)
automatic_future = automatic.forecast(horizon=2)
np.testing.assert_allclose(automatic_future.t, [4 + 2 / 3, 4 + 4 / 3], atol=1e-12)
np.testing.assert_allclose(automatic_future.y, [[24.0], [26.0]], atol=1e-10)

fixed = ramp_model(resample_dt=0.75, resample_method="pchip").fit(irregular)
fixed_future = fixed.forecast(horizon=2)
np.testing.assert_allclose(fixed_future.t, [4.75, 5.5], rtol=0, atol=1e-12)
np.testing.assert_allclose(fixed_future.y, [[24.25], [26.5]], atol=1e-10)

The fixed grid above is [2.5, 3.25, 4.0]. A later trajectory supplied as forecast history is resampled to the fitted interval, keeping each recurrent step at the duration used for training. Its component names and order must match the training trajectory. Duplicate, decreasing or nonfinite times are rejected before execution. The time origin and interval must also remain distinguishable at float64 precision. If a large absolute time prevents a uniform grid, subtract a time origin or choose a coarser interval.

docs.title: Keep tensors on the model device
docs.text:
Choose return_type="tensor" to receive the usual Torch output on the model device. Trajectory output makes a detached CPU/NumPy copy after forecasting; the tensor path makes no such copy. Since NumPy has no bfloat16 dtype, bfloat16 trajectory values are converted to float32 at that output boundary.

tensor_future = ramp.forecast(horizon=4, return_type="tensor")
assert isinstance(tensor_future, torch.Tensor)
torch.testing.assert_close(tensor_future, torch.from_numpy(future.y))

tensor_history = torch.from_numpy(observed.y.copy())
tensor_continuation = ramp.forecast(
    history=tensor_history, horizon=4, return_type="tensor"
)
torch.testing.assert_close(tensor_continuation, tensor_future)

return_type="auto" is the default: trajectory fitting or explicit trajectory history selects trajectory output; a tensor-only workflow selects tensors. Tensor history supplies no timestamps, so requesting trajectory output from it raises a clear error. Supply a trajectory history or request tensor output. A successful tensor refit returns the default to tensors.

docs.title: Restore a checkpoint
docs.text:
The ordinary state dictionary includes scaling, the observed tail, sampling options, component names, clock information and portable source metadata. Rebuild the same named graph before loading.

import io

checkpoint = io.BytesIO()
torch.save(fixed.state_dict(), checkpoint)
checkpoint.seek(0)
restored = ramp_model()
restored.load_state_dict(torch.load(checkpoint, map_location="cpu", weights_only=True))
restored_future = restored.forecast(horizon=2)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(restored_future.t, fixed_future.t)
np.testing.assert_allclose(restored_future.y, fixed_future.y, rtol=0, atol=0)
assert restored_future.variables == ("position",)

The producing system is a transient reference and is not serialized. A restored forecast retains its source identity in .meta["source"], while .system is None. Model device/dtype conversions move tensors and fitted scaling; physical timestamps retain float64 precision. Source arrays become plain lists in checkpoint metadata. Opaque Python metadata values are represented by type markers instead of serialized objects.

Bare trajectory fitting infers shifted targets for one input/output of equal width. prediction_lead can select a larger distance. Warmup outputs then start at that lead's historical timestamp, while future predictions still begin at the first unseen sample. Named inputs and explicit trajectory targets are supported by the named trajectory workflow, which aligns all ports on a shared observed range and applies per-head leads to physical target timestamps. Tensor targets remain caller-aligned.

Both bare and named trajectory checkpoints use the current version 2 clock envelope. Older common-workflow trajectory metadata is rejected; reconstruct and refit those models to save a current checkpoint. There is no automatic converter. Ordinary tensor forward and explicit-state calls retain the PyTorch behavior described in the common model guide.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The Start and Build sections describe the API. This section specifies what the library computes: the exact update equations, which index is zero, which direction the target shift points, and what is and is not centered. Each formula is cross-referenced with the code that implements it, so the implementation can be checked against your own derivations or a published result.

Each page is self-contained, equations cite their implementing code, and conventions are stated explicitly rather than assumed.
