docs.title: Design of the library
docs.text: Presets and custom DAGs share a Model workflow around ordinary PyTorch modules. Reservoirs split into a single-step cell and a sequence layer; algebraic fitting traverses shared upstream work once. Initializers and custom components have explicit extension interfaces.

docs.title: The package map
docs.text:
resdag/
├── facade.py         ESN — ready-made Model workflow, eager or lazy construction
├── core/             Model workflow, ESNModel graph, feedback, state and execution
├── artifacts/        portable DAG/state codecs and explicit trusted bundles
├── layers/
│   ├── cells/          single-step updates, one per family: ESNCell, NGCell, …
│   ├── reservoirs/     sequence loop + state API: ESNLayer, NGReservoir, …
│   ├── readouts/       ReadoutLayer (an nn.Linear) + CGReadoutLayer, …
│   └── transforms/     Concatenate, Power, SelectiveExponentiation, …
├── init/
│   ├── topology/       registry + GraphTopology / MatrixTopology
│   ├── input_feedback/ registry + input/feedback initializers
│   ├── graphs/         NetworkX graph builders
│   └── matrices/       direct matrix builders (orthogonal, antisymmetric, …)
├── models/           premade factories: classic_esn, ott_esn, …
├── ensemble/         coupled ensembles + aggregators
├── training/         ESNTrainer — hook-based algebraic fitting
├── hpo/              Optuna integration (optional extra)
├── data/             data prep, I/O, window datasets, DataLoader factory
├── datasets/         public time-series generators
├── metrics/          forecast, dynamical, and attractor diagnostics
└── utils/            RNG helpers, esp_index, compatibility data imports

docs.title: The cell/layer split
docs.text:
Reservoirs follow PyTorch's own LSTMCell/LSTM pattern. The cell — every reservoir family implements one, such as ESNCell — owns all parameters and defines one timestep: forward(inputs, state) -> (output, new_state). The layer (BaseReservoirLayer and its subclasses) owns the time loop and the entire state-management API — lazy init, reset, get/set, detach semantics — once, for every cell type. Adding a new reservoir means writing a single-step update and inheriting the rest.

The split also carries a performance contract: project_inputs / step. A leaky ESN's pre-activation separates into an input-dependent part and a state-dependent part, and only the latter must live inside the loop. The layer asks the cell to precompute \(W_{fb}\,u_t + W_{in}\,d_t + b\) for the whole sequence in one batched matmul, then iterates with step, where torch.addmm fuses the recurrent matmul with the precomputed slice. This moves input projection out of the sequential recurrence. Actual kernels and speed depend on device, dtype, layout and compilation; the split alone establishes no fixed launch count or CPU/GPU crossover. Cells that cannot split (NG-RC's buffer update) return None from project_inputs and the layer falls back to per-step forward.

docs.title: Dense parameters and compressed buffers
docs.text:
Dense reservoir weights use frozen Parameters by default for three reasons:

  • state_dict parity. A frozen and a trainable reservoir serialize identically; checkpoints do not care which experiment produced them.
  • trainable is a single flag. Construction is one code path; trainable=False calls requires_grad_(False) on every parameter, and unfreezing is the same call in reverse.
  • PyTorch integration. Optimizers can discover the same parameters after unfreezing. A frozen reservoir still propagates gradients to upstream inputs that require them; freezing weights does not detach the computation graph.

Compact sparse reservoirs instead keep compressed weights as buffers, without a duplicate dense square matrix. They still pass gradients through the supported Torch operations to upstream inputs. Inspecting a dense copy or making all connections trainable requires an explicit representation choice; see sparse storage. Parameter discovery and checkpoint representation consequently depend on that choice.

docs.title: The trainer is a hook
docs.text:
ESNTrainer.fit resets recurrence once and evaluates a continuous warmup-plus-training prefix in topological order. Each readout's pre-hook fits only the training suffix, then its normal forward computes fitted outputs for the complete prefix. A downstream reservoir consequently warms up with the fitted upstream mapping and continues through training without replaying any upstream nodes. Each reservoir consumes its samples once; shared branches are cached until their last consumer.

Normal PyTorch calls preserve module hooks. Declare dependencies as separate functional graph nodes or use standard torch.nn.Sequential containers. Opaque custom containers mixing readouts and reservoirs are rejected because their internal ordering cannot be inferred safely. The common Model.fit also supports internal targets without exposing additional outputs and stages the fit before committing. See training. fit_stream has its own independent incremental-readout contract; it cannot retroactively refit upstream heads after consuming their downstream inputs.

docs.title: Registries, but callables first
docs.text:
Topologies and weight initializers resolve through one spec type: a registry name ("erdos_renyi"), a (name, params) tuple, any bare callable — fn(n) -> matrix | graph, fn(rows, cols) -> matrix, or an in-place torch.nn.init.*_ function — a (callable, params) tuple, or a configured initializer object. The registry exists for discoverability and for string-based specification in HPO search spaces; the callable path exists because reservoir research routinely involves weight structures that have no registry name yet. A new structure requires only a function definition; register_matrix_topology / register_input_feedback promote it to a named, reusable component.

Convention

Resolution happens eagerly at layer construction (resolve_topology / resolve_initializer inside ESNCell.__init__), so an invalid spec raises at construction time rather than partway through an experiment.

docs.title: Workflow and extension boundaries
docs.text:
rd.ESN and rd.Model support training-only preprocessing, named signals, explicit feedback routes/delays, tuning, and complete model artifacts. Seed streams and custom initializer registration are public controls. Single-step state is available through step_stateless; incremental readouts also support streaming fitting.

Public extension contracts are documented in the API reference and contributing guide. Private execution planners, fit-preparation helpers and serialization plumbing are implementation details. Torch's checkpoint hooks retain their required method names but are omitted from ordinary method listings. Current compiler/export limits are stated in graph tooling and the roadmap.

docs.title: Reservoir dynamics
docs.text: Theory · Dynamics

docs.title: Reservoir dynamics
docs.text: Each reservoir family is defined by a single rule: an update equation for ESN layers, a feature map for NG-RC layers. This page states both rules exactly as the code computes them, then explains how spectral radius, leak rate, and bias relate to the dynamical properties they control.

docs.title: The leaky-ESN update
docs.text:
ESNCell implements the standard leaky-integrator update (Jaeger 2001; Lukoševičius 2012) as a nonlinear pre-activation followed by a linear leak:

\[ \tilde h_t = f\!\left(W_{rec}\,h_{t-1} + W_{fb}\,u_t + W_{in}\,d_t + b\right) \] \[ h_t = (1-\alpha)\,h_{t-1} + \alpha\,\tilde h_t \]

The activation \(f\) wraps only the pre-activation. The leak mixes the old state with the activated candidate outside \(f\) — in code, torch.lerp(state, new_state, leak_rate), which is exactly \(h_{t-1} + \alpha(\tilde h_t - h_{t-1})\). When leak_rate=1.0 (the default) the lerp is skipped and \(h_t = \tilde h_t\): a standard RNN update.

Symbols map to ESNCell attributes one-to-one:

Symbol Code Shape / value \(h_t\) layer.state (batch, reservoir_size) \(u_t\) (feedback) first forward argument (batch, feedback_size) per step \(d_t\) (driver) second forward argument, optional (batch, input_size) per step \(W_{fb}\) weight_feedback (reservoir_size, feedback_size), default \(\mathcal U(-1,1)\) \(W_{in}\) weight_input (reservoir_size, input_size), None without input_size \(W_{rec}\) weight_hh (reservoir_size, reservoir_size) \(b\) bias_h (reservoir_size,), \(\mathcal U(-\beta, \beta)\) with \(\beta\) = bias_scaling \(f\), \(\alpha\) activation, leak_rate "tanh" default; \(\alpha \in [0, 1]\), default 1.0

docs.title: Spectral radius
docs.text:
After the topology builds \(W_{rec}\), the matrix is rescaled so its largest absolute eigenvalue hits the target:

\[ W_{rec} \leftarrow \frac{\rho_{\text{target}}}{\rho(W_{rec})}\, W_{rec}, \qquad \rho(W) = \max_i |\lambda_i(W)| \]

(scale_to_spectral_radius in init/topology/base.py.) Every positive measured radius can be rescaled, including values smaller than \(10^{-8}\). An exactly zero radius cannot be multiplied into a positive one: zero and nilpotent matrices retain their weights and emit a warning for a positive target. A bare ESNLayer defaults to spectral_radius=None, meaning no scaling at all; the premade factories pass 0.9.

The echo state property. The reservoir is usable when its state forgets initial conditions: two copies started from different states and driven by the same input must converge. \(\rho < 1\) is the standard heuristic for this, and a good default — but it is neither necessary nor sufficient for a general driven nonlinear reservoir. In the special case of zero bias and a tanh reservoir at its zero fixed point, it gives local stability of the unforced linearization. A strongly driven reservoir can keep the ESP well above \(\rho = 1\), because the input pushes units into their saturating region where the effective gain drops. The property can be measured directly: esp_index (importable as from resdag import esp_index) runs one orbit from the zero state and iterations orbits from standard-normal random states \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) (the same convention as set_random_reservoir_states) under the same input, and reports \(\overline{\lVert h^{\text{base}}_t - h^{\text{rand}}_t \rVert}\) averaged over time, batch, and restarts. An index near zero means the tested trajectories merged for that finite input window; it is empirical evidence, not a proof for all inputs or initial states. A plateau means the reservoir still remembers where it started. Because a healthy reservoir converges fast, the full-window mean is dominated by the early transient — pass window=k to average only the last k steps (the asymptotic regime), and relative=True to normalise by the base-state norm for a scale-free index comparable across reservoirs.

Leak rate as timescale. For \(0 < \alpha < 1\), the direct retained-state term has decay factor \((1-\alpha)\) and relaxation time \(\tau = -1/\ln(1-\alpha) \approx 1/\alpha\) steps for small \(\alpha\). This describes that term, not the full reservoir's memory. The recurrent candidate also depends on the old state; its local Jacobian is \((1-\alpha)I + \alpha\,\mathrm{diag}(f')W_{rec}\). Recurrent weights, the driving signal and saturation therefore also determine memory and stability.

docs.title: Bias and broken symmetry
docs.text:
tanh is odd, and so is every term of the bias-free update: with \(b = 0\),

\[ h_t(-u, -d \mid -h_{t-1}) = -\,h_t(u, d \mid h_{t-1}) \]

so the zero-initialized input-to-state operator satisfies \(H(-x) = -H(x)\). It distinguishes opposite inputs, but its features obey an odd-symmetry constraint. A linear readout of those features has the same odd part plus its intercept, which can restrict fitting a target with different symmetry. This global sign reversal differs from Lorenz's partial reflection \((x,y,z) \mapsto (-x,-y,z)\); one does not imply the other.

A fixed random bias \(b \sim \mathcal U(-\beta,\beta)\) removes the enforced odd symmetry. bias_scaling controls \(\beta\) (default 1.0); choose bias=False or bias_scaling=0.0 for a zero-bias baseline. Whether bias helps prediction is a validation question, not a guarantee from symmetry alone.

docs.title: The NG-RC feature map
docs.text:
NGCell (Gauthier et al. 2021, Eqs. 5–10) has no weights and no recurrent dynamics — its "state" is a FIFO buffer of past inputs, and its output is a deterministic feature vector. For input dimension \(d\), \(k\) delay taps spaced \(s\) steps apart, and polynomial degree \(p\):

Linear features — the delay embedding, dimension \(D = d\,k\):

\[ O_{\text{lin},i} = \big[\,x_i \,\Vert\, x_{i-s} \,\Vert\, \cdots \,\Vert\, x_{i-(k-1)s}\,\big] \]

Nonlinear features — every degree-\(p\) monomial over \(O_{\text{lin}}\), i.e. all multisets of size \(p\) from \(D\) entries (itertools.combinations_with_replacement), counted by the stars-and-bars coefficient:

\[ n_{\text{nonlin}} = \binom{D + p - 1}{p} \]

Assembly — constant, linear, and nonlinear blocks concatenated:

\[ O_{\text{total}} = [\,1\,] \oplus O_{\text{lin}} \oplus O_{\text{nonlin}}, \qquad \dim O_{\text{total}} = \mathbb 1_{\text{const}} + \mathbb 1_{\text{lin}}\,D + \binom{D+p-1}{p} \]

with the first two blocks present iff include_constant / include_linear. The delay buffer holds \((k-1)\,s\) rows and starts zero-filled, so the first \((k-1)\,s\) outputs mix real data with zeros and should be discarded. This is the NG-RC warmup; it is typically much shorter than the hundreds of steps an ESN needs. The monomial count grows combinatorially in \(k\), \(p\), and \(d\); the cell warns when \(\dim O_{\text{total}} > 10{,}000\).

docs.text:

  • M. Lukoševičius, A practical guide to applying echo state networks, in Neural Networks: Tricks of the Trade (2012).
  • D. J. Gauthier, E. Bollt, A. Griffith, W. A. S. Barbosa, Next generation reservoir computing, Nature Communications 12, 5564 (2021), arXiv:2106.07688.

docs.title: Readout solvers
docs.text: Theory · Readout

docs.title: Readout solvers
docs.text: A readout learns a linear map from reservoir features to targets. The friendly rd.ESN preset uses AutoReadoutLayer: it checks numerical suitability and chooses among primal/dual Cholesky, augmented QR and direct SVD without increasing the requested L2 penalty. Lower-level model factories retain a direct ridge default; pass readout="auto" to select the same policy explicitly. See the practical solver guide for examples, diagnostics, device fallback and forcing an algorithm.

docs.title: The ridge objective
docs.text:
Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{N\times F}\) contain \(N=B\,T\) feature rows and \(Y\in\mathbb R^{N\times M}\) contain targets. Batch and incremental ridge with bias=True minimize

\[ \lVert XW+\mathbf1c^\top-Y\rVert_F^2+\alpha\lVert W\rVert_F^2. \]

The intercept \(c\) is unpenalized. Center both matrices first:

\[ X_c=X-\mathbf1\bar x^\top,\qquad Y_c=Y-\mathbf1\bar y^\top. \]

Then solve

\[ (X_c^\top X_c+\alpha I)W=X_c^\top Y_c, \qquad c=\bar y-W^\top\bar x. \]

Centering before multiplying matters. The algebraically equivalent \(X^\top X-N\bar x\bar x^\top\) subtracts two potentially enormous nearly equal numbers. It can lose the meaningful variation even in float64. ResDAG forms products from centered matrices, including for explicit-noise ridge fits and CG. With bias=False, it uses raw products and no intercept: centering would change that different objective.

SVD and pseudoinverse solvers work directly with the centered design matrix. They avoid squaring its condition number through normal equations and do not allocate an unused feature-by-feature Gram matrix.

docs.title: Choosing a solver
docs.text:
Readout / factory key Method Useful when AutoReadoutLayer / auto Checked primal/dual Cholesky, augmented QR or design-matrix SVD A common L2 objective with automatic numerical checks and explicit overrides RidgeReadoutLayer / ridge Cholesky, or explicit solver="solve" for LU Regularized, well-conditioned batch fitting CholeskyReadoutLayer / cholesky Direct Cholesky ridge You want that method by name CGReadoutLayer / cg Iterative conjugate gradient on a full Gram matrix Iterative fitting is preferable for your feature width and tolerance LSMRReadoutLayer / lsmr SciPy iterative least squares through matrix/vector products An explicit CPU float64 fit without a feature-by-feature matrix SVDReadoutLayer / svd Design-matrix SVD with ridge filter factors Correlated or rank-deficient features; more features than samples PinvReadoutLayer / pinv Least squares / pseudoinverse with an rcond cutoff Unregularized least squares with explicit rank tolerance IncrementalRidgeReadoutLayer / incremental Merge chunk statistics, then solve once The complete feature sequence does not fit in memory RLSReadout / rls Sequential inverse-correlation updates Online adaptation, optionally with forgetting FISTAReadoutLayer / fista Accelerated proximal iterations Sparse coefficients through L1 / elastic-net regularization

These algorithms do not all minimize the same objective. Pseudoinverse fitting has no ridge penalty. RLS applies its initial delta prior to an augmented bias feature too, and forgetting changes sample weights. FISTA adds an L1 penalty; l1_ratio controls the balance with its quadratic penalty. Check each class's reference when comparing coefficients.

Auto always keeps the L2 objective and requested alpha: FISTA, RLS and pseudoinverse are never automatic substitutes for a positive-ridge fit. It tries the smaller normal system, checks full inverse-norm conditioning and estimated Gram roundoff, and checks a normalized optimality residual. QR/SVD recovery does not increase the penalty. A forced Auto algorithm never switches to another algorithm; unsuitable forced paths warn or raise. The immutable last_solve report identifies the actual method, placement, precision, residuals and reasons for recovery.

For alpha=0, a Cholesky or LU solve needs adequate rank; use SVD or pseudoinverse for rank-deficient designs. Cholesky's recovery path can add rescue jitter or project a numerically indefinite Gram, emitting a warning. This is a numerical fallback, not evidence that the original requested problem was well-conditioned. This rescue behavior belongs to the explicit ridge classes, not Auto's unchanged-penalty recovery policy.

SVD computes \(X_c=U\,\mathrm{diag}(s)V^\top\) and, for positive ridge,

\[ W=V\,\mathrm{diag}\!\left(\frac{s}{s^2+\alpha}\right)U^\top Y_c. \]

The filter is evaluated in scaled form to avoid overflowing \(s^2\) for large finite singular values. It preserves alpha; this numerical improvement does not guarantee accurate decomposition or coefficients for arbitrary data scales. For zero penalty, rcond discards small singular values and defines the numerical minimum-norm solution. Auto uses a dtype/dimension-aware default cutoff; the explicit SVD class defaults to 1e-15. No cutoff truncates positive-ridge SVD. Both SVD and Auto reject nonfinite or negative penalties/cutoffs.

Very weak regularization on dependent features can produce large cancelling coefficients in finite precision, even with small training and optimality residuals. Auto warns and records the final severe-conditioning risk when detected. Rescaling, an explicitly stronger penalty or higher precision can help; held-out autonomous forecast accuracy remains a separate validation target.

CG still stores an \(F\times F\) Gram matrix: it is not matrix-free. It solves output columns together with separate step sizes, warns on under-convergence, and checks its absolute residual tolerance every ten iterations. Increasing max_iter or changing tol trades work against the quality of that approximate solve. Compare predictions as well as residuals before choosing it for speed.

LSMR instead applies the design and its transpose through a linear operator, centering bounded row blocks when fitting an intercept. Its damping is sqrt(alpha), preserving the same ridge objective. It uses relative stopping tests, per-output target scaling, and fails explicitly on iteration or condition limits. The feature matrix remains resident and accelerator fitting requires a warned CPU bridge; see the LSMR guide.

FISTA uses an exact Gram eigenvalue by default. Optional power_iters>0 estimates curvature more cheaply, but an estimate plus a fixed margin is not a guaranteed upper bound. Quadratic-majorizer backtracking verifies each proximal update. A power vector that misses a nonzero eigenspace therefore cannot turn a real fitting problem into a false converged zero solution.

docs.title: Working precision and device placement
docs.text:
Auto uses solve_dtype: float64 on CPU/CUDA by default, and an initial native float32 attempt on MPS. Unsafe or unavailable MPS decompositions use an explicit CPU float64 bridge, with a warning and the actual device recorded in the report. cpu_fallback=False raises instead of bridging. The fitted parameters keep their ordinary model dtype/device, and a forced algorithm remains forced across a bridge. Unlike the explicit solvers below, Auto does not accept use_float64 or gram_dtype; choose the options of the selected readout class.

Direct and incremental ridge form their Gram in the solve dtype by default: float64 with use_float64=True. CG retains a different historical default: solve precision on CPU, input precision on CUDA. Explicit gram_dtype overrides these choices. Lower-precision products can be faster on some accelerators, but a later float64 solve cannot recover information already lost during multiplication.

Incremental accumulation and RLS recursion retain their configured working precision across parameter conversions. For example, .float() makes their weights float32 while retaining float64 statistics when use_float64=True. With use_float64=False, statistics follow the parameter dtype. Values are moved directly into the destination working dtype, without an intermediate narrowing cast that would destroy accumulated precision.

MPS cannot store float64 statistics. Moving such an incremental or RLS readout to MPS raises before changing its parameters. Keep it on CPU for float64 training, or explicitly use use_float64=False for operations supported by your installed PyTorch. This does not guarantee every MPS solver operation is available. Ordinary ridge readouts fitted on CPU can still be moved to float32 MPS for inference.

Choose precision using held-out forecast quality and measured runtime. Feature scaling fitted on training data helps conditioning; it does not replace a stable solver or justify discarding precision automatically.

docs.title: Stable streaming and checkpoints
docs.text:
Incremental ridge merges each chunk's centered cross-products and means with the Chan covariance update. For chunks with counts \(n_a,n_b\) and mean differences \(\Delta_x,\Delta_y\), the cross-product correction is

\[ C_{xy}=C_{xy,a}+C_{xy,b} +\frac{n_an_b}{n_a+n_b}\Delta_x\Delta_y^\top. \]

The feature covariance uses the same formula with \(\Delta_y=\Delta_x\). This keeps \(O(F^2+FM)\) statistics independently of total sequence length, avoids subtracting large raw moments at finalization, and preserves the batch ridge objective up to floating-point differences between chunk orders.

XtX and Xty now contain centered cross-products when bias=True, and raw products when bias=False. Checkpoints include running means and a statistics format version. Legacy raw-moment checkpoints upgrade automatically, with a warning when samples were accumulated. Conversion cannot reconstruct precision already lost in an old checkpoint: reset and refit highly offset or ill-conditioned streams before continuing. No second feature-by-feature covariance is retained.

Fresh RLS partial_fit starts from zero weights, matching fit_online and reset_state. An unobserved feature therefore does not retain a random coefficient prior. Existing saved RLS weights and inverse-correlation state remain loadable.

docs.title: Fitting, gradients and customization
docs.text:
ReadoutLayer.fit flattens sequence inputs, validates shapes and finite values, asks solve for coefficients and intercept, then copies them into standard nn.Linear parameters. The fitted layer remains an ordinary PyTorch module. Set trainable=True to refine its parameters with a gradient optimizer.

Custom solvers return coefficients shaped (in_features, out_features) and a vector intercept when bias=True; return None for an absent bias. See custom solvers for a complete example that handles both cases.

Continue with streaming, training, or forecast timing.

docs.title: Timing conventions
docs.text: Theory · Timing

docs.title: Timing conventions
docs.text:
A next-step readout consumes feedback \(x_t\) and an optional driver \(d_t\) and predicts \(x_{t+1}\). This same rule applies to training, teacher-forced evaluation, and autonomous forecasting.

The examples below describe default next-sample timing and the explicit low-level ESNModel/ensemble APIs. The common rd.Model and rd.ESN share that default; their optional prediction leads and named delayed connections are explained in feedback and timing. Their future drivers use future_inputs, and each forecast reconstructs its rollout from history; the raw continuation arguments below do not apply to that interface.

docs.title: Training and validation
docs.text:
After discarding any initial transient, let W = warmup_steps and L = train_steps. Both counts must be positive integers. Preparation builds:

warmup = data[:, :W]
train = data[:, W:W+L]
target = data[:, W+1:W+L+1]
f_warmup = data[:, L+1:W+L+1]
val = data[:, W+L+1:W+L+1+H]

The trainer fits each input row to the matching target row without another shift. The final training target, data[:, W+L], has already been observed during fitting. Forecast warmup includes it; validation starts after it. f_warmup always contains W observations, even when L < W.

Normalization statistics are fitted on training inputs alone and reused across all windows. Validation therefore contributes neither targets to fitting nor statistics to preprocessing.

docs.title: Forecast the immediate unseen sample
docs.text:
If observed contains x[:, :N], then:

predictions = model.forecast(observed, horizon=H)
# predictions[:, i] estimates x[:, N+i]

The last warmup readout already predicts the next sample. Forecast slot zero uses that prediction. Only the remaining H-1 predictions need further model updates. horizon must be a positive integer; zero is rejected. A one-step forecast is useful and does not require any future drivers.

Output Feedback consumed Driver consumed Sample estimated last warmup output / forecast slot 0 \(x_{N-1}\) \(d_{N-1}\) \(x_N\) forecast slot 1 \(\hat x_N\) \(d_N\) \(x_{N+1}\) forecast slot 2 \(\hat x_{N+1}\) \(d_{N+1}\) \(x_{N+2}\)

For a driven model, future drivers start immediately after the observed driver history. They accompany the input being consumed, not its next-sample target:

predictions = model.forecast(
    (x[:, :N], d[:, :N]),
    forecast_inputs=d[:, N:N+H-1],
    horizon=H,
)
truth = x[:, N:N+H]

Longer driver windows are accepted; only the required prefix is consumed. With return_warmup=True, historical predictions are prepended. The final warmup prediction is already slot zero, so it appears once: total length is W-1+H. Core, coupled ensemble, and parallel models share these semantics. With the default lead/delay of one, the ESN preset retains washout+1 observations and therefore returns washout+H values when including historical predictions. Larger leads/delays can require a longer cached history. The common workflow's general length is W - max(model.prediction_leads.values()) + H, where W is the history actually supplied or cached.

docs.title: Explicit seeds and continuation
docs.text:
This section uses the raw graph APIs, not rd.Model or the rd.ESN preset.

initial_feedback is a distinct extra input consumed after the complete warmup. Slot zero predicts the sample after that seed. Do not repeat the last warmup observation as the seed. Explicit seeds need H future driver samples, starting at the same time as the seed, and return_warmup=True has length W+H.

A forecast leaves its final returned prediction unconsumed. Continue the same trajectory without replaying history by consuming it as the next explicit seed:

first = model.forecast(observed, horizon=100)
next_part = model.forecast(
    observed[:, :0],
    initial_feedback=first[:, -1:],
    horizon=100,
    reset=False,
)

For driven models, pass empty history for every stream and future drivers beginning at the seed's time. Empty warmup without an explicit seed raises. reset=False uses current states; reset=True starts from zero states.

windowed_forecast fills gaps at their own timeline indices. It consumes the final predicted gap input before the next observed window so recurrent state remains continuous. Score only gap positions using its returned mask.

docs.title: Reproducing earlier low-level forecasts
docs.text:
alignment="legacy" preserves the old core and ensemble convention: it consumes the last warmup prediction before returning slot zero, skipping the immediate unseen sample. It requires H drivers and prepends W predictions when return_warmup=True. Pair it with prepare_esn_data(..., alignment="legacy"), whose forecast history ends one sample earlier. Training and validation splits stay unchanged.

Earlier ParallelESN forecasts already started at the immediate unseen sample; keep the default to preserve their future timing. Their old return_warmup prefix contained raw observations; the prefix now contains predictions. See Migration for the compatibility recipe.

docs.title: State across calls
docs.text:
Ordinary model(x) calls carry reservoir state. warmup and forecast reset by default. Use reset_reservoirs() between independent trajectories or use model.as_module() for independent PyTorch minibatches. The full model's forward_stateless(..., states=...) returns predictions and explicit state without changing stored reservoir buffers; it supports deliberate chunking and backpropagation across chunks.

Stored states move with .to(device) and dtype conversion. Inputs must match the model's device and dtype. By default, stored state detaches at ordinary call boundaries. Set detach_state_between_calls=False only when managing backpropagation across those calls. Explicit stateless states retain gradients until you detach them yourself.

docs.title: Workflows
docs.text: Work

docs.title: Workflows
docs.text:
A reservoir computing project iterates through the same cycle: fit the readout (an algebraic solve that takes seconds), forecast against held-out validation data, adjust the hyperparameters that affect forecast quality, then scale the result with larger reservoirs, ensembles, GPU execution, and model persistence. The guides below cover that cycle. Optional calibration adapts reservoir activity on training data before fitting the readout.

For the new named-graph interface, start with the common model workflow, then use tuning for preset and custom-DAG searches. The roadmap distinguishes implemented features from remaining work.

  • Train

    Three training approaches — the one-pass algebraic solve, frozen features with a gradient head, and full BPTT — and when each is appropriate.

  • Calibrate

    Optional intrinsic plasticity and flow control, with training-only inputs and checkpoints that retain the adaptation.

  • Forecast

    The two-phase forecast procedure, driver alignment during autoregression, coupled ensembles, and Lyapunov-time limits on forecast horizons.

  • Lyapunov time

    Report forecast horizons in Lyapunov times, measure valid prediction time, and read a reservoir's own edge-of-chaos exponent.

  • Tune

    Tune a preset or custom DAG with fixed seeds, forecast starting points and training-only scaling. Inspect the study and keep a refitted winner ready to forecast; customize recipes, search spaces and objectives.

  • Scale & deploy

    When to move to the GPU, saving and loading models, and embedding frozen reservoirs in larger PyTorch pipelines.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: Work · Benchmarks

docs.title: Current measurement protocol
docs.text:
The comparison harness checks alignment, numerical precision and timing before publishing new rankings. The heldout-v1 protocol uses raw shared data and fits normalization on the supervised training targets after washout. Training inputs end at index T-1, their next-sample targets end at T, and forecasts begin at the first unseen sample, T+1. Every adapter receives the same transformed data.

Accuracy is the uninterrupted prefix with per-step RMS error below 0.3, using fixed training component scales. The report also includes 0.5. Compute each seed/origin's horizon separately, then report its median and spread. A forecast that stays valid throughout the evaluated window gives a lower bound. Report actual dt, system parameters and the Lyapunov exponent when converting steps to Lyapunov times.

The forecast experiment shows how to build, draw, train, save and score vanilla, OTT and custom DAG models. Its untuned examples are separate from a controlled comparison. The phase-five design records the agreed 7–8 Lyapunov-time median target and the remaining experiment work.

Run a bounded Python-adapter smoke check from the repository:

python -m pip install -r benchmarks/requirements.txt
cd benchmarks
python -m rc_bench.run --quick --only resdag-cpu reservoirpy --report --out results/local-smoke.json

This checks both real Python adapters, chronological preparation and reporting. An execution failure from an available adapter makes the command fail; unavailable optional adapters are explicit skips. The settings and random weights are realized by each library independently. Equal nominal settings alone do not establish identical numerical models or an equal tuning budget.

docs.title: Equal tuning time
docs.text:
The new headline protocol gives each library and each system ten CPU minutes to tune a vanilla ESN: ResDAG, reservoirpy and ReservoirComputing.jl on Lorenz and Rössler. It uses Optuna's ordinary study.optimize, one worker and one CPU thread, with the same seven controls: reservoir size, spectral radius, leak, input scale, random bias scale, mean degree and ridge penalty.

Every complete candidate fits once for each of three initialization seeds, then forecasts from three validation starts using that fitted model. Adapter initialization and one fixed synthetic warmup are reported separately; this does not measure total process startup, including common CLI imports. Construction, fitting, history synchronization, rollout, scoring and Julia IPC count toward the budget. Failed, unfinished or deadline-overrun candidates cannot win; their work and actual overrun remain in the report. There are no automatic retries.

All six winners are saved before reading final test values. Final evaluation uses five unseen seeds and three later starts, with the same training-only normalization, 0.3 headline and 0.5 secondary thresholds. The JSON keeps every seed/start, failure, divergence flag and censored horizon; the Markdown report shows the median and full range. This compares achievable accuracy under equal tuning time. Separate matched-configuration measurements compare throughput without confusing different winning architectures.

The common model explicitly uses Gaussian recurrent weights, directed connectivity at mean_degree / reservoir_size including possible self-loops, dense uniform input weights and a random uniform reservoir bias. Initial memory is zero. A linear readout sees only reservoir states, with no direct input features or readout intercept. Native random streams, sparse-mask construction and direct readout solvers still differ. ResDAG's native Gram solver can increase the effective regularization or repair a numerically indefinite Gram matrix; ReservoirPy uses its symmetric Gram solve, while Julia uses augmented QR. Equal requested penalties therefore do not imply identical effective fits. The precise protocol, commands and accounting are in benchmarks/BUDGET_PROTOCOL.md.

The pinned Julia environment has been executed with Julia 1.12.5 and ReservoirComputing.jl 0.12.23. Independent NumPy ridge and recurrent-update oracles check Float64 fitting, the first unseen forecast, history resets, future-data isolation and requested timing repetitions. This verifies the adapter; it does not establish a cross-library speed ranking.

docs.title: CPU implementation checks
docs.text:
Use the paired CPU harness when changing execution code:

python benchmarks/cpu_workflows.py --before BASE_COMMIT --after HEAD \
  --reservoir-forward --artifacts-dir /tmp/resdag-cpu-workflows

Run it from a repository checkout after installing benchmarks/requirements.txt. Each revision loads the same baseline weights and synthetic observations. Public Model.fit timing includes preprocessing, graph staging, warmup and the readout solve; Model.forecast includes history synchronization and returning predictions in their original units. Construction, external cloning and correctness hashing are outside the timers. No hooks alter execution.

Two fresh-process ABBA blocks compare the old and new implementation, with seven timed repetitions per process after warmup. The report keeps raw samples, process medians, paired ratios and their spread. Torch and native BLAS thread settings are set to one and verified; this is not a measurement of operating-system thread occupancy.

The default matrix includes vanilla, OTT, cycle and sparse random reservoirs, plus batches 1, 4 and 16. --profile storage compares the same ER weights as dense and CSR matrices at 400, 1,000 and 2,000 units. Predictions must agree exactly between revisions within each case. Cross-storage differences are reported separately because multiplication order can change roundoff. --profile smoke is a small execution check, not performance evidence.

See the complete CPU protocol for dimensions, timing boundaries and commands. These are implementation checks; the forecast accuracy results remain a separate experiment. Automatic storage and compilation defaults are unchanged.

docs.title: Archived comparisons
docs.text:
Historical results; use the current comparison separately

These tables are archived measurements, not evidence for the current release. The phase-one audit found mismatched forecast indexing and unsupported optional adapter paths in the comparison harness. Treat its accuracy rankings and cross-library speed ratios as unverified. The current equal-time comparison reports the completed aligned study separately. Internal CPU regression gates compare ResDAG execution paths and do not establish superiority to another library.

The historical measurements below compare ResDAG 0.6.0 head-to-head with two established reservoir-computing libraries — reservoirpy (NumPy/SciPy) and ReservoirComputing.jl (Julia) — on the same Echo State Network architecture, the same data, and the same three tasks every forecasting practitioner runs: fitting a readout, fitting on a lot of data, and rolling out long autoregressive forecasts.

The harness is in benchmarks/; it is re-runnable and adding a library is a single adapter file. Numbers below were produced by python -m rc_bench.run followed by python -m rc_bench.report. They describe that version and workload; rerun the harness to measure the current release on your own hardware. The repository's benchmark report records later sweeps with their own environment and settings.

Reading the tables

Speedups are relative to reservoirpy, so reservoirpy is always 1.00× and a value above 1× means faster than reservoirpy. Each cell is the median wall-clock time over repeated runs (a warmup iteration is discarded; GPU work is synchronized before the clock stops).

Archived observations (RTX 3060 laptop, vs reservoirpy)

The following tables preserve the recorded timings and scores for that historical setup. Their indexing, initialization and solver caveats prevent using them to claim that a current library is faster or more accurate. GPU suitability depends on the actual model, precision and workload; no new CUDA throughput claim has been verified in this phase.

docs.title: Forecast precision (valid prediction time)
docs.text:
Predictive skill, not speed: after an identical warmup, how many steps the closed-loop forecast tracks the true Lorenz trajectory before the normalized error crosses the threshold. Higher is better.

Reservoir size reservoirpy (CPU) resdag (CPU) resdag (GPU) ReservoirComputing.jl (CPU) 500 52 steps (0.9 Λt) 146 steps (2.6 Λt) 148 steps (2.7 Λt) 89 steps (1.6 Λt) 1000 143 steps (2.6 Λt) 146 steps (2.6 Λt) 144 steps (2.6 Λt) 27 steps (0.5 Λt) 2000 342 steps (6.2 Λt) 147 steps (2.7 Λt) 149 steps (2.7 Λt) —

Valid prediction time: steps until the normalized forecast error first exceeds 0.5, also in Lyapunov times (Λt). Higher means the model stays on the true trajectory longer. Predictive skill is hyper-parameter-dependent; these use matched nominal settings (not tuned per library), so each library leads in different regimes.

Archived setup: NVIDIA RTX 3060 laptop GPU / 16-thread i7-10870H, Python 3.14, resdag 0.6.0, reservoirpy 0.4.2, ReservoirComputing.jl 0.12, torch 2.10 (cu128). Median of recorded repetitions; — means the old sweep did not measure that cell. Current commands below run the corrected protocol and will not reproduce these historical values.

docs.title: What is being measured
docs.text:
The matched-workload harness builds a single reservoir feeding a ridge readout with the same nominal settings and byte-identical transformed data. Its native initializer distributions are recorded separately from the explicit common distributions in the equal-budget track.

  • Training runs the reservoir over the training sequence and solves for the readout. The current ResDAG adapter uses RidgeReadoutLayer, a direct solver; reservoirpy uses Ridge, and Julia uses StandardRidge. An earlier adapter used CG; those historical results do not describe the current direct-solver path.
  • Forecasting warms the reservoir up on a seed window, then generates closed-loop: each prediction is fed back as the next input. This loop is inherently sequential in time.

A short-horizon forecast RMSE is recorded alongside each timing as a sanity check that all libraries are doing comparable work — not just racing to produce garbage.

docs.title: Fairness & caveats
docs.text:
Read the protocol and implementation choices alongside every result:

  • Connectivity and storage are separate. ResDAG supports native sparse recurrent storage through sparse=True. The historical/default timing adapter builds a dense tensor, reservoirpy uses SciPy sparse storage, and the Julia timing worker currently requests a dense matrix from its sparse initializer. A sparsely connected mathematical reservoir does not imply a sparse storage backend. The new equal-budget recipe records its explicit storage policy separately.
  • Precision. CPU rows run float64 (NumPy/Julia's natural dtype); the resdag GPU row runs float32, the realistic choice for consumer GPUs (which run float64 at a small fraction of float32 throughput).
  • Sequential forecasting is launch-bound. The autoregressive forecast loop issues one tiny operation per timestep. On the GPU each step is dominated by kernel-launch overhead, so the eager GPU loop does not help long forecasts at small reservoir sizes — and may be slower than CPU there. forecast(compile=True) requests the supported compiled path; its setup cost, fallback behavior and steady-state benefit depend on the graph and backend. The tables above are historical eager measurements and do not establish a compilation speedup. Measure both fitting and forecasting on the target device before choosing it. See Scale & deploy for when the GPU is worth it.
  • ReservoirComputing.jl coverage. The current adapter has no implicit reservoir-size cap and honors the requested repeats and warmups. Julia's standalone matched-workload timings are measured inside the worker after warmup, excluding startup/JIT. The budget track keeps one Julia process alive and reports its startup/synthetic warmup separately. Missing Julia or an uninstantiated optional environment must be reported, without treating it as a measured performance result.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
# resdag + torch (use a CUDA torch build for the GPU rows)
uv pip install -e ".[dev]"
uv pip install -r benchmarks/requirements.txt   # reservoirpy

# optional Julia comparison (skipped automatically if Julia is absent)
julia --project=benchmarks/julia -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()'

cd benchmarks
python -m rc_bench.run                            # -> results/latest.json
python -m rc_bench.report --in results/latest.json

Adding another library — pytorch-esn, PyRCN, the reservoir-computing PyPI package, ... — is one new adapter implementing is_available / time_train / time_forecast; see benchmarks/README.md.

docs.title: Calibrate a reservoir
docs.text:
Calibration changes the reservoir using training inputs only, before the readout is fitted. It needs no targets. It is optional: start with a normal ESN, then compare calibration on held-out data if its neurons saturate or its activity is poorly scaled.

import torch
from resdag import ESNLayer
from resdag.training import calibrate_intrinsic_plasticity

training = torch.randn(1, 800, 2)
reservoir = ESNLayer(64, feedback_size=2, spectral_radius=0.8, seed=5)
report = calibrate_intrinsic_plasticity(
    reservoir, training,
    epochs=2, warmup=50, learning_rate=1e-3,
    target_mean=0.0, target_std=0.2,
)

Inputs may be (time, features) or (batch, time, features). Pass (feedback, driver) for a driven reservoir. Every batch slot represents an independent trajectory; time order is preserved. Calibration replays the training sequence for each epoch and resets state between replays. A successful calibration resets the layer's carried state, ready for a fresh readout warmup. It restores the layer's training/evaluation mode. Invalid inputs fail before committing adapted values.

docs.title: Intrinsic plasticity
docs.text:
Gaussian-target intrinsic plasticity adapts each neuron's gain and offset in tanh(a * drive + b). target_mean and target_std describe the desired activity distribution. The learning rate controls the adaptation speed; an aggressive value can make the procedure unstable. The result is not guaranteed to become exactly Gaussian or to improve forecast accuracy.

This implementation supports the standard tanh ESN and its documented leak behavior. It records adaptations in registered buffers, so .to(), state_dict() and model checkpoints carry them with the reservoir. It leaves all ordinary weights frozen unless you explicitly enable training.

docs.title: Flow control
docs.text:
Flow control adapts per-neuron gains on the recurrent contribution. It balances recurrent input power against the previous activity's power:

from resdag.training import calibrate_flow_control

reservoir = ESNLayer(64, feedback_size=2, leak_rate=1.0, seed=5)
report = calibrate_flow_control(
    reservoir, training,
    target_radius=0.9, learning_rate=1e-3,
    warmup=50, epochs=2, mode="local",
)

mode="local" uses each neuron's own activity; "global" averages the control signal across neurons. This is a data-driven adaptation rule, not an exact eigenvalue rescale. Strong correlations in the inputs can move the achieved radius away from its target. The report includes the measured before/after effective radius and activity statistics for inspection. For example, inspect report.activity_std_before, report.activity_std_after, and report.spectral_radius_after.

Flow control requires unit leak and does not combine with an existing intrinsic-plasticity adaptation. Unsupported cell types and parameter combinations are rejected explicitly; frozen dense and frozen sparse ESNs use the same adaptation math; consult the function reference for the exact supported contract.

docs.title: Fit after calibration
docs.text:
Calibrate the layer, then use that same instance in the normal model graph:

from resdag import ESNModel, ESNTrainer, SVDReadoutLayer, reservoir_input

inp = reservoir_input(2)
model = ESNModel(
    inp, SVDReadoutLayer(64, 2, name="output")(reservoir(inp)),
)
ESNTrainer(model).fit(training[:, :50], training[:, 50:-1], training[:, 51:])
model.eval()

After calibration, refit any existing readout: its old weights were fitted to the previous reservoir features. Never calibrate on validation/test samples, and fit normalization on the training period too. Use chronological validation to decide whether the extra calibration helps your task.

The update rules follow the original Gaussian-tanh adaptation paper and local flow-control paper.

docs.title: Scale & deploy
docs.text: Work · Scale & deploy

docs.title: Scale & deploy
docs.text: A ResDAG model is a standard torch.nn.Module: it moves to the GPU, checkpoints, and embeds in a larger network like any other module. The reservoir-specific part is knowing when each of those is worth doing.

docs.title: GPU
docs.text:
import resdag as rd

model = rd.ESN(3000, input_size=3, device="cuda").fit(training.to("cuda"))
preds = model.forecast(horizon=1000)   # original units, on cuda

CUDA has an optional self-hosted GPU test workflow; it was not run for this continuation. MPS does not support float64, which the algebraic solvers and some diagnostics use by default. For MPS inference, fit on CPU, move a float32 model and its inputs to "mps", and validate your workload. Passing "mps" to device discovery does not guarantee that every solver or diagnostic supports it.

.to("cuda") moves parameters and buffers, including a warmed-up reservoir state. Device or dtype moves preserve that state's values; move the inputs to the same device and dtype too. A different batch size initializes the configured reset state (zeros by default), unless you deliberately restored a state with set_state, in which case a mismatched batch size raises instead of discarding it.

Measure the complete workflow. Recurrent state depends on the previous timestep, limiting parallelism across time. Larger batches and reservoirs provide more matrix work per step, while small single-trajectory workloads can spend much of their time in dispatch and kernel launches. Device, dtype, solver and batch size all affect the crossover; there is no fixed reservoir size at which GPU execution is guaranteed to win. Measure representative fitting and forecasting with examples/11_gpu_benchmark.py, including device transfers and synchronization. Earlier GPU numbers are historical measurements, not current release guarantees. Phase-five continuation measured CPU execution and native MPS correctness; it did not measure CUDA throughput.

Readout precision and GPU throughput

Direct readouts such as RidgeReadoutLayer form their normal equations in the solve dtype by default: float64 with use_float64=True, on CPU and CUDA. This favors accuracy for correlated reservoir features, but float64 throughput can be substantially lower on consumer GPUs. For normalized, sufficiently regularized problems, explicitly setting gram_dtype=torch.float32 can improve throughput; compare forecast accuracy before adopting that tradeoff. CGReadoutLayer has a different default: it forms the Gram matrix in the input dtype on CUDA and uses float64 for the subsequent solve when use_float64=True. Pass gram_dtype=torch.float64 there when the input-dtype Gram loses accuracy.

docs.title: Long horizons: compile the step
docs.text:
The autoregressive loop can spend substantial time in Python and kernel launches. forecast(compile=True) unrolls chunks of the flat executor into torch.compile (mode="reduce-overhead", fullgraph=True). For a hook-free symbolic graph with ordinary next-step feedback from its first output to its first input, the default chunk contains 64 forecast steps. This amortizes dispatch across the chunk rather than compiling and calling each step separately:

preds = model.forecast(history=observed, horizon=10_000, compile=True)

For hook-free models, the default eager path already uses a flat executor. Models with PyTorch execution hooks automatically use native module calls so their pre-hooks, output changes and backward hooks keep ordinary PyTorch semantics. On backends that support compiled forecasts, compile=True emits a warning and uses compatible eager execution while hooks are registered. Removing the hooks restores the lean path. Named non-first, multiple or delayed feedback routes use the sequence executor; they do not use this 64-step flat rollout. Full-history execution and the parallel/coupled workflow backends reject compile=True. Check the execution capabilities for your graph. Compiled results should be compared with floating-point tolerances, especially for chaotic dynamics; compilation can change rounding. Warm compiled executors are reused for matching shapes, devices, and dtypes. compile=True is an opt-in execution choice and transparently falls back to eager on torch < 2.10 or a compilation failure (emitting a RuntimeWarning). Measure cold compilation separately from repeated warm calls: setup can cost more than it saves, and a long horizon alone does not guarantee improvement. The low-level ESNModel.forecast API also supports a differentiable no_grad=False rollout, which is mutually exclusive with compile=True (Train · Differentiable forecast) — requesting both raises. The common rd.ESN/rd.Model.forecast workflow performs inference; use ordinary module calls, explicit states or the raw graph API for gradient-based composition.

Compiling the teacher-forced pass too

Warmup and training run the teacher-forced sequence loop, which also accepts an opt-in compile=True: reservoir(feedback, compile=True) routes it through a compiled chunked scan (same reduce-overhead mode, same eager fallback) when CUDA inference is eligible. CPU and MPS use eager execution for this scan, as do calls requiring gradients. This control belongs to the reservoir call; the common model.fit(...) API has no compile option. Compare setup and repeated-call timing on your own workload; the default remains the eager loop.

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
The common rd.ESN and rd.Model workflow saves a complete model by default:

model = rd.ESN(reservoir_size=500, seed=7).fit(series)
model.save("run.pt")
restored = rd.load("run.pt", map_location="cpu")
prediction = restored.forecast(horizon=1000)
model.save("run.svg")

The checkpoint describes the graph and includes fitted preprocessing, observed history and current reservoir memory. A larger PyTorch application can instead save model.state_dict() and load it into a matching architecture. Ordinary forward memory supports continuing a stream; autonomous forecasts reconstruct delayed feedback queues from history each call. Saving reservoir tensors alone does not preserve a forecast cursor. See the complete persistence guide for registered components, explicitly trusted notebook bundles and formats.

docs.title: Inside a larger pipeline
docs.text:
A frozen reservoir is a feature extractor with zero trainable parameters — sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad) is 0 by design — so optimizers, gradient bookkeeping, and checkpoint diffs all treat it as a constant. Wrap it like any frozen backbone:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import resdag as rd

class ReservoirClassifier(nn.Module):
    """Frozen reservoir features, gradient-trained head."""

    def __init__(self, n_classes: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = rd.ReservoirFeatureExtractor(
            reservoir_size=500, feedback_size=3, stateful=False,
        )
        self.head = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(500, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, n_classes)
        )

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:   # (batch, time, 3)
        states = self.features(x)                          # (batch, time, 500)
        return self.head(states[:, -1])                    # classify on last state

clf = ReservoirClassifier(n_classes=4)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(clf.head.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

for xb, yb in loader:                                      # (B, T, 3), (B,)
    loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(clf(xb), yb)
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

stateful=False starts each minibatch from the configured initial state (zeros by default) and never changes stored reservoir states, so independent or shuffled sequences do not leak history into each other. The default stateful=True carries state for streaming; reset it between independent trajectories. Gradients flow through a frozen reservoir to a trainable encoder upstream, while its weights stay fixed. To fine-tune a readout instead of adding a separate head, use the combination pattern from Train: build it with trainable=True, solve algebraically, then continue with a small learning rate.

Reuse a trained model's reservoirs with rd.ReservoirFeatureExtractor.from_model(trained_model, stateful=False). This shares reservoir weights and extracts their features; it does not include the trained readout or reproduce arbitrary parallel branches and transforms. To retain the complete trained model, place trained_model itself inside your larger nn.Module and reset its reservoirs between independent sequences.

For explicit state threading, call features, states = extractor.forward_stateless(x) and continue with extractor.forward_stateless(next_chunk, states=states). This leaves stored states untouched and keeps gradients across chunks; detach the returned states yourself when you want truncated backpropagation.

One operational note: reservoir layers carry mutable state, so a model instance is not thread-safe — give each thread its own model. CoupledEnsembleESNModel.fit(n_workers=...) parallelizes exactly this way, one sub-model per thread.

docs.title: Forecast
docs.text: Work · Forecast

docs.title: Presets and named DAGs
docs.text:
rd.ESN and rd.Model forecast in the original signal units. Supply observed history explicitly, or use the history retained by fit:

import torch
import resdag as rd

observed = torch.sin(torch.linspace(0, 20, 400))[:, None]
model = rd.ESN(reservoir_size=32, washout=30, seed=7).fit(observed)
prediction = model.forecast(horizon=100)
resynchronized = model.forecast(history=observed, horizon=100)
assert prediction.shape == resynchronized.shape == (100, 1)

The first prediction estimates the sample immediately after the last observation. Forecasts synchronize on their history and then feed predictions back into the model; no future truth is needed. One output returns a tensor; several named outputs return a dictionary. Trajectory-trained models return TSDynamics trajectories unless return_type="tensor" is requested.

For custom networks, named feedback connections route outputs to chosen inputs with explicit delays. Prediction lead and connection delay have separate controls. Inputs without feedback routes need known future values through future_inputs={"port": values}. Temporal modules can use history execution when they cannot advance one frame at a time.

docs.title: Raw symbolic graphs
docs.text:
The lower-level examples below use ESNModel and raw factory results. Their tensors use the graph's own units; they do not apply a surrounding Model's fitted scaling. f_warmup, train, target and val denote the aligned splits from prepare_esn_data. Use the common workflow unless you need to own this preparation and state management yourself.

forecast(observed, horizon=H) predicts the H samples immediately after an observed history. With next-sample targets, the last warmup readout already estimates the first unseen sample. Slot zero uses it; each later prediction feeds the previous prediction back into the reservoir.

docs.title: Anatomy
docs.text:
preds = model.forecast(f_warmup, horizon=2000)  # (batch, 2000, features)
error = ((preds - val) ** 2).mean()             # prepared val aligns directly

full = model.forecast(f_warmup, horizon=2000, return_warmup=True)
# (batch, warmup_steps - 1 + 2000, features): no repeated boundary prediction

States reset by default. Pass reset=False to continue current states. horizon must be a positive integer; horizon=1 returns the immediate unseen prediction. Multi-output models return a tuple; the first output supplies feedback and must match the feedback input width.

An explicit initial_feedback supplies a distinct additional observation after all warmup observations. The first output predicts the sample after that seed. This is useful for continuing a rollout with empty warmup:

more = model.forecast(
    f_warmup[:, :0],
    initial_feedback=preds[:, -1:],
    horizon=100,
    reset=False,
)

The final returned prediction has not been consumed yet. Passing it as the next seed consumes it exactly once. With an explicit seed, including historical predictions gives warmup_steps + horizon outputs.

docs.title: Driver alignment
docs.text:
Training pairs (feedback_t, driver_t) → feedback_{t+1}. Warmup supplies the driver needed for forecast slot zero. The remaining H-1 outputs need drivers beginning immediately after the warmup driver window:

N, horizon = 200, 300
preds = model.forecast(
    (x[:, :N], d[:, :N]),
    forecast_inputs=d[:, N:N+horizon-1],
    horizon=horizon,
)
truth = x[:, N:N+horizon]

A one-step forecast needs no future driver. Explicit seeds need H future drivers, beginning at the seed's own time index. Extra trailing driver samples are accepted and ignored. Theory · Timing derives these indices and explains continuation for driven models.

docs.title: Windowed reconstruction
docs.text:
windowed_forecast() fills the gaps in a sparsely-observed trajectory. You hold the full ground-truth series but only trust it in periodic windows; between them the model free-runs. Each cycle re-synchronizes the reservoir on a short teacher-forced window, then forecasts across the unobserved gap. Each new observed window can synchronize the state again, limiting accumulated drift when the reservoir and observations support it. This does not guarantee accurate reconstruction or an indefinite forecast. The method loops over forecast() (inference uses no_grad=True by default): the reservoir is reset once (on the first window, and only when reset=True) and its state is carried across the whole pass.

[== warmup W ==][~~ gap P ~~][= teacher F =][~~ gap P ~~][= F =] ...
   observed        filled        observed       filled       obs
 (teacher-forced) (forecast)  (teacher-forced) (forecast)

recon, mask = model.windowed_forecast(
    series,            # (batch, T, feedback_dim) ground truth
    predict_len=200,   # P: autonomous steps per gap
    teacher_len=40,    # F: real steps teacher-forced to re-sync
    warmup_len=200,    # initial sync window (defaults to teacher_len)
    return_mask=True,  # mask[t] True where observed, False where forecast
)
# recon: real values on observed steps, forecasts on the gaps.
# Score the steps the model never saw:
gap_rmse = ((recon[:, ~mask] - series[:, ~mask]) ** 2).mean().sqrt()

The returned mask is a 1-D boolean of length T: True on observed (teacher-forced) steps and any untouched trailing remainder, False on the forecast gaps. The gaps are exactly what you score — recon[:, ~mask] against series[:, ~mask] — the values the model had to infer without ever seeing them. Observed segments are copied verbatim, so recon[:, mask] equals series[:, mask].

For driven models, pass one full-timeline driver series per driver positionally; each is sliced per cycle internally (unlike forecast(), which takes separate warmup and forecast driver tuples):

recon = model.windowed_forecast(feedback, driver, predict_len=100, teacher_len=50)

Keep predict_len short relative to the system's predictability horizon (a few Lyapunov times for chaotic systems): sparse sampling still rebuilds the attractor, but phase tracking degrades before the attractor shape does. For multi-output models the first output is fed back, as in forecast(), and only that channel is reconstructed.

docs.title: Coupled ensembles
docs.text:
A coupled ensemble runs N independently initialized models, trained separately, in a single forecast loop: at every autoregressive step each member receives the same aggregated output (mean, median, or a custom module) as its next feedback. The shared signal couples the members. Their spread measures member disagreement; it is not a calibrated uncertainty interval and need not contain the true trajectory. Wrap the ensemble with rd.Model(graph=ensemble) for the common original-unit workflow. The example below uses its raw API.

import torch
import resdag as rd

ensemble = rd.coupled_ensemble_esn(
    n_models=5,
    model_factory=rd.classic_esn,   # default: rd.ott_esn
    aggregate="mean",               # "median" | nn.Module: (N, B, T, F) -> (B, T, F)
    seed=42,                        # sub-model i is built under seed + i
    reservoir_size=300, feedback_size=3, output_size=3,
)

ensemble.fit((warmup,), (train,), {"output": target})   # same contract as ESNTrainer
preds = ensemble.forecast(f_warmup, horizon=400)        # (batch, 400, 3)

agg, members = ensemble.forecast(f_warmup, horizon=400, return_individuals=True)
spread = torch.stack(members).std(dim=0)                # (batch, 400, 3)

fit trains each member independently on the same data — diversity comes purely from the random initializations (n_workers > 1 fits members in a thread pool). If a member diverges mid-forecast, an outlier-filtering aggregator excludes it from the shared signal:

from resdag.ensemble.aggregators import OutliersFilteredMean

ensemble = rd.coupled_ensemble_esn(
    n_models=10,
    aggregate=OutliersFilteredMean(method="z_score", threshold=2.0),
    reservoir_size=300, feedback_size=3, output_size=3,
)

docs.title: How far you can forecast
docs.text:
For a chaotic system, small initial and modeling errors can grow rapidly. A forecast that tracks the observed continuation for several Lyapunov times may later lose pointwise alignment. Remaining bounded or tracing a similar phase portrait does not establish accurate statistics or the correct invariant measure; those require separate checks.

A fixed Lorenz display case from the independent-trajectory study. Both panels include the entire recorded test window. The trajectory, reservoir seed and forecast start were fixed before final evaluation. The [complete results](../project/phase-five-robustness.md) report error thresholds and accuracy across all cases; the picture alone does not measure accuracy.

Use TSDynamics plots and animations to inspect component traces and attractor geometry together.

If forecasts diverge early, compare hyperparameters on validation data before increasing reservoir size. To quantify how far a forecast tracks — and to report it in the hardware- and system-independent unit of Lyapunov times — see Work · Lyapunov time.

docs.title: Locking the forecast — golden regression fixtures
docs.text:
The forecast path is the library's most-revised code, so its behaviour is pinned by committed golden trajectories. For every forecast-capable premade model (classic_esn, ott_esn, power_augmented) plus an NG-RC forecaster, a fully-seeded warmup → forecast on a canonical Lorenz-63 series is checked in under tests/fixtures/golden_forecast/ and asserted by tests/test_models/test_golden_forecast.py:

  • the first forecast steps must match the golden within a tight tolerance — the structural guard that catches any silent shift in the autoregressive loop (slot-0, the warmup/forecast seam, the flat single-step engine);
  • the Valid Prediction Time against the true continuation must clear a committed floor — a coarser "forecast quality didn't collapse" guard.

If you intentionally change the forecast path (or the canonical data generators), regenerate the goldens and review the diff:

python tools/regen_golden_forecasts.py --check   # verify only — write nothing (CI-style drift check)
python tools/regen_golden_forecasts.py --all     # rewrite every fixture

docs.title: Lyapunov time
docs.text: Work · Lyapunov time

docs.title: Lyapunov time
docs.text: A forecast horizon of "347 steps" means nothing on its own: it depends on the integration step, the system, and the sampling rate. resdag.metrics reports horizons in Lyapunov times instead — the natural clock of a chaotic attractor — so a number is comparable across systems, integration steps, and papers.

docs.title: Why Lyapunov times
docs.text:
On a chaotic system, two trajectories that start infinitesimally close separate on average like \(e^{\lambda_\mathrm{max} t}\), where \(\lambda_\mathrm{max}\) is the largest Lyapunov exponent. One Lyapunov time

\[ t_\lambda = \frac{1}{\lambda_\mathrm{max}} \]

is the timescale over which that separation grows by a factor of \(e\). It is the system's own unit of "how far ahead is hard", so it makes forecast horizons directly comparable: a valid prediction of \(6\,t_\lambda\) on the Lorenz system and \(6\,t_\lambda\) on Rössler span the same multiple of the intrinsic instability timescale. Comparing predictive skill still requires matching error thresholds, normalization, observation noise, and evaluation conditions.

A horizon in steps converts to Lyapunov times by the headline formula

\[ \text{VPT}_{\Lambda t} = \text{steps} \cdot dt \cdot \lambda_\mathrm{max}, \]

where \(dt\) is the integration step. This is steps_to_lyapunov; its inverse is lyapunov_to_steps, and steps_per_lyapunov_time gives \(1/(dt\,\lambda_\mathrm{max})\) — how many samples span one \(t_\lambda\).

docs.title: Canonical exponents
docs.text:
For resdag's built-in chaotic generators the literature \(\lambda_\mathrm{max}\) values are tabulated in CANONICAL_LAMBDA_MAX (and, keyed by the Mackey-Glass delay \(\tau\), in MACKEY_GLASS_LAMBDA):

Generator \(\lambda_\mathrm{max}\) (per unit \(t\)) \(dt\) lorenz (σ, ρ, β = 10, 28, 8/3) 0.9056 0.02 rossler (a, b, c = 0.2, 0.2, 5.7) 0.0714 0.05 mackey_glass (τ = 17) 0.0086 1.0

The exponent is in inverse natural-time units, so multiply by \(dt\) to turn a step count into Lyapunov times. Passing a dataset= name to the metrics below looks these up for you.

docs.title: Measuring forecast quality
docs.text:
The Valid Prediction Time (VPT) is the standard forecast-skill metric on chaotic systems: the number of contiguous steps a closed-loop forecast tracks the truth before its normalised error (NRMSE) first crosses a threshold. valid_prediction_time returns it in raw steps by default, or in Lyapunov times with units="lyapunov" — pass dt and lambda_max explicitly, or a known dataset= name to infer both.

import torch

import resdag as rd
from resdag.datasets import lorenz
from resdag.metrics import reservoir_lyapunov, steps_to_lyapunov, valid_prediction_time
from resdag.utils import prepare_esn_data

torch.manual_seed(0)

# Fit scaling on training history only; validation must not set its statistics.
series = lorenz(6000, normalize=None)  # (1, 6000, 3), dt = 0.02
history = series[:, :500 + 4000 + 1]
mean = history.mean(dim=(0, 1), keepdim=True)
scale = history.std(dim=(0, 1), keepdim=True, correction=0).clamp_min(1e-8)
series = (series - mean) / scale
warmup, train, target, f_warmup, val = prepare_esn_data(
    series, warmup_steps=500, train_steps=4000, val_steps=1000
)

# Train an Ott-augmented ESN in one algebraic pass.
model = rd.ott_esn(reservoir_size=400, feedback_size=3, output_size=3, seed=0)
rd.ESNTrainer(model).fit((warmup,), (train,), {"output": target})

# Forecast aligns one-to-one with the validation split.
preds = model.forecast(f_warmup, horizon=val.shape[1])

# VPT in raw steps and in Lyapunov times (dt / lambda_max inferred from the name).
vpt_steps = valid_prediction_time(preds, val)
vpt_lyap = valid_prediction_time(preds, val, units="lyapunov", dataset="lorenz")
print(f"VPT = {vpt_steps:.0f} steps  =  {vpt_lyap:.2f} Lyapunov times")

# The same conversion done by hand from the canonical exponent.
print("check:", round(steps_to_lyapunov(vpt_steps, dt=0.02, lambda_max=0.9056), 2))

# The reservoir's own maximal Lyapunov exponent (edge-of-chaos diagnostic).
lam = reservoir_lyapunov(model, f_warmup, horizon=500)
print(f"reservoir lambda_max = {lam:.4f} per step  (< 0 => sampled contraction)")

Results depend on reservoir weights, the data split, preprocessing and the numerical backend. The example deliberately computes scaling before preparing the split, using only the history that belongs to training. Built-in generators return raw data by default. An explicit normalize="standard" or normalize="minmax" acts on the entire returned window; keep it disabled when fitting scaling separately on a training prefix.

Report the normalized horizon alongside the threshold, data scaling, and evaluation conditions. Lyapunov-time conversion removes the arbitrary step unit; it does not make different forecasting tasks identical.

docs.title: The reservoir's own exponent
docs.text:
reservoir_lyapunov estimates the maximal Lyapunov exponent of the trained reservoir's own driven dynamics — a distinct quantity from the attractor's \(\lambda_\mathrm{max}\) above. It runs Benettin's algorithm with QR reorthonormalisation of the analytic tangent map along an input-driven trajectory, using Torch on a local CPU float64 copy with no optional dependency. It preserves the caller's weights, device, cached state and training/evaluation mode.

It is the standard edge-of-chaos diagnostic. The Echo State Property requires trajectories from different initial states to converge under the same drive. A negative measured exponent supports contraction along the sampled trajectory; it does not establish the global ESP for every input. A positive value indicates local sensitivity and motivates further stability checks. The returned exponent is in inverse-step units (per reservoir update); multiply by \(1/dt\) to compare it with a natural-time attractor exponent.

lam = reservoir_lyapunov(model, f_warmup, horizon=500)   # scalar, k=1
spectrum = reservoir_lyapunov(model, f_warmup, horizon=500, k=4)   # top-4 as (4,) array

Pass a single ESNLayer or a model containing exactly one ESN reservoir; the reservoir must use the standard tanh ESNCell. The diagnostic includes scalar or per-neuron leakage, recurrent calibration gains and intrinsic gains/biases. Alternative cell update equations raise an explicit error until their tangent maps are validated. Training-only state noise is disabled during measurement. Inputs are used for an initial warmup, then repeated for transient + horizon additional steps; transient growth is discarded and exactly horizon steps are averaged. Repeating a short drive can alter the measured dynamics, so use a representative input window.

docs.title: Arbitrary systems — the dynamics extra
docs.text:
For systems that are not in the canonical tables, largest_lyapunov dispatches on its argument:

  • a generator name ("lorenz", "rossler", "mackey_glass") returns the canonical constant — no dependency;
  • a measured series gives a noisy, data-driven diagnostic estimate (opt in with from_="data", and pass dt);
  • a tsdynamics System computes a numerical Benettin spectrum estimate; check convergence as you increase its averaging time.
from resdag.metrics import largest_lyapunov

largest_lyapunov("lorenz")                 # 0.9056  — canonical, no dependency
largest_lyapunov("mackey_glass", tau=17)   # 0.0086  — canonical, no dependency

Optional dependency: resdag[dynamics]

The series- and System-based paths of largest_lyapunov require the optional tsdynamics package, which needs Python ≥ 3.12:

pip install "resdag[dynamics]"   # or: uv sync --extra dynamics

Every tsdynamics import is lazy and guarded, so this extra is only needed to estimate an exponent for an arbitrary system. The Lyapunov-time conversions, the canonical constants, valid_prediction_time, and reservoir_lyapunov all work with no extra installed.

docs.title: Memory capacity and effective spectral radius
docs.text:
These diagnose different aspects of a reservoir; evaluate autonomous forecast accuracy separately on chronological held-out data.

from resdag import ESNLayer
from resdag.metrics import memory_capacity, effective_spectral_radius

scalar_reservoir = ESNLayer(40, feedback_size=1, bias=False, seed=7)
capacity, curve = memory_capacity(
    scalar_reservoir, max_delay=80, n_samples=2000,
    test_samples=4000, seed=3, return_curve=True,
)

# Use consecutive states from each trajectory: leakage inversion needs neighbours.
representative = torch.sin(torch.arange(300).float()).reshape(1, -1, 1)
scalar_reservoir.reset_state(batch_size=1)
states = scalar_reservoir(representative)
radius = effective_spectral_radius(scalar_reservoir, states, max_states=64)

Memory readouts fit one random input stream and score a separate, independently warmed stream. Ridge fitting uses an augmented least-squares solve, so correlated states do not lose the regularizer through normal equations. Increasing test_samples and repeating seeds helps assess sampling noise. The theoretical population capacity bound is the state count; a finite-sample sum of squared correlations can exceed it. Capacity is not guaranteed to increase with spectral radius. Earlier versions scored fitting samples and could substantially overstate capacity; old numbers must be remeasured.

Effective radius averages local Jacobian eigenvalue radii. It includes the same calibration and per-neuron leakage as the actual standard tanh ESN update and preserves model state and mode. It does not bound transient amplification for non-normal matrices and is not a global stability guarantee.
