docs.title: NG-RC
docs.text: Work · NG-RC

docs.title: NG-RC
docs.text:
Next-generation reservoir computing (NG-RC, Gauthier et al. 2021) replaces the random recurrent reservoir with a deterministic feature map: time delays and the polynomial products of those delays. There are no recurrent weights, no spectral radius, no leak rate, and no seed — two runs with the same k, s, p produce identical features. It slots into the same DAG position as any other reservoir, so the rest of the pipeline — algebraic readout, autoregressive forecast — is unchanged from an echo-state model.

This page is the end-to-end workflow. For the layer itself — every parameter, the feature-count formula, the cumulative-degree convention — see Build · NGReservoir.

docs.title: The feature map
docs.text:
NGReservoir builds three blocks and concatenates them:

  1. a constant 1.0 feature (include_constant),
  2. the delay embedding — the current input stacked with k-1 earlier taps spaced s steps apart (include_linear), giving \(D = \text{input\_dim} \cdot k\) linear features,
  3. the monomials — by default every product of exactly degree p formed from those \(D\) linear features.

The output dimension is

\[ \text{feature\_dim} = \mathbb{1}[\text{constant}] + \mathbb{1}[\text{linear}]\,D + \binom{D+p-1}{p}. \] 
import torch
from resdag import NGReservoir

layer = NGReservoir(input_dim=3, k=2, s=1, p=2)  # delay taps k, spacing s, degree p
x = torch.randn(1, 500, 3)                       # (batch, time, input_dim)
features = layer(x)                              # (1, 500, feature_dim)

print(layer.feature_dim)    # 28 = 1 (constant) + 6 (linear, D=6) + 21 (degree-2 monomials)
print(layer.warmup_length)  # (k-1)*s = 1 — steps before this contain buffer zeros

Exact degree, not degree-up-to-p (default)

By default the nonlinear block holds monomials of exactly degree p — the lower-order cross terms (degrees 2, …, p-1) are excluded, which matches the single-degree bases in Gauthier et al. (2021). If you are porting a config that expects the full "degree up to p" basis common in other NVAR implementations, pass cumulative=True. The layer page has the cumulative feature-count formula.

docs.title: End to end
docs.text:
NG-RC is wired exactly like an echo-state model: a reservoir_input, the feature map, a CGReadoutLayer, then ESNModel. The only NG-RC-specific step is reading feature_dim off the layer to size the readout, since the feature count depends on k, s, p rather than a reservoir_size you chose directly. Build the layer once so you can both query its dimension and wire it into the graph.

import torch
import resdag as rd
from resdag import ESNModel, NGReservoir, reservoir_input, lorenz
from resdag.layers import CGReadoutLayer

data = lorenz(5000, seed=0)                      # (1, 5000, 3) — chaotic benchmark
warmup, train, target, f_warmup, val = rd.utils.prepare_esn_data(
    data, warmup_steps=20, train_steps=3000, val_steps=1000, normalize=True
)

ngrc = NGReservoir(input_dim=3, k=2, s=1, p=2)   # build once: query + wire the same layer

inp = reservoir_input(3)
features = ngrc(inp)
out = CGReadoutLayer(ngrc.feature_dim, 3, name="output", alpha=1e-6)(features)
model = ESNModel(inp, out)

rd.ESNTrainer(model).fit(
    warmup_inputs=(warmup,),                     # short: warmup only fills the (k-1)*s buffer
    train_inputs=(train,),
    targets={"output": target},                  # keyed by the readout name
)

forecast = model.forecast(f_warmup, horizon=200)  # (1, 200, 3) autoregressive rollout

Everything after the feature map is the standard workflow: ESNTrainer.fit solves the readout by ridge regression in one pass, and model.forecast runs the two-phase autoregressive rollout. alpha on the readout is the only fitting hyperparameter; sweep it on a log scale exactly as for an echo-state model.

Warmup is short on purpose

NG-RC's only state is the FIFO delay buffer, which fills in (k-1)*s steps — 1 step for k=2, s=1. The warmup_steps=20 above is generous; NG-RC needs nothing like the hundreds of steps an echo-state reservoir spends washing out its random initial condition. The first layer.warmup_length outputs still contain buffer zeros, so keep the warmup at least that long and discard those steps from a loss if you score one directly.

docs.title: When to prefer NG-RC over an ESN
docs.text:
NG-RC and the echo-state reservoir occupy the same slot, so the choice is a modeling decision rather than an API one:

Reach for NG-RC when… Reach for an ESN when… The dataset is short — the (k-1)*s-step warmup wastes almost no data. You have plenty of data and warmup length is not a constraint. You need exact reproducibility — the map is deterministic, no seed. A random projection into a large state is acceptable or desirable. The system is low-dimensional with smooth polynomial structure. The signal is high-dimensional — monomials explode combinatorially. You want few, interpretable knobs — three small integers, grid-searchable. You are comfortable tuning spectral radius, leak rate, and topology.

The trade-off is the binomial term in feature_dim: it grows fast in k, p, and input_dim, and NGReservoir warns once feature_dim exceeds 10,000. For high-dimensional signals, an echo-state reservoir that compresses into a fixed-size state is usually the better fit. Because NG-RC is a plain feature map with no learnable parameters, it also drops into the frozen-features training path unchanged — gradients flow through it to any upstream module.

docs.title: Save, load & diagrams
docs.text: Work · Save and load

docs.title: Save, load and inspect a model
The everyday workflow
docs.text:
import torch
import resdag as rd

series = torch.sin(torch.linspace(0, 18, 220, dtype=torch.float64))[:, None]
model = rd.ESN(reservoir_size=24, washout=15, seed=7).double().fit(series)
expected = model.forecast(horizon=20)
model.save("run.pt")

restored = rd.load("run.pt", map_location="cpu")
actual = restored.forecast(horizon=20)
torch.testing.assert_close(actual, expected, rtol=0, atol=0)

You do not rebuild the graph. The file contains the model's construction, weights, fitted preprocessing, named ports, feedback settings, prediction leads, observed history and current reservoir memory. Presets and custom rd.Model DAGs use the same commands. Parallel and coupled graphs keep their geometry and member structure. Trajectory sampling metadata and signal names are retained; a live TSDynamics system object is not bundled into portable files.

A loaded model remains an ordinary nn.Module, so .to(device), .float(), model(x) and integration into a larger PyTorch network work as usual. state_dict() remains useful when the surrounding application already owns its architecture. Complete artifacts do not store your optimizer, autograd graph, compiled executors, active execution hooks or live Optuna study connection. Built-in checkpoint integrity hooks remain available.

docs.title: Reservoir memory and forecasts
docs.text:
Saving includes current reservoir memory by default. After processing one chunk, saving and loading, an ordinary restored(next_chunk) continues from that memory. Use model.reset_state() for an unrelated sequence, or save with include_state=False to start with fresh recurrent memory on reload. Fitted weights, preprocessing and observed training history are retained either way. Moving between device types can restart a backend-specific noise RNG stream; the loader reports that limitation. Stored memory still moves with the tensors.

A forecast uses its saved or explicitly supplied history to synchronize and construct delayed feedback queues. A checkpoint does not save an in-progress forecast iterator or its clock. Do not treat ordinary reservoir state as an autonomous forecast cursor. Temporal layers that need full history may produce larger files because that history is part of their forecasting context.

docs.title: Diagrams and formats
docs.text:
model.save("structure.dot")  # text; no visualization dependencies
model.save("structure.svg")
model.save("structure.png")
model.save("structure.pdf")
model.save("wide", format="svg", rankdir="LR", show_trainable=True)
source = model.plot_model()  # notebook-displayable Graphviz source
assert "pt" in model.save_formats

Install pip install 'resdag[viz]' and the Graphviz system executable to render SVG, PNG or PDF (brew install graphviz on macOS; apt install graphviz on Debian/Ubuntu). DOT needs neither. The suffix selects the format; a name without a suffix defaults to .pt, or gains the explicit requested format. A format that disagrees with the suffix raises an error. Exports write one file at the returned path and never launch a system viewer.

Diagrams show branches, merges, layer names, feature widths, named input/output ports and delayed feedback. Coupled members have separate clusters; parallel graphs show periodic patch geometry and the shared reservoir/readout. Graph inspection does not execute layers, advance reservoir state or change modes.

docs.title: Custom components: portable registration
docs.text:
A portable file contains configuration and tensors, with versioned component identifiers. Built-in components are registered by ResDAG. For your own class, register a small recipe that describes how to construct it. Learned parameters and buffers are handled separately by the standard Torch state mechanism.

from torch import nn

class Gain(nn.Module):
    supports_framewise = True

    def __init__(self, factor=2.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.factor = float(factor)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.factor * x

rd.register_component(
    "myproject.Gain", Gain,
    encode=lambda layer: {"factor": layer.factor},
    decode=lambda config: Gain(**config),
    version=1,
)

x = rd.reservoir_input(1, dtype=torch.float64)
y = rd.SVDReadoutLayer(1, 1).double()(Gain(2.0)(x))
custom = rd.Model(inputs={"signal": x}, outputs={"prediction": y}, washout=5)
custom.fit(series)
custom.save("custom.pt")
loaded = rd.load("custom.pt")
assert loaded.input_names == ("signal",)

Import your registration module before loading in another process. Configuration can contain tensors, primitive values and other registered components. Use a stable project-specific name and increase the codec version when its contract changes. Unknown classes or versions fail with a registration remedy; the file does not import arbitrary Python paths. Custom subclasses require their own registration so custom behavior cannot silently disappear. Initializer registration remains the separate weight-generation extension point. A trained raw graph can restore its weights without an initializer-only callback; a callback without a portable codec may be omitted from that raw graph's recipe. Register its codec or use a trusted bundle to retain that recipe for reuse. Presets retain their factory recipe for tuning and reject unsupported recipe components instead of silently dropping them.

You can provide a local ComponentCodec through rd.load(path, custom_objects={"myproject.Gain": codec}) instead of changing the global registry. Its identifier, exact class and version must match. The decoder is application code you have explicitly installed.

Portable loading restores realized weights without rerunning original initializer callbacks. Some structured cells still perform constructor work, such as QR factorization or Legendre discretization, before those weights are restored. Treat loading as setup work when measuring performance.

docs.title: Notebook-defined Python code
docs.text:
For experiments that define classes or functions inside a notebook, an optional bundle can carry that Python code too:

# Requires pip install 'resdag[artifacts]'.
custom.save("notebook.pt", trusted=True)
notebook_model = rd.load("notebook.pt", trusted=True)

Both operations require the explicit flag. Only load a trusted bundle when you trust its producer: restoring bundled Python executes code. Normal portable checkpoints use restricted Torch loading and require no bundled Python.

docs.title: Low-level graph checkpoints
docs.text:
The raw graph, parallel and ensemble classes also provide weight checkpoints through save/load. Their metadata and custom extra state must contain tensors and primitive containers; unsupported Python objects are rejected before saving. Loading uses Torch's restricted weights_only=True mode. For complete portable models, prefer the common Model.save/rd.load workflow above.

Raw save_full files pickle Python. Their corresponding load_full methods require trusted=True explicitly, before reading the file. Use this only for a known producer; the portable artifact format is the default recommendation. Bundles use the standard cloudpickle package and need a compatible Python and dependency environment; keep experiment environments pinned when archiving.

docs.title: Metadata and failure behavior
docs.text:
model.save("annotated.pt", metadata={"experiment": "sine", "seed": 7})
loaded, metadata = rd.load("annotated.pt", return_metadata=True)
assert metadata == {"experiment": "sine", "seed": 7}

Metadata uses primitive values and tensors. Saves write to a temporary file and replace the destination only after successful serialization. Unsupported formats, unknown artifact versions and missing components raise useful errors. Keep an independent copy of valuable experiments and their environment specification.

docs.title: Keep large models within memory
docs.text: Three allocations grow for different reasons: recurrent weights with reservoir size, collected features with sequence length, and solver workspaces with the number of features. Choose a remedy for the allocation that limits your model.

docs.title: Compressed reservoir weights
docs.text:
For supported frozen ESN reservoirs, sparse=True keeps only compressed recurrent weights. It no longer retains a full square matrix alongside them. The same fit, forecast and save commands work:

import torch
import resdag as rd

t = torch.arange(400, dtype=torch.float64) * 0.05
training = torch.stack((t.sin(), t.cos()), dim=-1)
model = rd.ESN(
    64, input_size=2, washout=30, seed=7, dtype=torch.float64,
    topology=("erdos_renyi", {"p": 6 / 64}), sparse=True,
    readout="lsmr", alpha=1e-3,
    readout_kwargs={"max_iter": 1000, "chunk_size": 128},
).fit(training)
prediction = model.forecast(horizon=40)
assert prediction.shape == (40, 2)

cell = next(layer.cell for layer in model.graph.modules()
            if isinstance(layer, rd.ESNLayer))
assert cell.weight_hh.layout == torch.sparse_csr
model.save("compact.pt")
restored = rd.load("compact.pt")
expected = model.forecast(history=training[-60:], horizon=40)
actual = restored.forecast(history=training[-60:], horizon=40)
torch.testing.assert_close(actual, expected, rtol=0, atol=0)

The weight_hh attribute is a CSR Tensor view over ordinary persistent index and value buffers. It is no longer a dense Parameter for a sparse reservoir. cell.weight_hh.to_dense() explicitly makes an inspection copy. Change existing connection values with cell.weight_hh.values() under torch.no_grad(). The view shares those values; there is no stale operator cache to refresh.

The readout remains a normal Torch layer. Gradients can pass through the frozen reservoir to earlier layers. Setting cell.trainable = True explicitly expands the recurrent weights into a dense Parameter and warns about that allocation; create an optimizer after changing the set of trainable parameters. Freezing again restores the original sparse request. model.requires_grad_(True) affects registered Parameters; compressed recurrent buffers remain fixed. Set cell.trainable = True first when the recurrent connections themselves must become trainable.

CSR is available on CPU and supported CUDA devices. MPS uses dense weights; moving a model to MPS can therefore increase its memory requirement. Returning to CPU restores an explicit sparse=True request. No CUDA throughput was measured for this work.

docs.title: Compact does not always mean faster
docs.text:
Dense remains the default. sparse="auto" currently uses size/density heuristics, not a hardware calibration. Earlier Apple Silicon measurements include cases where dense multiplication beat CSR at 400–2,000 units; these observations do not cover every density, batch or dtype. Choose explicitly and measure your actual batch, precision and reservoir size. Sparse storage can still be valuable when memory is the binding constraint.

Initialization also matters. The built-in Erdős–Rényi sparse route uses bounded random blocks and produces the same unscaled edges and signs as its dense definition. Edge-native graph builders avoid a dense adjacency as well. Some other graph functions allocate dense NumPy arrays internally, so this is not a universal constant-memory initialization claim.

Sparse spectral scaling uses SciPy Arnoldi or an analytic spectrum for triangular matrices and matrices with at most one stored entry per row. In the latter case, SciPy identifies the directed cycles, whose radii are the geometric means of their edge magnitudes; branches contribute zero eigenvalues. This avoids iterative convergence failures for simple cycles and signed permutations, without allocating a dense square matrix. For example:

cycle = rd.ESNLayer(
    400, feedback_size=2, topology=("simple_cycle", {"weight": 0.7}),
    spectral_radius=0.9, sparse=True, seed=7, dtype=torch.float64,
)
assert cycle.weight_hh.layout == torch.sparse_csr

Only matrices of size one or two use a bounded dense fallback. An unsuccessful large sparse estimate raises instead of allocating a hidden dense fallback. Its scaling may differ in the last digits from dense eigvals, especially when initializing in float32. New sparse runs can therefore differ from older seeded experiments. Dense initialization and execution keep their existing path.

docs.title: Register a sparse-native initializer
docs.text:
Ordinary registered matrix builders can return a Torch CSR Tensor or a SciPy sparse matrix. No full dense destination is allocated for these build-style callables. Placement and dtype are passed when declared in the signature:

@rd.init.register_recurrent_initializer("my_sparse_cycle", prescaled=True, weight=0.8)
def sparse_cycle(n, weight=0.8, *, dtype=None, device=None):
    rows = torch.arange(n + 1, dtype=torch.int64, device=device)
    columns = (torch.arange(n, dtype=torch.int64, device=device) + 1) % n
    values = torch.full((n,), weight, dtype=dtype, device=device)
    return torch.sparse_csr_tensor(rows, columns, values, size=(n, n))

layer = rd.ESNLayer(
    64, feedback_size=2, recurrent_initializer="my_sparse_cycle",
    spectral_radius=None, sparse=True, dtype=torch.float64,
)
assert layer.weight_hh._nnz() == 64

Existing in-place builders remain supported through a temporary dense scratch matrix. A custom TopologyInitializer subclass can override build_sparse(n, *, dtype, device, spectral_radius) to construct CSR directly. Its normal initialize(...) method still supports dense models. Returned storage is copied into model-owned components; later edits to the initializer's own matrix cannot change an already built model.

docs.title: Readout and sequence memory
docs.text:
The example opts into LSMR, which avoids a full feature-by-feature Gram matrix. It solves on CPU and reports convergence; automatic readout selection is unchanged. This is a separate choice from compressed recurrence.

Batch fitting still collects feature sequences. Reducing a dense N × N recurrent allocation does not remove a time × features history. For long sequences, use the streaming workflow with a compatible incremental readout. Explicit-state DAG evaluation releases intermediate feature tensors after their last consumer, while keeping requested outputs, final states and tensors needed by autograd alive.

Tuning's optional memory-budget planner remains conservative: its default estimate reserves dense preset weights and general direct-solver workspaces, even when a candidate selects sparse storage or LSMR. It can therefore reject a model that would actually fit. Supply a workload-specific memory_estimator when you need tighter admission; see tuning resources. This estimate does not change the model's actual storage or solver.

docs.title: Streaming & DataLoaders
docs.text:
Because ResDAG models are ordinary torch.nn.Modules, they slot straight into the PyTorch data stack. TimeSeriesWindowDataset slices a long trajectory into fixed-length windows and make_dataloader wraps it in a standard DataLoader whose batches are (B, window_len, D) — exactly what ESNLayer and ESNModel consume. The same loader drives gradient descent and an algebraic ridge fit that never holds the whole state matrix in memory.

The runnable end-to-end recipe behind this page is examples/14_streaming_dataloader.py.

docs.title: Windowing a trajectory
docs.text:
make_dataloader builds the dataset and loader in one call. Each window is an (input, target, washout) triple: in the default forecasting mode the target is the input shifted forward horizon steps, and washout marks the leading steps to drop from the loss while the reservoir synchronizes. Windows never straddle a trajectory boundary, so per-window state resets keep one trajectory from leaking into the next.

import torch
from resdag import make_dataloader, lorenz

series = lorenz(4000, seed=0, normalize="standard")[0]           # (4000, 3) — drop the batch axis: lorenz is (1, T, 3)

loader = make_dataloader(
    series,
    batch_size=16,
    window_len=250,                        # timesteps per window
    horizon=1,                             # one-step-ahead target (input shifted +1)
    stride=125,                            # 50% overlap between successive windows
    washout=50,                            # leading steps excluded from the loss
    shuffle=True,
)

x, y, washout = next(iter(loader))
print(x.shape, y.shape, washout)           # (16, 250, 3) (16, 250, 3) 50

These examples use the entire generated series for training, so their explicit standardization uses training observations only. For held-out evaluation, split the raw series first and reuse statistics fitted on the training prefix. The common Model.fit workflow owns that scaling automatically.

series may be a single (T, D) tensor, a batched (B, T, D) tensor (each slice becomes one trajectory), or a ragged list of (T, D) tensors of differing length — windows are generated per trajectory in every case. For a regression task, pass an aligned targets= tensor instead of relying on horizon. Input stats normalize inputs and shifted forecast targets; external regression targets keep their own units. Pass separate target_stats and target_norm_method to normalize external targets. Need the underlying dataset for a custom loader? Build a TimeSeriesWindowDataset directly and wrap it yourself.

docs.title: The SGD loop
docs.text:
The canonical loop trains a head on frozen reservoir features, minibatched over the loader. Reset the reservoir at the top of each window so state does not carry across independent windows; skip the washout steps when computing the loss.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from resdag import ESNLayer, make_dataloader, lorenz

series = lorenz(4000, seed=0, normalize="standard")[0]
loader = make_dataloader(series, batch_size=16, window_len=250,
                         horizon=1, stride=125, washout=50, shuffle=True)

reservoir = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9, trainable=False)
head = nn.Linear(200, 3)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(head.parameters(), lr=5e-3)   # head only — reservoir is frozen
criterion = nn.MSELoss()

for epoch in range(6):
    for x, y, washout in loader:
        reservoir.reset_state()                            # each window is independent
        pred = head(reservoir(x))
        loss = criterion(pred[:, washout:], y[:, washout:])  # skip the washout transient
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

detach_state_between_calls is on by default, so even without the per-window reset_state() the stored state is severed from the autograd graph at every forward-call boundary and consecutive backward() calls never raise "backward through the graph a second time". To backpropagate through the recurrence as well (full BPTT through each window), build the reservoir with trainable=True and add its parameters to the optimizer — see Train · Path 3.

docs.title: Algebraic over the DataLoader
docs.text:
When the reservoir is fixed and you want the classic ridge readout — but the full state matrix would not fit in memory — accumulate the fit incrementally. IncrementalRidgeReadoutLayer keeps the ridge sufficient statistics (the Gram matrix and cross term), so partial_fit per batch followed by a single finalize is algebraically identical to one full-batch solve over the concatenated data, to floating-point tolerance.

import torch
from resdag import ESNLayer, make_dataloader, lorenz
from resdag.layers import IncrementalRidgeReadoutLayer

series = lorenz(4000, seed=0, normalize="standard")[0]
loader = make_dataloader(series, batch_size=16, window_len=250,
                         horizon=1, stride=125, washout=50)

reservoir = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9, trainable=False)
readout = IncrementalRidgeReadoutLayer(200, 3, name="output", alpha=1e-4)

readout.reset_accumulators()
with torch.no_grad():
    for x, y, washout in loader:
        reservoir.reset_state()
        states = reservoir(x)
        readout.partial_fit(states[:, washout:], y[:, washout:])  # accumulate, hold no full matrix

print(f"accumulated {readout.n_seen} post-washout samples")
readout.finalize()                          # one ridge solve from the running statistics

with torch.no_grad():
    x, y, washout = next(iter(loader))
    reservoir.reset_state()
    pred = readout(reservoir(x))            # is_fitted is now True

finalize must be called once before inference — forward on an unfitted IncrementalRidgeReadoutLayer raises with a clear message. Calling partial_fit again after finalize keeps accumulating and re-marks the layer unfitted, so finalize again to refresh; reset_accumulators starts a fresh fit.

docs.title: fit_stream — the trainer over a stream
docs.text:
For a full ESNModel whose readouts are all IncrementalRidgeReadoutLayer, the trainer wraps the accumulate-then-finalize pattern in fit_stream. It warms the reservoir once, then consumes chunks one at a time, accumulating each readout's statistics and solving once at the end — no more than a single chunk's states are ever in memory.

import torch
import resdag as rd
from resdag import ESNLayer, ESNModel, reservoir_input, make_dataloader, lorenz
from resdag.layers import IncrementalRidgeReadoutLayer

series = lorenz(4000, seed=0, normalize="standard")                # keep (1, T, D): one continuous stream

inp = reservoir_input(3)
states = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9)(inp)
out = IncrementalRidgeReadoutLayer(200, 3, name="output", alpha=1e-4)(states)
model = ESNModel(inp, out)

warmup = series[:, :300]                    # (1, 300, 3)

def chunk_stream():
    # Adjacent input chunks, with next-sample targets and fixed batch slots.
    for start in range(300, series.shape[1] - 1, 250):
        stop = min(start + 250, series.shape[1] - 1)
        yield (series[:, start:stop],), {"output": series[:, start+1:stop+1]}

rd.ESNTrainer(model).fit_stream(warmup_inputs=(warmup,), chunks=chunk_stream())
forecast = model.forecast(series[:, -300:], horizon=200)

Chunks must be contiguous and in order

fit_stream flows reservoir state from the end of one chunk into the start of the next, exactly as a single long forward pass would. Do not shuffle or overlap chunks feeding fit_stream — that desynchronizes the reservoir. Keep the same batch size and trajectory in each batch slot. Ordinary sliding-window batches represent independent windows and should use the per-window reset/partial_fit path above. (The shuffled loader earlier on this page is fine for the SGD and per-window partial_fit paths, which reset state per window.) Every readout in the model must be an IncrementalRidgeReadoutLayer; mixed readouts raise, and fit is the in-memory path for single-pass readouts. Readouts on separate branches may share the stream; stacked readouts require separate fitting passes because their input features depend on upstream fitted weights.

docs.title: When to use which path
docs.text: Path Use when SGD loop (frozen head) The head is nonlinear or the loss is not least-squares; you want minibatched gradient training. SGD loop (trainable=True) You need full BPTT through the recurrence (rarely worth it — see Train). Per-window partial_fit A fixed reservoir, the classic ridge readout, and a state matrix too large to materialize, with manual control over the loop. fit_stream The same algebraic streaming fit for a full ESNModel, with warmup and the contiguous-chunk bookkeeping handled for you.

docs.title: Train

docs.title: Train
docs.text: Three training paths coexist because ResDAG models are ordinary torch.nn.Modules. The algebraic solve is the standard reservoir-computing approach and the usual starting point; use gradient-based training when the problem is not a least-squares fit.

docs.title: Path 1 — the algebraic solve
docs.text:
ESNTrainer.fit fits every readout in the model algebraically, all inside a single forward pass; for a CGReadoutLayer each fit is one ridge regression:

import torch
import resdag as rd
from resdag import ESNLayer, ESNModel, reservoir_input
from resdag.layers import CGReadoutLayer

data = torch.load("series.pt")        # (1, 7500, 3) — (batch, time, features)
warmup, train, target, f_warmup, val = rd.utils.prepare_esn_data(
    data, warmup_steps=300, train_steps=5000, val_steps=2000, normalize=True
)

inp = reservoir_input(3)
states = ESNLayer(500, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9)(inp)
out = CGReadoutLayer(500, 3, name="output", alpha=1e-6)(states)
model = ESNModel(inp, out)

rd.ESNTrainer(model).fit(
    warmup_inputs=(warmup,),          # tuple: (feedback, driver1, ...)
    train_inputs=(train,),            # same number of tensors as warmup
    targets={"output": target},       # keyed by readout name
)

What fit does, in order:

  1. Validates — warmup and train tuples must hold the same number of tensors, targets must match train in sequence length, and every readout needs a key in targets (a missing key raises; an extra one warns).
  2. Owns one concatenated warmup-plus-training prefix and resets reservoir states once.
  3. Visits graph operations in dependency order. Each reservoir processes the complete prefix once, carrying its state across the warmup/training boundary.
  4. At each readout, fits on training rows only, then applies the fitted mapping to the entire prefix. Downstream reservoirs therefore receive the fitted upstream predictions during both warmup and training.
  5. Reuses branch results and releases cached values after their last consumer. It never replays the whole graph for a later readout. Normal PyTorch hooks still run. A standard nn.Sequential can express nested dependencies; opaque custom containers mixing readouts and reservoirs are rejected.

Warmup contributes recurrent context, not regression rows. Sequence-dependent layers see the uninterrupted prefix too. Compared with the former replaying trainer, stochastic layers, including reservoir noise, consume random draws in a different order; seeded runs remain repeatable, but old noisy-fit results may change. Ordinary deterministic, framewise cascades retain numerical parity. Temporal graphs use the corrected full-prefix features. See the controlled depth benchmark.

Multi-readout models need one key per readout name:

rd.ESNTrainer(model).fit(
    warmup_inputs=(warmup,),
    train_inputs=(train,),
    targets={"position": pos_target, "velocity": vel_target},
)

docs.title: Internal readouts without extra prediction outputs
docs.text:
Use rd.Model.fit for automatic input/output scaling and failed-refit isolation. An internal head can have its own supervision without becoming a public output:

import torch
import resdag as rd

x = rd.reservoir_input(1, dtype=torch.float64)
hidden = rd.SVDReadoutLayer(1, 1, name="stage1").double()(x)
states = rd.ESNLayer(12, feedback_size=1, seed=7, dtype=torch.float64)(hidden)
y = rd.RidgeReadoutLayer(12, 1, alpha=1e-3).double()(states)
model = rd.Model(inputs={"signal": x}, outputs={"prediction": y}, washout=10)

series = torch.sin(torch.linspace(0, 12, 150, dtype=torch.float64))[:, None]
inputs, final_values = series[:-1], series[1:]
model.fit(inputs, targets=final_values, readout_targets={"stage1": 2 * inputs})
forecast = model.forecast(horizon=20)  # one tensor: only the declared prediction
assert forecast.shape == (20, 1)
assert model.internal_readout_names == ("stage1",)

Internal targets use the internal head's desired output units, unchanged by public output scaling. Include the same full time axis as the inputs, including warmup; fit discards the warmup labels. With implicit next-value targets it also excludes the unsupervised final input origin. Choose explicit readout names for convenient keys; unnamed heads use their graph paths. Coupled members use models.0.stage1, models.1.stage1, and so on. Missing, extra, nonfinite or incorrectly shaped internal targets fail before fitting.

For trajectory inputs, internal target tensors must already match the prepared shared input clock. Keep reservoirs as separate functional nodes for forecasting; reservoirs nested inside containers support ordinary stateful calls and fitting, but cannot currently use the explicit-state forecast engine.

The raw ESNTrainer changes its graph in place if a later readout fails. The common Model.fit stages the complete fit and commits only on success, preserving the live model and caller input tensors after failure.

What alpha does. Each CGReadoutLayer solves \(\min_W \lVert XW - Y \rVert^2 + \alpha \lVert W \rVert^2\); alpha is its only fitting hyperparameter and it lives on the layer, not the trainer. Larger values shrink the weights, giving smoother, more stable forecasts at the cost of one-step accuracy. It acts on a log scale: sweep \(10^{-8}\) to \(10^{-2}\) in decade steps, not linearly.

docs.title: Preparing the data
docs.text:
prepare_esn_data cuts one series into the five tensors used above:

[ discard ][ warmup ][———————————— train ————————————][seam][ val ]
                      [—— target = train shifted +1 ——]

Each training input is paired with the next sample in the original series: target[:, t] = data[:, discard_steps + warmup_steps + t + 1]. The final target is the seam sample, immediately after the training inputs. With train_end = warmup_steps + train_steps measured after discarding, validation starts at data[:, train_end + 1]. The seam is therefore used for training and excluded from held-out scoring.

With the default alignment="next", f_warmup contains the last warmup_steps observed samples, including the seam at data[:, train_end]. When training is shorter than warmup, it includes part of the earlier warmup history. Its last output predicts the first held-out sample, data[:, train_end + 1], so the forecast aligns directly with val. The required source length is discard_steps + warmup_steps + train_steps + 1 + val_steps. With normalize=True, statistics are fitted on training inputs only and applied to every split; return_stats=True also returns those statistics for inverting predictions with rd.data.denormalize_data.

docs.title: Path 2 — frozen reservoir, gradient head
docs.text:
When the head must be nonlinear or the loss is not least-squares, use the reservoir as a fixed feature extractor and train any PyTorch head on top. ReservoirFeatureExtractor packages a reservoir as a plain nn.Module that drops straight into nn.Sequential ahead of the head — single positional input, frozen by default, one optimizer over model.parameters():

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from resdag import ReservoirFeatureExtractor

model = nn.Sequential(
    ReservoirFeatureExtractor(500, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9),
    nn.Linear(500, 64),
    nn.Tanh(),
    nn.Linear(64, 3),
)
extractor, head = model[0], model[1:]
opt = torch.optim.Adam(head.parameters(), lr=1e-3)  # head only — reservoir is frozen

with torch.no_grad():                        # frozen features: compute once
    extractor.on_epoch_start()               # epoch-reset hook (alias of reset_state)
    feats = extractor(torch.cat([warmup, train], dim=1))[:, warmup.shape[1]:]

for step in range(300):
    loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(head(feats), target)
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

The reservoir is frozen by default (extractor.is_frozen is True), so the optimizer only ever sees the head's parameters. Precomputing feats once avoids re-running the reservoir on every optimization step; this is the main efficiency advantage of a frozen base. Streaming also works: push fresh batches through the reservoir inside the loop and consecutive backward() calls succeed without resets, because the stored state is detached at every forward-call boundary (detach_state_between_calls=True) and no autograd graph survives to trigger "backward through the graph a second time".

The epoch hook. The reservoir is stateful, so re-zero it between epochs with extractor.on_epoch_start() (a readable alias of reset_state()) at the top of each epoch — otherwise a trajectory from the previous epoch bleeds into the next one:

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    extractor.on_epoch_start()               # re-zero the reservoir state
    for batch_feedback, batch_target in loader:
        loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(head(extractor(batch_feedback)), batch_target)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

A non-regression head. Because the extractor is just an nn.Module, any torch head works. Feeding the last-timestep feature vector into a linear classifier and a cross-entropy loss turns the same frozen reservoir into a sequence classifier:

extractor = ReservoirFeatureExtractor(500, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9)
classifier = nn.Linear(500, num_classes)

with torch.no_grad():
    extractor.reset_state()
    summary = extractor(sequences)[:, -1, :]   # (batch, 500) — last-step features

opt = torch.optim.Adam(classifier.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
for step in range(150):
    loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(classifier(summary), labels)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

Reusing an existing model. ReservoirFeatureExtractor.from_model(esn) wraps the reservoir layers of an already-built ESNModel by reference — the parameters are shared, not copied — so an algebraically-fitted model can double as a feature source without rebuilding the reservoir:

from resdag import ESNModel, ESNLayer, reservoir_input

inp = reservoir_input(3)
states = ESNLayer(500, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9)(inp)
esn = ESNModel(inp, states)
extractor = ReservoirFeatureExtractor.from_model(esn)  # shares esn's reservoir

To backpropagate through the recurrence as well (full BPTT, Path 3), pass trainable=True or call extractor.unfreeze(). The runnable end-to-end recipe — regression head, classification head, and from_model reuse — is examples/12_feature_extractor.py.

docs.title: Path 3 — full BPTT
docs.text:
trainable=True unfreezes the recurrent and input weights; gradients then flow through the recurrence itself:

reservoir = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9, trainable=True)
head = nn.Linear(200, 3)
opt = torch.optim.Adam([*reservoir.parameters(), *head.parameters()], lr=1e-3)

for epoch in range(30):
    reservoir.reset_state()                      # fresh state each epoch
    pred = head(reservoir(train[:, :400]))       # truncate: BPTT cost grows with T
    loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(pred, target[:, :400])
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(reservoir.parameters(), 1.0)
    opt.step()

Clip gradients (backpropagation through hundreds of recurrent steps is prone to exploding gradients) and keep the windows short. Use this path when validation shows a frozen reservoir is insufficient. Backpropagation retains intermediate states and repeats the sequence across optimizer steps; measure its memory and training cost on your workload. Updates can move the recurrent matrix away from the spectral radius you configured.

Combining paths

The paths compose. Build the readout with trainable=True, run ESNTrainer.fit to obtain the ridge solution (the solve writes the weights directly, regardless of trainable), then fine-tune from there with a small learning rate. The algebraic solution is a better initialization than random weights.

docs.title: Path 4 — differentiable forecast (BPTT through the rollout)
docs.text:
Paths 1–3 train on a teacher-forced pass — every step sees ground truth. But the quantity you usually care about is free-running forecast quality, where each prediction is fed back as the next input and errors compound. To optimize that directly, roll the forecast out differentiably and backpropagate the multi-step loss through the autoregressive loop.

forecast(no_grad=False) does exactly this: instead of running under torch.no_grad() (the default), it builds an autograd graph through the warmup and every autoregressive step, so loss.backward() reaches the trainable reservoir and readout parameters:

inp = reservoir_input(3)
states = ESNLayer(200, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9, trainable=True)(inp)
model = ESNModel(inp, nn.Linear(200, 3)(states))     # any differentiable head
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

for step in range(50):
    preds = model.forecast(f_warmup, horizon=60, no_grad=False)  # differentiable rollout
    loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(preds, val[:, :60])            # multi-step forecast loss
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()                                              # BPTT through the loop
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
    opt.step()

The returned tensor carries requires_grad=True, and gradients flow back through every fed-back step — this is BPTT through the closed-loop forecast, not just a teacher-forced window. Keep the horizon short (backprop through a long autoregressive chain is memory-heavy and prone to exploding gradients — clip), and use this only when free-running skill genuinely matters more than the one-step fit the algebraic solve optimizes.

Two constraints:

  • no_grad=False is mutually exclusive with compile=True — the compiled flat engine is inference-only, so requesting both raises ValueError.
  • Something in the loop must be trainable (trainable=True on the reservoir, and/or a gradient head); with everything frozen the backward pass has nothing to update.

docs.title: Tune a model
docs.text:
Call model.tune(data) to choose a configuration using autonomous forecasts. It returns the same model, fitted with the winning settings and ready for forecast(). rd.ESN and custom rd.Model networks use the same commands.

Install the optional tuning tools:

python -m pip install "resdag[hpo]"

docs.title: Start with a preset
docs.text:
Keep a final test segment separate from tuning. This small example uses a sine wave so the complete workflow is easy to run:

import torch
import resdag as rd

series = torch.sin(torch.arange(600, dtype=torch.float64) * 0.05)[:, None]
development, test = series[:500], series[500:540]

model = rd.ESN(reservoir_size=64, washout=30, readout="svd", dtype=torch.float64)
model.tune(development, preset="quick", horizon=40, seed=7)
prediction = model.forecast(horizon=len(test))

print(model.tuning_report.best_params)
print("Test RMSE:", (prediction - test).square().mean().sqrt().item())
assert prediction.shape == test.shape

The tuner first fits on the earliest 80% of development and checks forecasts against its final 20%. After choosing a winner, it refits on all supplied development observations. forecast() then starts after their final sample. Scaling is learned during each fit; predictions remain in the original units. The untouched test segment gives a separate final evaluation.

model.tuning_report.study is the full Optuna study. model.tuning_report.best_params includes fixed values returned by your search function as well as values sampled by Optuna.

docs.title: Choose the amount of work
docs.text:
Preset New trial attempts Initialization seeds Forecast starting points "quick" 8 1 1 "balanced" (default) 24 3 3 "thorough" 80 5 5

Seeds and starting points are reused across configurations. A starting point is a later moment in the held-out segment: the model sees observations before that moment to synchronize its state, then forecasts without seeing future feedback values. Its readout and preprocessing stay fixed during these checks. Windows may overlap; they are several checks of one series, not independent experiments.

Set n_trials, seeds and n_origins to override those counts. There can be fewer starting points when the data cannot support more distinct full windows. All use the same horizon. Omitting it uses half the available validation span, with a minimum of one sample; changing presets does not change that horizon. An unsupported explicit horizon raises before any trial starts.

Built-in vanilla and OTT models search reservoir size, spectral radius, leak, input strength, bias strength, recurrent connection density and readout regularization (alpha). The trial and repetition budgets above stay the same. Vanilla recipes also try input_to_readout=True and False: the readout can use current input plus reservoir memory, or memory alone. Ordinary model construction still defaults to True. OTT keeps its augmented feature layout. For an OTT model, the command is identical:

ott = rd.Model(
    graph=rd.ott_esn(64, 1, 1, readout="svd", seed=7, dtype=torch.float64),
    washout=30,
)
ott.tune(development, preset="quick", horizon=40, seed=7)
ott_prediction = ott.forecast(horizon=len(test))
assert ott_prediction.shape == test.shape

The automatic recipe retains the chosen initializer, activation, readout and current preprocessing/workflow settings. It varies only controls supported by that configuration: for example, it keeps a custom non-random topology and does not invent a bias for a bias-free reservoir. See the exact default ranges.

An unmodified rd.Model(graph=rd.classic_esn(...)) also gets this automatic recipe. If you change its layers, wiring or reservoir weights, it becomes a custom DAG: tuning keeps those changes and uses the fixed-DAG behavior below. Provide a recipe to rebuild that customized architecture.

docs.title: Choose your own ranges
docs.text:
search_space replaces the automatic search. Fixed values stay fixed; omitted settings keep the current recipe's values. For example, keep 64 units and vary only input strength and regularization:

def narrower_search(trial):
    return {
        "reservoir_size": 64,
        "input_scaling": trial.suggest_float("input_scaling", 0.05, 0.5, log=True),
        "alpha": trial.suggest_float("alpha", 1e-9, 1e-4, log=True),
    }

model.tune(
    development, search_space=narrower_search, preset="quick",
    n_trials=2, horizon=40, seed=7,
)
assert model.forecast(horizon=len(test)).shape == test.shape

docs.title: Optionally screen candidates first
docs.text:
Full evaluation remains the default. To shortlist candidates before spending the complete repetition budget, enable screening:

screened = rd.ESN(reservoir_size=32, washout=20, readout="svd", dtype=torch.float64)
screened.tune(
    development, preset="balanced", horizon=40, seed=7,
    screening=True, memory_budget="8GiB",
)
print(screened.tuning_report.resources)

This checks all 24 candidates on one seed and one starting point, using the complete 40-sample forecast. The best eight then receive the full three-seed, three-origin evaluation. Only a fully evaluated candidate can win. Candidates outside the shortlist are recorded as PRUNED; they still consume attempts. Screening may discard a configuration that would perform better across other seeds or starting points.

Screening(...) lets you choose repetition counts, promotion fraction and cohort size. Memory planning can reduce concurrency or skip an individually oversized candidate; it does not change its architecture or precision. A budget is an estimate, not an OS/RSS/GPU allocation limit. See tuning resources for the controls and custom factory estimates.

docs.title: Tune a custom DAG
docs.text:
The functional construction stays the same: connect layers with layer(x) and wrap named inputs and outputs in rd.Model. Here two reservoirs process the same signal at different update rates:

def make_model(width=64, alpha=1e-6, seed=0):
    x = rd.reservoir_input(1, dtype=torch.float64)
    slow = rd.ESNLayer(
        width, feedback_size=1, leak_rate=0.2,
        spectral_radius=0.9, seed=seed, dtype=torch.float64,
    )(x)
    fast = rd.ESNLayer(
        width, feedback_size=1, leak_rate=1.0,
        spectral_radius=0.7, seed=seed + 1, dtype=torch.float64,
    )(x)
    joined = rd.Concatenate()(slow, fast)
    y = rd.SVDReadoutLayer(2 * width, 1, alpha=alpha).double()(joined)
    return rd.Model(inputs={"state": x}, outputs={"next": y}, washout=30)

custom = make_model()
custom.tune(development, preset="quick", horizon=40, seed=7)
custom_prediction = custom.forecast(horizon=40)
assert custom_prediction.shape == (40, 1)

Without a recipe, a custom DAG keeps its wiring and reservoir weights. Its default search varies alpha; a custom search may vary alpha and washout. Only one initialization seed is evaluated, since copying the same weights would not create new initializations. Readouts must support the selected settings; supply your own search or recipe for other readout types.

docs.title: Change sizes, layers or initializers
docs.text:
Provide an ordinary Python recipe, factory(params, seed), when candidates need new structure or weights. It rebuilds the whole candidate, so changing a reservoir's width also updates its readout automatically:

def search_space(trial):
    return {
        "width": trial.suggest_int("width", 32, 96, step=32),
        "alpha": trial.suggest_float("alpha", 1e-9, 1e-3, log=True),
    }

def factory(params, seed):
    return make_model(width=params["width"], alpha=params["alpha"], seed=seed)

custom.tune(
    development,
    factory=factory,
    search_space=search_space,
    preset="quick",
    horizon=40,
    seed=7,
)
custom_prediction = custom.forecast(horizon=40)
assert custom_prediction.shape == (40, 1)

Use the recipe to choose any supported layers, topology, registered initializer or custom module. Return a built rd.Model (or a compatible rd.ESN). Candidates must preserve the task: input/output names and widths, prediction leads, feedback routes/delays, and resampling settings. Their hidden structure, preprocessing and trainable settings can differ.

search_space(trial) uses standard Optuna suggestions, including conditional branches. Return a mapping of finite JSON-compatible settings (tuples are retained). Capture Python objects such as custom initializers in the recipe instead. rd.ESN rebuilds itself and therefore uses its own recipe; use rd.Model for a custom factory.

docs.title: Tune a TSDynamics trajectory
docs.text:
Install resdag[hpo,dynamics] on Python 3.12 or newer. The same tuning call accepts a trajectory and returns forecasts with future times and signal names:

import numpy as np
import tsdynamics as ts

trajectory = ts.systems.Lorenz().run(final_time=6.0, dt=0.02)
dynamics_development, dynamics_test = trajectory[:241], trajectory[241:261]
dynamics_model = rd.ESN(
    reservoir_size=48, washout=20, readout="svd", dtype=torch.float64,
)
dynamics_model.tune(dynamics_development, preset="quick", horizon=20, seed=7)
trajectory_prediction = dynamics_model.forecast(horizon=len(dynamics_test))
tensor_prediction = dynamics_model.forecast(horizon=20, return_type="tensor")

assert isinstance(trajectory_prediction, ts.Trajectory)
assert trajectory_prediction.variables == dynamics_test.variables
np.testing.assert_allclose(trajectory_prediction.t, dynamics_test.t, atol=1e-12)
assert tensor_prediction.shape == (20, 3)

This is an interface example, not a forecast-quality benchmark. The named trajectory guide explains multiple inputs and targets. Tuning uses the same physical alignment, component names and configurable resampling. Raw source observations are split before interpolation, so held-out values cannot influence training interpolation. Scoring stays in tensors; trajectory output converts to CPU only when requested.

docs.title: Supply your own validation segment
docs.text:
Use validation=(inputs, targets_or_None) when a particular held-out segment must decide the winner. It is excluded from both candidate fits and final refitting:

held_out = rd.ESN(reservoir_size=64, washout=30, readout="svd", dtype=torch.float64)
held_out.tune(
    series[:400],
    validation=(series[400:500], None),
    preset="quick",
    horizon=40,
    seed=7,
)
# Use the later observations as history without fitting on them.
held_out_prediction = held_out.forecast(history=series[400:500], horizon=40)
assert held_out_prediction.shape == (40, 1)

Without that explicit history, this model's cached forecast begins after its training segment at sample 399. Tensor validation is treated as the continuation of training, with the same batch and feature layout. Explicit trajectory validation must occur later in time and preserve component names/order.

For separate input/target tensors, targets are already aligned to each input origin, as in fit(inputs, targets). A head with lead three expects target row zero to describe the signal three samples after input row zero. Tuning withholds labels beyond each observed fit boundary; the shared supervision window stops at the largest head lead while retaining the complete observed history. Explicit Tensor validation starts scoring after its first max(prediction_leads) observations, so every head has labels originating within validation. Trajectory targets instead supply physical timestamps and are queried directly. Actual origins and discarded target rows are recorded in tuning_report.validation.

Named input/target mappings and (batch, time, features) tensors work as in fit. Inputs without a feedback route become known future drivers during validation. Future observed feedback signals are withheld from the rollout. See feedback connections for leads and independent delays.

docs.title: Understand the score
docs.text:
The default winner has the longest contiguous accurate forecast, measured in samples. At each sample, errors are divided by fixed training channel scales, then combined with an RMS across features. A sample counts while this error is strictly below threshold=0.2; counting stops at the first failure. Scales come from training labels after the original model's washout, and stay fixed across trials, seeds, starting points and forecast prefixes.

For batches, each output uses the median horizon across batch items. With several outputs, the weakest output determines the score: position lasting 400 samples and velocity lasting 100 gives a score of 100. Set aggregation="mean" to average outputs instead. Each trial then takes the median score across its initialization seeds and starting points. The winner is refitted using the first seed in that fixed bank.

The report also includes full-window normalized error (nrmse), per-output horizons/errors and fit/forecast timings. These diagnostics do not break ties in the default horizon objective. For trajectory data, multiply sample counts by the recorded validation["dt"] to obtain physical duration.

docs.title: Choose an error objective
docs.text:
A callback can replace the ranking while retaining the normal fit, forecast and reporting workflow. ScoreContext contains named predictions and truth in original units, fixed training scales, and the current seed/origin. Truth and scales are copied for the callback so it cannot alter later evaluations.

from resdag.hpo import ScoreContext

def normalized_error(context: ScoreContext):
    errors = [
        ((context.predictions[name] - context.truth[name]) / context.scales[name])
        .square().mean()
        for name in context.predictions
    ]
    return torch.stack(errors).mean().sqrt().item()

error_model = rd.ESN(reservoir_size=64, washout=30, readout="svd", dtype=torch.float64)
error_model.tune(
    development, preset="quick", horizon=40, seed=7,
    objective=normalized_error, direction="minimize",
)

Return one finite scalar per seed/origin. Scores are aggregated by their median. direction="minimize" chooses the smallest error; the built-in horizon objective requires "maximize". Custom metrics can remain on the tensor device until the final scalar conversion.

docs.title: Stop unpromising forecasts early
docs.text:
An Optuna pruner can stop future forecast generation at a checkpoint:

pruned_model = rd.ESN(reservoir_size=32, washout=20, readout="svd", dtype=torch.float64)
pruned_model.tune(
    development, preset="quick", horizon=40, seed=7,
    pruner="median", checkpoint_interval=10,
)

Forecasting proceeds in chunks of at most ten scored samples here. The parent process owns the real Optuna trial and makes pruning decisions, including when numerical work runs in joblib workers. A rejected checkpoint prevents later chunks, origins and seeds from running. Fitting and work before that checkpoint have already happened. Pruning is disabled by default, and the median pruner also has its own startup/warmup rules.

For the built-in objective, intermediate values are positive accurate-horizon scores with the same fixed training scales. pruner="threshold" uses a lower score bound of 0.1 after a warmup of 2 * checkpoint_interval resource steps. This is separate from threshold=0.2, which defines an accurate forecast sample. The raw runner uses negated horizon losses and a different threshold-pruner preset; its bounds are not interchangeable.

Custom objective callbacks still receive a complete forecast. Without an explicit prefix callback, pruning is checked only after each complete seed/origin forecast and can skip later evaluations. Opt in to within-forecast pruning when your metric makes sense on partial predictions:

from resdag.hpo import PrefixScoreContext

def prefix_error(context: PrefixScoreContext):
    # Predictions/truth contain only the completed prefix. The same fixed
    # training scales used by normalized_error are available here.
    return normalized_error(context)

prefix_model = rd.ESN(reservoir_size=32, washout=20, readout="svd", dtype=torch.float64)
prefix_model.tune(
    development, preset="quick", horizon=40, seed=7,
    objective=normalized_error, pruning_objective=prefix_error,
    direction="minimize", pruner="median", checkpoint_interval=10,
)

PrefixScoreContext.completed_steps is the admitted prefix length; horizon is the complete requested scored length. Return a finite scalar with the same direction and comparable meaning at matching resource steps. The complete objective still decides the final ranking. Custom callbacks retain prediction prefixes; the built-in scorer accumulates its statistics without retaining a full output trajectory.

docs.title: Run and resume a study
docs.text:
Optuna provides samplers, queued starting configurations and study inspection. For example, enqueue a known configuration before asking for more candidates:

import optuna

study = optuna.create_study(
    direction="maximize", sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=7),
)
study.enqueue_trial({
    "reservoir_size": 64, "spectral_radius": 0.9,
    "leak_rate": 0.5, "alpha": 1e-6,
})
resumable = rd.ESN(reservoir_size=64, washout=30, readout="svd", dtype=torch.float64)
resumable.tune(
    development, study=study, preset="quick", horizon=40, seed=7,
    n_trials=4, n_jobs=2,
)
resumable.tune(
    development, study=study, preset="quick", horizon=40, seed=7,
    n_trials=2, n_jobs=2,
)
assert len(study.trials) == 6

n_trials counts new attempts per call, including failed, pruned, memory-rejected and screened-out candidates. A timeout can stop a call before it uses the whole budget. catch_exceptions=True records evaluation failures as FAIL trials, with messages in trial attributes; they cannot win. Set it to False while debugging to raise the original error. If no valid candidate completes, tuning raises. The source model changes only after a winner refits successfully. Construct optimizers after tuning, since the winning configuration can replace parameters.

The default n_jobs=1 runs in the caller. Other values use joblib/loky process workers and its standard worker-count conventions, including -1 for available CPUs. Workers evaluate parent-sampled windows of candidates; inner_max_num_threads=1 limits worker BLAS threads. Search suggestions, Optuna storage and pruning stay in the parent; workers receive prepared numerical jobs. Submission uses finite windows bounded by remaining attempts and estimated memory, so a worker queue cannot exceed the new-attempt budget. timeout stops dispatching new windows, while an in-flight window and the final winner fit finish normally. It is not a hard wall-clock deadline. Changing worker count can change an adaptive sampler's sequence, even though candidates reuse the same evaluation seeds and origins.

On errors or interruption, joblib cancels outstanding work and this call's unfinished trial reservations are finalized. An error during final refitting or owned-storage cleanup leaves the original model unchanged.

Use storage="tuning.log", study_name="my-experiment" for a persistent journal, or a .db path for SQLite. Pass those options instead of study=; a caller-owned study also owns its sampler and pruner. Resuming checks data, validation, task, seed bank, objective and captured configuration against the stored protocol. Keep callback configuration stable, and use a fresh study when the experiment changes. Unverified prior evaluated scores are rejected; queued trials are supported. Caller-owned studies remain usable, and returned owned studies reconnect after storage cleanup when needed.

Forecast execution defaults to execution="auto": compatible DAGs use the fast step loop, while temporal custom layers use history replay. Force "fast" or "history" to select a mode explicitly. See forecast capabilities.

docs.title: Reuse settings from another experiment
docs.text:
reused = rd.ESN(reservoir_size=64, washout=30, readout="svd", dtype=torch.float64)
reused.tune(
    development, warm_start=model.tuning_report.study,
    preset="quick", horizon=40, seed=7, n_trials=2,
)

The default transfer_mode="reevaluate" queues complete configurations from the source, best first, then evaluates them on the destination task. Old scores are not copied. Fixed returned settings and source-trial provenance are kept. Queued configurations consume new attempts when evaluated; any beyond the budget remain WAITING. This is the useful choice when data, architecture or the objective changes. Adapt incompatible settings explicitly.

transfer_mode="scores" is an explicit import of prior evaluated scores. It requires identical bound task protocols and objective directions, including the actual prepared data and model/objective configuration. Imported scores do not consume the budget for new attempts. Use reevaluation when the experiment changes; matching parameter names alone do not make scores comparable.

docs.title: Plot and animate a forecast
docs.text:
Use ResDAG for the model diagram and TSDynamics for trajectories, component plots and movies. The examples below keep values in their original units. A phase portrait shows geometry; use a time plot and an error measure to judge whether predictions stay aligned with the observed continuation.

Install the Python visualization packages and Graphviz:

python -m pip install "resdag[dynamics,viz]" "tsdynamics[viz]"
# macOS: brew install graphviz
# Debian/Ubuntu: apt install graphviz

TSDynamics requires Python 3.12 or newer. GIF export uses Pillow through Matplotlib. MP4 export also needs the FFmpeg executable on your path.

docs.title: Build a custom DAG and train it
docs.text:
Two reservoirs see the same observed state, with different memory rates. Their states feed one shared readout. Each branch has an explicit seed. The held-out continuation is sliced before fitting and is never used as a training target.

import torch
import tsdynamics as ts
import resdag as rd

trajectory = ts.systems.Lorenz(ic=[1, 1, 1]).run(final_time=70, dt=0.02)
training, truth = trajectory[500:3001], trajectory[3001:3501]

x = rd.reservoir_input(3, dtype=torch.float64)
seeds = rd.SeedStreams(7)
fast = rd.ESNLayer(
    48, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9, leak_rate=1.0,
    seed=seeds["fast"], dtype=torch.float64,
)(x)
slow = rd.ESNLayer(
    48, feedback_size=3, spectral_radius=0.9, leak_rate=0.25,
    seed=seeds["slow"], dtype=torch.float64,
)(x)
features = rd.Concatenate()(fast, slow)
y = rd.SVDReadoutLayer(96, 3, alpha=1e-6).double()(features)
model = rd.Model(inputs={"state": x}, outputs={"prediction": y}, washout=200)
model.fit(training)
prediction = model.forecast(history=training, horizon=len(truth))

These small branches illustrate composition. Their parameters are not a validated long-range Lorenz recipe. For accuracy experiments, use separate validation data and repeated seeds, then evaluate on a new continuation. The forecast experiment writes model artifacts, exact split data, scores and a replay manifest.

docs.title: Draw or save the graph
docs.text:
model.save("forecast-model.svg", rankdir="TB", show_trainable=True)
model.save("forecast-model.dot", rankdir="TB", show_trainable=True)

DOT is readable source and needs no Graphviz executable. The top-to-bottom layout keeps both branches readable in the page. Use rankdir="LR" for a wide left-to-right layout. In a notebook, display model.plot_model() directly. Diagrams include named ports, feature widths, branches and feedback connections. Drawing does not execute the model or advance recurrent state. The save and diagram guide lists supported formats and custom-component behavior.

Two reservoir branches merge before a common prediction head. A diagram describes the computation; it does not establish forecast quality.

docs.title: Compare the values over time
docs.text:
The model returns a TSDynamics trajectory because it was fitted on one. Its future timestamps match the held-out continuation. Draw a component to check phase drift and amplitude error:

observed_x = ts.plot(truth, "time_series", components="x", color="#b06a18")
forecast_x = ts.plot(prediction, "time_series", components="x", color="#2a63d4")
comparison = ts.plot(
    observed_x, forecast_x,
    labels=["Observed continuation", "Autonomous forecast"],
)
comparison.save("forecast-x.png")

Change components="x" to another signal name. For an original-unit RMSE:

error = torch.as_tensor(prediction.y) - torch.as_tensor(truth.y)
print(f"Forecast RMSE: {error.square().mean().sqrt().item():.4g}")

A single RMSE averages the whole window. The Lyapunov-time guide measures how long the uninterrupted accurate prefix lasts and explains how threshold and normalization affect that result.

docs.title: Save an attractor movie
docs.text:
ts.plot overlays the two recorded paths. Animation reveals those samples in time order; it does not generate new observations or change the model's forecast. Keep the full path with trail(None):

orbit = ts.plot(
    truth, prediction,
    labels=["Observed continuation", "Autonomous forecast"],
)
orbit.recolor("#b06a18", "#2a63d4").camera(elev=18, azim=-60)
orbit.save("forecast-phase.png", size=(960, 640))
movie = orbit.animate(duration=12, fps=24).trail(None)
movie.save("forecast.gif", size=(720, 480), dpi=100)
# movie.save("forecast.mp4", size=(960, 640), dpi=120)  # needs FFmpeg

duration is playback time in seconds; dt remains the physical interval between recorded samples. More animation frames do not improve the prediction. The camera is fixed and every forecast sample is retained, including divergence.

Download the Lorenz forecast recording. Lorenz: a fixed display case from the independent-trajectory study. The complete recorded test window is shown in original state coordinates. Brown shows observations; blue shows the autonomous forecast. Open the static image. Download the Rössler forecast recording. Rössler: the corresponding fixed display case. A recognizable attractor shape does not imply continued pointwise agreement. Brown shows observations; blue shows the autonomous forecast. Open the static image.

Both displayed cases use final trajectory 0, reservoir seed 7849201 and forecast start 0, chosen before observing final results. Each model's settings were selected using separate validation trajectories. These cases illustrate the recordings; the complete study reports accuracy across all independent trajectories, initializations and starting points. The source observations, predictions and provenance are downloadable. Documentation figure generation only reads those arrays; it never refits models, selects a favorable test case or clips divergent paths.

docs.title: delay_line_backward
docs.text:
Build a forward delay line plus a backward superdiagonal connection.

Connectivity and weight matrix on a small reservoir. 
from resdag.layers import ESNLayer

reservoir = ESNLayer(500, feedback_size=3, recurrent_initializer='delay_line_backward', spectral_radius=0.9, seed=7)
parameter default weight 0.1 backward_weight 0.1 shift 1 backward_shift 1 dtype torch.float32 device None

Override parameters with recurrent_initializer=("delay_line_backward", {...}) or pre-configure with get_recurrent_initializer("delay_line_backward", ...). The existing topology= spelling and get_topology() also work.

A layer spectral_radius rescales this matrix after construction. Use get_recurrent_initializer(..., rescale=False) to keep the native scale.

from resdag.layers import ESNLayer

reservoir = ESNLayer(500, feedback_size=3, feedback_initializer='pseudo_diagonal', seed=7)
parameter default input_scaling None binarize False

Works for feedback_initializer= and input_initializer= alike; override parameters with ("pseudo_diagonal", {...}) or get_input_feedback("pseudo_diagonal", ...).
